Sunday AI · Semiconductor Study Group

AI Infrastructure and Semiconductors

A seven-session self-study guide for readers with a background in statistics, computing or AI. Instead of memorizing terms, you set up a few equations and plug in the numbers yourself.

Edited by Bowon Kwon, Presiding Judge, Daegu District Court

Contents · How to use + 7 sessions + 3 appendices
Quantitative exercises · 32, with full solutions
Interactive figures · 12 (HTML edition; the print edition shows a still image in the same place)
Glossary index · 114 terms
Suggested pace · 8 weeks, about 2 hours a week

Printing · Press Ctrl+P and save as PDF; all collapsible solutions open automatically.
Offline · This single file is self-contained. The interactive figures work without an internet connection; links open when you are online.

Edition 2.0.1-en · translated from the Korean edition 2.0.1 (October 22, 2026) · compiled with generative AI. Errors may remain, and corrections will continue.

Introduction

How to Use This Book

Before you start

The editor compiled this book with a generative AI system (Claude). Each session was checked against primary sources several times, but errors may remain. Please confirm figures and quotations against the originals. The book will keep being revised; the edition and date you are reading are on the cover and in the colophon (edition 2.0.1-en, translated from Korean edition 2.0.1 of October 22, 2026).

To the extent the editor holds rights in it, this book is released under CC BY-NC 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International). You may adapt and share it for noncommercial purposes if you credit the author, name the license (with a link), and indicate any changes you made. You may not restrict others' use with legal terms or technological measures. This summary is for convenience; the license text governs. The code of the interactive figures in the screen edition (HTML, CSS and JavaScript) is released separately under the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0. Noncommercial use, modification and redistribution are permitted on that license's terms; for commercial use, please contact the editor in advance through the repository's issue tracker to agree on separate terms. Tables, quotations and figures reproduced or redrawn from original works are not covered by these licenses and remain subject to the rights of their authors. If you hold rights in such material, tell us through the repository's issue tracker and we will correct or remove it.

This English edition is a translation of Korean edition 2.0.1 (October 22, 2026). The editor made it with the same AI system and had it checked against the Korean text and, where a quotation was originally in English, against that original wording. Its numbers keep the Korean edition's reference date of October 8, 2026 (see "A note on the numbers" below). Sources that exist only in Korean are listed with translated titles and marked "(in Korean)."

This edition keeps the Korean edition's Korean examples as they are. In a few places where a Korean case carries the argument, a box headed "Comparable cases elsewhere" adds an example from another country. Those examples may not fit your jurisdiction, your date or your industry, so check the source cited in the box before you rely on one.

This is a self-study guide compiled for the semiconductor sessions of Sunday AI, a study group, and covers AI infrastructure and semiconductors in seven sessions. It is written for readers with a background in statistics, computing or AI who never studied semiconductors. Instead of asking you to memorize terms, it sets up a handful of equations and has you plug in the numbers yourself. Every session comes with calculation exercises and full solutions, so you can check your answers on your own. In the screen edition (HTML), interactive figures placed next to the equations let you change the values; the print edition (PDF) carries the same figures in their initial state at the same spots. You are welcome to read it the same way in another group, or alone.

What this book covers

The seven sessions follow one question: "Where are the limits of the physical equipment that runs AI set?"

Session Topic Tool the session builds
1 How the AI semiconductor industry is laid out, and how to read its numbers The habit of asking for the definition first
2 Compute chips (GPU, NPU, TPU, ASIC) The roofline model
3 Memory (DRAM, HBM, HBF) Separating bandwidth from capacity
4 Fabless, foundries and the value chain The yield equation
5 Front-end processes (lithography, etching, deposition, metrology) The Rayleigh criterion
6 Back-end processes and advanced packaging Chiplet trade-offs, the thermal-resistance chain
7 AI data centers (power and cooling) Synthesis

The two equations set up in Sessions 2 and 4 govern everything else. If you are short of time, work through at least those two by hand.

What each session contains

Every session follows the same structure.

Order Name What it does
1 Key takeaway A three-line preview of the session's conclusion
2 Learning objectives Questions you should be able to answer at the end
3 0. Self-study guide For readers working alone. What to bring from the previous session, a prerequisite check, reading order and time budget, and detours around the usual sticking points
4 Main text
5 Common misconceptions Things that are often stated wrongly
6 Quantitative exercises Problems to solve by hand
7 Discussion questions Questions without a single right answer
8 Self-study appendix A Full solutions to the exercises. They are folded; solve first, then open them
9 Self-study appendix B The axes along which the discussion questions divide
10 Self-study appendix C Key terms of the session
11 Self-study appendix D Self-assessment checklist. Do not move on to the next session until you pass the ★ items
12 Before the next session Open questions paired with where the next session answers them

The solutions in appendix A are folded. On screen, click the heading to open them; when you print, they all open automatically.

An eight-week schedule

There are seven sessions, but eight weeks works better. Session 5 (front-end processes) is one and a half times as long as the others.

Week Read Time Must solve by hand that week
1 Session 1, how the AI semiconductor industry is laid out 100 min The three number-audit problems
2 Session 2, AI chips 120 min Exercises 1 and 2
3 Session 3, AI memory 110 min Exercises 1 and 2
4 Session 4, fabless and foundries 110 min Exercises 1, 2 and 4
5 Session 5, front-end processes, first half (sections 1–4) 95 min Exercises 1 and 2
6 Session 5, front-end processes, second half (sections 5–9) 65 min Exercises 3, 4 and 5
7 Session 6, back-end processes and advanced packaging 130 min Exercises 1, 2 and 4
8 Session 7, AI data centers, plus synthesis 190 min Exercise 5 (required)

That is about two hours a week. If one session is too much at a sitting, break it at the steps in that session's "Reading order" table.

Update the same picture every week

What breaks down most easily in self-study is "I read it, but nothing stayed." There is one remedy. Draw the skeleton below on one sheet of paper (or one screen), and add the layer you learned each week on top of it.

[request] → [model/software] → [compute chip] → [memory] → [package]
                                                                   ↓
[power/cooling] ← [DC/rack] ← [server/board] ← [fab/supply chain] ←┘

Three rules for updating it

  1. Put one number on every arrow. (For example, on the arrow from compute chip to memory: "ridge point ≈ 295 FLOP/byte".)
  2. Mark on every box whether it is the bottleneck. As the sessions go on, you should see the bottleneck mark move.
  3. Do not erase last week's picture. Draw over it in a different color.

"The seven sessions in one line" at the end of Session 7 is the final answer key. If in week 8 you can reconstruct it without looking, you are done.

When you get stuck

Symptom Cause What to do
Everything from Session 2 on feels like it slides past You have not digested "the whole set of weights is read" in Session 1, section 3 Go back to the library analogy in Session 1's self-study guide. If this does not land, nothing after it will
I can follow the equations but not why they matter You have not plugged in numbers Do appendix A with the solutions covered. The book is designed so that reading without calculating leaves nothing behind
Too many terms You are trying to memorize them all at once Do not memorize; keep the Appendix II glossary beside you and look terms up as they come
The lithography part of Session 5 will not go in Not enough optics background Start with the camera-aperture analogy in Session 5's self-study guide. If that fails, read only sections 3 and 4, move on, and come back after Session 6
The volume is overwhelming You are trying to read it all at once Break it at the steps in each session's "Reading order" table
I read everything but cannot connect it You read session by session without building the chain Start the cumulative picture above, even now

A note on the numbers (read this)

The calculation exercises in this book use many assumed values. They are examples meant to show the direction of a conclusion, not measurements.

The reference date is October 8, 2026. Statements that change over time, such as volume-production and shipment status, power-demand projections, standards and product specifications, were rechecked on that date against primary sources (manufacturer announcements, standards documents and agency reports), and the text gives the date each was checked.

Assumed values that must not be quoted as facts

  • The price of one wafer (USD 15,000), electricity (USD 0.08 per kWh), the price of an accelerator node (USD 250,000)
  • ASIC and GPU unit prices and NRE, defect density D0, assembly yield, interface overhead ratios
  • Any other settings stated in individual exercises

Values taken from public spec sheets that change with each generation

  • Compute performance and memory bandwidth of accelerators (A100, H100, B200). All are dense (no sparsity) figures. Vendor material also lists a figure twice as high with sparsity, so always check which one you are looking at
  • HBM specifications, the reticle limit, microbump and hybrid-bonding pitch

Things that are structurally stable and safe to quote

  • The equations themselves: the roofline, the yield model, the Rayleigh criterion, thermal resistance, the definition of PUE
  • The direction of the relationships that follow from them: yield falls exponentially as die area grows, depth of focus worsens with the square of NA, small batches are bandwidth-bound, and so on

This book deliberately leaves out absolute figures for market size and market share. Each source defines and counts them differently, so they vary widely. Section 4 of Session 1 explains why.

Read alongside other material

The thinner parts of this book are the following.

Topic Coverage here
AI compilers and the software stack Session 2, section 7 treats them only from the angle of lock-in. There is almost nothing on the compilation pipeline itself — the largest gap
Links to primary sources Links are given in the "Primary sources" box at the head of each session and in each session's sources section. Paid standards and papers are given with bibliographic data and DOI only
Diagrams and images There are redrawn diagrams and interactive figures, but no photographs or micrographs

Session 1

Mapping the AI Semiconductor Industry

Key takeaway

"AI semiconductors" is not a single product but a loose category that spans compute chips and memory chips, and that vagueness is the first trap when you read market statistics. The industry splits into three layers: design (fabless), manufacturing (foundry/IDM), and equipment and materials. The layer that earns the most and the layer that cannot be replaced are not the same. Demand is moving from training to inference, and that shift has pushed the memory bottleneck to the center of the whole industry. The goal of this session is not to memorize numbers but to get into the habit of checking which definition a number stands on.

Primary sources

KDB Future Strategy Research Institute, "AI Semiconductor Technology and Industry Trends" (in Korean; KDI Economic Information and Education Center) · Samil PwC, "Global Semiconductor Industry Outlook 2026" (in Korean, PDF) · PwC Consulting Korea, "The Paradox of the Semiconductor Supercycle" (in Korean) · LBNL press release on its 2024 U.S. data center energy report · NVIDIA DGX H100/H200 User Guide — power specifications · eCFR 15 CFR §734.9 (FDP rules)

Learning objectives

By the end of this session you should be able to answer the following.

  1. When you see a news story saying "the AI chip market is worth trillions of dollars," what should you check first?
  2. How do profit margins and irreplaceability differ across the layers of the value chain?
  3. As demand moves from training to inference, how do the hardware requirements change?
  4. Into what types do semiconductor supply-chain risks fall, and how do they differ in character?

0. Self-study guide — for readers working alone

This is a reading session

It is the only one of the seven sessions with no calculations. Its real goal is not to acquire knowledge but to build one habit: whenever you see a number, first ask "what was counted to get this?" Section 4 is the training ground; the other sections set the stage on which you will use the habit.

Prerequisite check — can you explain each of these five in one line?

If any of them stops you, read the answer below and move on. That is all you need for this session.

Concept One-line answer
Parameter Each number the model fixed through training (a weight). A "70B model" has 70 billion of them
FLOP / FLOP/s FLOP is a count of floating-point operations; FLOP/s is the count per second (speed). The first is an amount of work, the second a processing capacity
Memory bandwidth The number of bytes per second that can be moved from memory to the chip [byte/s]. A completely different notion from capacity (GB)
Wafer A disk of silicon. Hundreds of chips are made on it at once and cut apart at the end
Fabless / foundry A company that only designs chips / a plant that manufactures other companies' designs under contract

Reading order (100 minutes recommended)

When you read alone, front to back is not the best order.

Step Section Time Why
1 Section 1, getting the intuition 15 min Fixes the scope of the term first
2 Section 3, from training to inference 25 min The heart of this session. The other six sessions all grow out of it
3 Section 2, the value chain 15 min After section 3 you can see why money gathers in this layer
4 Section 4, reading the numbers 20 min Together with the exercises below
5 Sections 5 and 6, risks and misconceptions 15 min
6 Self-study exercises 10 min

Never skip: "Why this shift put memory on the throne" in section 3. The single line "arithmetic intensity I≈B" found there leads straight to the roofline in Session 2, HBM in Session 3, packaging in Session 6, and the power problem in Session 7. If this paragraph does not make sense, Session 2 will keep sliding past you.

If section 3 is hard — a detour

Section 3 borrows ideas that have not yet been set up (arithmetic intensity, ridge point), so getting stuck on a first reading is normal. Get a feel for it with the analogy below, move on, and come back after reading Session 2. It will open up.

Suppose you fetch an entire book from the library, read one sentence, and send it back. Moving the book takes ten minutes; reading takes one second. The bottleneck is not "reading speed" but "moving speed." Decoding during inference is exactly like this. To produce one token, the whole set of model weights is read from memory. However fast the chip is, it makes no difference; how fast you can haul the weights in from memory decides everything. There is only one fix: once the book has been brought over, have many people share the reading (batching). This is where the importance of batching comes from.

1. Getting the intuition — what "AI semiconductor" actually means

It is not one thing

The term "AI semiconductor" refers to at least four things.

What people call it The actual object Typical examples
Narrow sense (compute) Accelerator chips specialized for AI computation GPU, TPU, NPU, inference ASIC
Broad sense (compute + memory) The above plus memory for AI + HBM
System sense The whole accelerator module or board HGX board, accelerator card
Industry sense Every semiconductor sold because of AI demand + network chips, power semiconductors, CPUs

When an article or report says "the AI chip market is worth X billion dollars," it often does not say which of the four it means. Different definitions produce numbers that differ several-fold. The first habit this book tries to build is asking "which scope is this?" every time you see a number.

Why this industry suddenly grew so large — three lines

  1. A transformer is a lump of matrix multiplications. Its computation reduces to massively parallel multiply-accumulate operations, so the gain from dedicated hardware is extreme.
  2. Scaling laws gave empirical support to "bigger model = better performance." The belief that compute input translates into performance justified the capital spending.
  3. But only a handful of places can make that hardware. Demand exploded while supply had no physical or financial elasticity. So prices and profits piled up at particular points.

You can read this book as a seven-session dissection of the "why only a handful" in point 3.

2. The value chain — who makes money where

Three layers

Between layers 1 and 2 of the figure sits one more thin layer. Design houses (design service companies) take the logical design handed over by a fabless company, implement and verify it physically for a particular foundry's process, and pass it on to manufacturing. Foundries tie them into partner networks. TSMC describes the members of its VCA (Value Chain Alliance; formerly Value Chain Aggregator) as "independent design service companies working closely with TSMC to help system companies, ASIC companies, and emerging start-up customers bring their innovation to production." They "provide specific services at each link in the IC value chain, including IP development, design backend, wafer manufacturing, assembly, and testing" (checked October 2026). The players and each foundry's programs are covered in Session 4.

Key insight — profit margin and irreplaceability are different things

  • Highest margins: the leading fabless companies in layer 1 and the leading foundry in layer 2
  • Highest irreplaceability: layer 3. EUV lithography tools in particular come effectively from ASML alone. Its revenue is far smaller than NVIDIA's, but if it stops, all of leading-edge logic stops.

This asymmetry explains why geopolitical controls do not stop at finished chips but also aim at layer 3 (equipment). Controls on finished chips block the flow of chips sold today; controls on equipment tie up the ability to make such chips yourself (section 5 ③).

Where Korea stands

This book was written for a study group in Korea, so the original keeps a short note on the country's position. It is kept here because it shows how the three-layer picture reads from one country's vantage point.

  • Strong: memory (DRAM, NAND, HBM). SK hynix and Samsung Electronics hold a large share of the world market. For example, by revenue in the first quarter of 2026, SK hynix ranked first in the world in HBM and second in DRAM (including HBM) and in NAND (IDC figures, as given in the prospectus SK hynix filed for its U.S. listing in July 2026; checked 2026-10-08).
  • Relatively weak: share of leading-edge foundry, the fabless ecosystem, the domestic share of equipment and materials.
  • Structural implication: memory has traditionally been a market with violent cycles. Whether AI demand has changed that cycle structurally or only widened its swings is the final discussion topic of Session 7.

Comparable cases elsewhere. Taiwan reads the same picture from layer 2. TSMC reported that it "represented 34 percent of the Foundry 2.0 industry, which we define as all logic wafer manufacturing, packaging, testing, mask-making and others, output value in 2024, as compared to 28 percent in the previous year" (TSMC 2024 business report, in the minutes of its June 3, 2025 shareholders' meeting). The definition is the company's own, so the share is also a small case of the problem in section 4: change the denominator and the number changes. (source)

3. The shift in demand — from training to inference

The concern behind every later session comes from this section.

Training and inference want different machines

Item Training Inference
Computation pattern Large-batch matrix multiplication (GEMM) Decoding is close to matrix-vector multiplication
Arithmetic intensity High (hundreds of FLOP/byte) Low (on the order of the batch size)
Main bottleneck Compute performance, communication between nodes Memory bandwidth, capacity, latency
Precision BF16/FP8 INT8/FP8/INT4 (aggressive quantization)
Memory needs Weights + activations + optimizer state Weights + KV cache
Latency sensitivity Low (batch processing) High (a user is waiting)
Cost structure One-off large investment Ongoing operating cost

Why this shift put memory on the throne

Training uses large batches, so it can keep the compute units busy. But in the decoding phase of inference, producing one token requires reading the whole set of model weights from memory. Each read of the weights supports only as many operations as there are sequences in the batch.

Roughly speaking, the amount of computation per byte of fp16 weights is proportional to the batch size B. Arithmetic intensity is about I≈B. As Session 2 will show, the ridge point of current GPUs is around 300 FLOP/byte. With a batch below 300, the GPU is bound by bandwidth and its compute units sit idle.

Yet latency requirements keep the batch from growing without limit, and the KV cache eats memory, so batch size is capped by memory capacity. In the end, the economics of an inference service are decided not by "how fast the chip is" but by "how wide and how large a memory is attached to it."

This is why HBM became the center of the industry (Session 3), why advanced packaging became a bottleneck (Session 6), and why data center power became a problem (Session 7).

4. How to read market figures critically

What actually happens

For the "AI accelerator market" of the same year, different sources give very different figures. The reasons:

  1. Differences in scope — Is it the accelerator chip only, the module and board too, or the whole AI server? Counting the whole server brings in the CPU, memory, network and power supply, and the number grows several-fold.

    Power figures hide the same trap. NVIDIA lists the maximum thermal design power (TDP) of the H100 (SXM) as "Up to 700W (configurable)", and gives the maximum input power of the DGX H100 server, which holds eight H100s, as 10.2 kW. Do the arithmetic: the TDP of eight chips adds up to 5.6 kW, and the gap to the server's maximum input power is 4.6 kW. Items such as the CPUs, memory, network, fans and power-conversion losses fall into that gap. Both values are ceilings, however, so this does not mean that 4.6 kW is used outside the chips during actual work. This session does not break the gap down into numbers. The next-generation DGX B200 has a maximum system power of about 14.3 kW. Each time you widen the boundary, from chip to server and from server to a facility that includes cooling and power distribution, the number grows. When you see the phrase "the power one AI chip uses," first ask at which boundary it was measured. The question comes back in the power-cost calculation of Exercise 4 in Session 2. Manufacturing has the same structure: wafer capacity, number of good dies, package output and shipments are different numbers.

  2. Differences in the unit counted — Revenue, units shipped, or deployed compute (FLOPS)? In-house chips (such as TPUs), for example, are not sold outside, so they are underestimated in revenue-based statistics and come out much larger when counted in deployed FLOPS.

  3. The interests of whoever publishes — chip companies, market research firms and investment banks each have different incentives.

  4. Differences in timing — this is a market whose forecasts are revised heavily every half year.

What can and cannot be pinned down

This book draws the line as follows.

Structurally settled (several sources agree)

  • NVIDIA holds the overwhelming majority of data center AI accelerator revenue. What the ratio is and which way it is moving depends on how you set the denominator, so it is not given here (Exercise 1).
  • The share of hyperscalers' in-house ASICs (Google TPU, AWS Trainium, Meta MTIA, Microsoft Maia) is rising fast, and Broadcom, Marvell and others have risen as their design partners.
  • Inference has overtaken, or is overtaking, training as a share of AI compute spending.
  • HBM is an oligopoly of three companies (SK hynix, Samsung, Micron), and SK hynix leads by revenue (confirmed with IDC figures for the first quarter of 2026, 2026-10-08). The order and gap between second and third place swing with each product generation, so they are not stated here.

Not settled (sources vary widely — mention only as ranges)

  • Absolute market size by year
  • Exact percentage shares by company (for example, the same company's HBM share differs by several percentage points depending on whether it is a quarterly result or an annual forecast, and whether it is counted by revenue or by shipments)
  • Total data center power consumption. Even authoritative estimates span a wide range. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) estimated U.S. data center electricity use in 2028 at 325–580 TWh (section 6, misconception 6)

If you read this in a group: make it a rule that the presenter must state "the source and definition of this number in one line." The learning effect of this session rises sharply.

5. Three axes of supply-chain risk

① Geographic concentration

Leading-edge logic manufacturing is heavily concentrated in Taiwan. That makes it a single point of failure, both for natural disasters and for geopolitics. Countries' policies to attract fabs (the U.S. CHIPS Act, the EU Chips Act, support in Japan and Korea) try to ease this concentration, but they are not short-term fixes: building one fab and raising its yield takes years.

② Single-supplier bottlenecks

Bottleneck Effective supplier
EUV lithography tools ASML (effectively the only one)
Advanced packaging (CoWoS and similar) Centered on TSMC
EDA tools Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens EDA
CPU IP Arm (licensing model)
High-purity wafers and photoresist Concentrated in Japanese firms

The important point here is that "can it be made technically" and "how much can actually be made" are different questions. For instance, the supply of AI accelerators runs into limits on CoWoS packaging capacity and HBM supply before it runs into limits on logic wafers. (Covered in detail in Session 6.)

Bottlenecks also form a chain on the demand side. EUV → CoWoS → HBM is the movement of the bottleneck seen from the supply side. The same movement can be traced from the demand side. As models grow and contexts lengthen, both compute and the KV cache grow, and so do the capacity and bandwidth demanded of the HBM that holds the weights and the KV cache. Attaching more HBM makes the package larger and more complex. Pack such accelerators densely into servers and the heat density rises, until the power and cooling of the racks and the facility reach their limits. When demand at one link rises, the pressure passes to the next. So what constrains the system is usually not performance within one layer but the interfaces where layers meet: between memory and chip, chip and package, server and facility. Session 3 (HBM), Session 6 (packaging) and Session 7 (servers and facilities) each take one of these links.

③ Policy risk

Export controls target equipment and manufacturing capability as well as finished chips. Because of extraterritorial reach (the foreign direct product rules and others), firms in third countries are affected too. As of October 2026, the text of the foreign direct product (FDP) rules in the U.S. Export Administration Regulations (EAR) (15 CFR §734.9) contains a separate advanced computing FDP rule (paragraph (h); advanced integrated circuits and computers) and a semiconductor manufacturing equipment (SME) FDP rule (paragraph (k)). The structure is that an item made with certain U.S. technology or software, or made in a plant built with such technology, can be subject to the EAR even if produced outside the United States. The text can be read through the eCFR link under "Further study" in section 8.

"The paradox of the supercycle"

The stronger the boom, the more everyone invests in expanding the bottleneck process. Because fabs and equipment have lead times of two to three years, the demand signal at the moment of the investment decision and the demand at the moment the capacity comes online diverge. This is the semiconductor industry's classic bullwhip effect, and it is especially severe in memory. One camp argues that AI demand has abolished this cycle; the other, that it has only widened the swings. (Final discussion of Session 7.)

6. Common misconceptions

Misconception 1: "AI chip = GPU" → GPUs dominate today, but the share of ASICs such as TPU and Trainium is rising fast. More important, memory (HBM) and packaging account for a large part of the performance and cost of an AI system.

Misconception 2: "The smaller the nanometer number, the better the chip, always" → Node names are marketing labels, not physical dimensions (Session 4). AI accelerator performance also depends more on memory bandwidth and packaging than on the node.

Misconception 3: "With enough money, you just build a fab" → Equipment lead times, skilled labor and the yield ramp (the learning curve to reach volume-production yield) are bigger constraints than capital. A fab building goes up in two years, but bringing yield to a competitive level takes longer.

Misconception 4: "China will soon catch up / will never catch up" → Both are oversimplifications. China has already secured considerable capacity at mature (legacy) nodes, while at the leading edge of logic it faces the structural constraint of having no EUV. It has to be looked at layer by layer.

Misconception 5: "The AI chip boom will end soon / will last forever" → The honest answer is: "Because the nature of demand has shifted from training to inference, it is uncertain whether the old cycle models still apply." Inference demand is more continuous and more like an operating expense than training, which could dampen the cycle, but the structure of capacity lead times is unchanged.

Misconception 6: "Once power-efficient chips arrive, total data center power will fall" → The efficiency of one chip and the total for a whole facility are different questions. According to LBNL's 2024 report on U.S. data center energy use, prepared with support from the U.S. Department of Energy, U.S. data center electricity use grew from 58 TWh in 2014 to 176 TWh in 2023, about 4.4% of total U.S. electricity in 2023. For 2028 it is estimated at 325–580 TWh, 6.7–12% of U.S. electricity (the share depends on how fast the rest of the economy grows). Use more than doubled between 2017 and 2023 alone, and the report names the growth of AI servers as the main cause. Over the same period, chips became more power-efficient with each generation. Yet the total tripled, so efficiency and total can move separately (this interpretation is this book's own, not a conclusion taken from the report). Note also that the 2028 estimate spans nearly a factor of two. That is why section 4 classes the total as "not settled" and gives it only as a range.

7. Discussion questions

  1. From a country's point of view, in which of the three layers of the value chain is it most efficient to put investment and policy resources? How does the answer change with the time horizon (5 years vs. 20 years)?
  2. Is it rational for hyperscalers to build their own chips? Under what conditions is it rational, and under what conditions not? (Taken up quantitatively in Session 4.)
  3. Are the wide differences among estimates of "the AI chip market size" a problem of measurement or a problem of definition? As someone trained in statistics, how should you treat these estimates?
  4. How should we understand the bottleneck in the supply chain moving from EUV (equipment) to CoWoS (packaging) and then to HBM (memory)? Why does the bottleneck keep moving?
  5. Is there evidence that the traditional memory cycle (boom → expansion → glut → slump) has been changed structurally by AI demand?

8. Further study

  • Overview of the industry structure: Chris Miller, Chip War (2022) — the standard popular book on the geopolitics of the semiconductor industry. Good background reading for this session
  • Regular tracking of technology trends: industry analysis from SemiAnalysis, TrendForce, Counterpoint Research and others. Allow for each one's slant
  • Primary material: quarterly earnings materials from TSMC, SK hynix, Micron and NVIDIA (especially the Q&A of the earnings calls). Often more accurate than market reports
  • Korean perspectives (in Korean): semiconductor industry analysis from the KDI Economic Information and Education Center, the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade (KIET), and ETRI's Electronics and Telecommunications Trends
  • Power demand: LBNL press release on the 2024 U.S. data center energy report — source of the figures in section 6, misconception 6
  • Export-control text: eCFR 15 CFR §734.9 — current text of the foreign direct product (FDP) rules

Self-study appendix A — number-audit exercises and solutions

This session has no calculation exercises. Instead it has three problems that put the "ask for the definition first" habit from section 4 to work. Write your answer on paper before you look.

Exercise 1 — Same company, different numbers

One article says "Company A's share of the AI accelerator market is 90%," and another says "70%." Assuming neither article is lying, what differences in definition could produce this gap? Give at least three.

SolutionSolution

There are three or more legitimate differences in definition.

  1. Whether in-house chips are in the denominator. Google TPU and AWS Trainium are not sold outside, so they barely register in a revenue-based market. Take in-house chips out of the denominator and Company A's share goes up; put them in on a deployed-units or deployed-compute basis and it goes down. This alone produces a 20-percentage-point difference.
  2. Chips only, or systems too. Shares at the accelerator-die level and at the server or rack level differ. A whole server includes the CPU, network and power supply, and the mix of suppliers for those items is different.
  3. Training only, or inference too. The inference market is fragmented, with CPU inference, low-cost accelerators and edge NPUs mixed in. Looking at the training market alone gives a much higher concentration.
  4. (Extra) Timing. Quarterly shipments or cumulative installed base? In a fast-growing market the two diverge widely.

What to take away: a share is decided not by the numerator but by the denominator. If an article does not state the denominator, the number is an unverifiable statement.

Exercise 2 — The growth-rate trap

In the same year, one article writes "the AI chip market grew 200% year on year," and another writes "the semiconductor market grew 25% year on year." Both are about the semiconductor industry. Is this a contradiction? Before answering, write down what each sentence counted.

SolutionSolution

It is not a contradiction. It mixes a part with the whole.

Check it with a simple numerical example. Say that out of a total semiconductor market of 100, AI-related sales are 5 and the rest 95. If AI triples to 15 (+200%) and the rest grows about 16% from 95 to 110, the total goes from 100 to 125, a 25% increase.

Both sentences are true. They simply speak of different levels.

What to take away: a growth rate means nothing unless the base is stated. Items that start from a small base always show dramatic growth rates. That is why section 4 put only the "structurally settled" points in the text and held back absolute figures.

Exercise 3 — Locating the bottleneck

Suppose the following three observations are reported at the same time.

  • Leading-edge logic wafer capacity has room to spare.
  • Lead times for accelerators exceed 40 weeks.
  • HBM is pre-contracted through next year's volume.

Where is the bottleneck? And why would a policy proposal to "expand wafer capacity" have no effect?

SolutionSolution

The bottleneck is in a stage after the wafer. If logic wafers are left over but finished products do not come out, the blockage lies after the wafer. The candidate the three observations point to directly is HBM supply. Advanced packaging (CoWoS and similar), which binds HBM and the logic die into one package, is also a candidate, but these three observations alone cannot tell whether packaging is blocked too: a shortage of HBM alone would produce exactly the same three observations. On the packaging side, you would have to check CoWoS capacity utilization or the packaging backlog separately.

In a serial process, output is set by the narrowest neck. Widening a stage that has spare room (wafers) does not raise total output by one unit; it only piles inventory up in front of the neck. What needs to grow is the HBM line, and, if a packaging queue is confirmed, CoWoS capacity as well.

One step further: if the HBM line is expanded, what gets blocked next? HBM uses DRAM dies, so it competes with ordinary DRAM capacity; it needs the TSV process and thermocompression and MR-MUF stacking equipment (and, in the next generation, hybrid-bonding equipment as well), and that equipment is again tied to a few suppliers. Bottlenecks are not removed; they move (section 5). This structure is the subject of Session 6 and Session 7.

What to take away: when you read industry news, set "what is left over" beside "what is short," and the location of the bottleneck shows. Look at only one side and you will always get the wrong prescription.

Self-study appendix B — leads for the discussion questions

The discussion questions in section 7 have no right answers. But a reader working alone may not even know what to base an answer on, so only the axes of the argument are given. The conclusions are yours to draw.

Question Where it divides Grounds that let you answer either way
1. Which of the three layers to invest in? Time horizon Over 5 years, design and people (fast payback); over 20 years, equipment and materials (irreplaceability compounds). Add a particular country's current position (for Korea, strong in memory and weak in equipment) and the answer changes again
2. Are in-house chips rational? Volume × control over the workload Quantified by the break-even formula N* in Session 4. The key is that the break-even volume is surprisingly small (about 3,000–5,000 units); the real constraint is whether the workload survives the two to three years of development
3. Measurement or definition? The nature of the error If it is measurement error, it converges as the sample grows. If it is a difference in definition, it does not converge however precisely you measure. The cases in section 4 are of the second kind → statistically, it is not the variance of the estimator but the estimand that differs
4. Why does the bottleneck move? Investment lags When a bottleneck shows, capital rushes there; when it opens up after a two-to-three-year lead time, the next narrowest point shows. The movement is evidence of normal operation, not failure. From the demand side, growth in models and context passes the pressure along KV cache → HBM → package → server heat density → facility power (section 5 ②). Overlay the two directions, and the next bottleneck is the link, among those the pressure has reached, where capacity expands most slowly
5. Has the memory cycle changed? The nature of demand Training demand is investment-like (one-off capital spending); inference demand is operational (ongoing billing). The "it has changed" side argues that as the latter's share grows, demand flattens. The other side argues that the lead-time structure of capacity is unchanged — even with flat demand, if supply comes in steps, the cycle remains

Self-study appendix C — key terms

Only the terms that first appear in this session. They are used from Session 2 on.

Term One-line definition
Fabless A semiconductor company that only designs and outsources production
Foundry A plant that manufactures other companies' designs under contract
Design house (design service company) A design service company that implements and verifies a fabless company's design physically for a particular foundry process and passes it on to manufacturing
IDM (integrated device manufacturer) A semiconductor company that designs, manufactures and sells
OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) A contractor specializing in back-end work (packaging and test)
EDA (electronic design automation) Software tools for chip design
HBM (high bandwidth memory) Memory that stacks DRAM vertically to maximize bandwidth
Accelerator Umbrella term for chips specialized for particular computations (GPU, TPU, NPU, etc.)
ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit) A custom chip built for a fixed purpose
Training / inference The process of building a model / the process of using a built model
Arithmetic intensity Operations performed per byte moved from memory [FLOP/byte]
KV cache (key-value cache) Memory that stores intermediate results of tokens already produced to avoid recomputing them
Quantization Representing weights with fewer bits to save capacity and bandwidth
(Process) node A process-generation name such as "3nm." A marketing label, not a physical dimension
Yield The share of what is made that works correctly
CoWoS (chip-on-wafer-on-substrate) TSMC's flagship 2.5D advanced packaging method
Hyperscaler A very large cloud operator (Google, AWS, Microsoft, Meta, etc.)
Bullwhip effect Demand fluctuations amplifying as they travel upstream in a supply chain
Single point of failure A point whose stopping stops the whole

Self-study appendix D — self-assessment

If you can answer each item in your own words, you are ready for the next session. If two or more stop you, go back to the relevant section in the "Reading order" above.

  • ☐ Given an article on "the AI chip market size," I can immediately name three things to check → sections 1 and 4
  • ☐ I can draw the three layers of the value chain and explain why margins and irreplaceability diverge in each → section 2
  • ☐ I can say in one sentence why export controls aim at manufacturing equipment as well as finished chips, and what equipment controls tie up that chip controls do not → sections 2 and 5
  • ☐ Without looking at the table, I can name four or more ways in which the hardware that training and inference need differs → section 3
  • ☐ I can explain why "reading the whole set of weights to produce one token" makes memory the bottleneck → section 3 ★
  • ☐ I can say why a larger batch raises efficiency and why it cannot grow without limit → section 3 ★
  • ☐ I can tell the three axes of supply-chain risk apart and explain why the remedy for each is different → section 5
  • ☐ I can explain the movement of the bottleneck from EUV → CoWoS → HBM as "normal operation" → section 5

The two ★ items must be passed. All of Session 2 is a refinement of those two sentences.

Before the next session

Three things were named in this session but left undefined. Session 2 sets them up properly.

Left open In Session 2
Arithmetic intensity I Formally defined as the horizontal axis of the roofline model
"Ridge point of 300 FLOP/byte" Derived as I*=Ppeak/B and checked against real chips
"Below a batch of 300, you are bound by bandwidth" Quantified with the decoding-ceiling formula

The question that carries over: if memory that cannot keep up makes a faster chip useless, where exactly is that limit drawn?

Session 2

AI Chips — Compute Semiconductors

Key takeaway

The first principle of accelerator design is not "make computation fast" but "move less data." Fetching a piece of data once from DRAM costs two orders of magnitude more energy than one multiplication. The differences among CPUs, GPUs, NPUs, TPUs and ASICs can all be explained along two axes: (1) how far the overhead per instruction is amortized, and (2) how many times data, once fetched, is reused. The roofline model built in this session is a shared tool that every later session uses again. The ridge point of current accelerators sits near 300 FLOP/byte, while the arithmetic intensity of LLM decoding is one or two orders of magnitude lower. That gap is the concern of the whole book.

Primary sources

Element Korea, "What Is an AI Chip?" (in Korean) · MSAP, "What Is an AI Accelerator?" (in Korean) · ScienceON JAKO202412457639314, "Research Trends in Domestic and International AI chips" (in Korean) · ScienceON JAKO202504350488400, "A Comprehensive Study of AI Semiconductors and Key Application Fields" (in Korean) · InitNode, "CPU vs GPU vs TPU vs NPU" · Williams et al., Roofline (CACM 2009) · Jouppi et al., TPU paper, arXiv:1704.04760 · NVIDIA H100 product specifications · NVIDIA Blackwell Architecture Technical Brief

Learning objectives

  1. Explain why CPUs are inefficient for AI computation in terms of energy, not "because the clock is slow."
  2. Tell apart how GPU tensor cores and TPU systolic arrays each gain their efficiency.
  3. Build the roofline model and determine by calculation whether a given workload is compute-bound or memory-bound.
  4. Weigh the break-even point of developing an in-house ASIC quantitatively.

0. Self-study guide — for readers working alone

This session builds the tool for the whole book

The one roofline inequality set up here is reused again and again in Session 3, Session 4, Session 6 and Session 7. You can read the other sessions once and move on, but this one will not stay with you unless you calculate it by hand. A calculator is all you need, and Exercise 1 takes 5 minutes.

What to bring from the previous session

From Session 1 In this session
"To produce one token, the whole set of weights is read" With fp16 weights, this sentence becomes the approximation I≈Bsz
"With a batch below 300, you are bound by bandwidth" You confirm that the 300 comes from I*=Ppeak/B
"The layer that earns the most and the layer that cannot be replaced are not the same" Here you see that in small-batch decoding the bottleneck of performance is bandwidth, not computation

Prerequisite check

Concept One-line answer Can you skip it?
Matrix multiplication (GEMM) The operation that multiplies two matrices. An n×n matrix multiplication takes about 2n3 FLOP ❌ Required
Log-log plot A plot with both axes on a logarithmic scale. Power-law relations show up as straight lines Needed to read the figure in section 6
fp16 / INT8 / INT4 One number represented in 2 bytes / 1 byte / 0.5 byte ❌ Required
Systolic array A structure that streams data through a grid and repeats multiply-accumulate operations ✅ The idea only
CUDA The programming environment for NVIDIA GPUs and its ecosystem ✅ The name only

Reading order (120 minutes recommended)

Step Section Time Note
1 Sections 1–5 (chip structure) 35 min Quickly. For now this is background
2 Section 6, the roofline 35 min Read closely. Copy the equations onto paper yourself
