If section 6 is hard — a detour in three sentences

The roofline has a grand name, but its content is grade-school arithmetic.

  1. To get work done you have to bring the materials in (bandwidth B) and process them (compute Ppeak).
  2. Whichever of the two is slower sets the overall speed. Hence the min.
  3. Which one is slower depends on "how long you process 1 kg of material" (I). If processing takes long, compute is the bottleneck; if it is over quickly, transport is.

Pattainable(I)=min(Ppeak,B×I)

That is all the equation says. The rest is plugging in real numbers.

1. Getting the intuition — computing is cheap, delivering data is expensive

A logistics analogy

Suppose machining one part in a factory takes 1 second. If fetching that part from the warehouse takes 3 minutes, adding more production lines will not raise output at all. There are only two ways to improve.

  • Move the warehouse closer (= on-chip SRAM, HBM placed right next to the chip)
  • Do several jobs with each part you fetch (= data reuse, tiling, larger batches)

Almost every idea in AI accelerator design is one of these two. Everything else is detail.

The shock in numbers

According to Horowitz's classic summary (ISSCC 2014, for a 45nm process), the energy gap between computation and memory access looks like this.

Operation Approximate energy
8-bit integer add 0.03 pJ
32-bit floating-point add 0.9 pJ
32-bit floating-point multiply 3.7 pJ
32-bit on-chip SRAM read (8 KB cache) 5 pJ
32-bit DRAM read 640 pJ

The top three rows (add and multiply) are taken directly from Figure 1.1.9 of Horowitz's paper. The two memory rows are the 32-bit access values of Han et al. (2015), who cite the same 45nm table. Horowitz's figure gives memory for 64-bit access: cache 10 pJ at 8 KB, 20 pJ at 32 KB and 100 pJ at 1 MB, and DRAM 1.3–2.6 nJ. The SRAM value of 5 pJ is half the 8 KB cache value, so it grows as the cache grows.

So reading data once from DRAM costs about 170 times as much as one floating-point multiplication. Halve Horowitz's DRAM range to get 32-bit values, and the ratio is about 180–350 times. As processes shrank, the energy of computation kept falling, but the energy of off-chip memory access fell much less, so the gap has widened over time.

The conclusion that follows: the objective function a chip designer must optimize is not FLOPS but "total energy per useful operation," and its dominant term is data movement.

2. Why the CPU will not do

First, clear away a misconception

"CPUs are slow because they have few cores" is only half right. The more fundamental reason is the fixed cost the CPU pays per instruction.

What actually happens when a CPU executes the single line c = a * b:

  1. Instruction fetch (I-cache access)
  2. Instruction decode
  3. Branch prediction, register renaming, out-of-order scheduling
  4. Register file read
  5. The actual multiplication ← only this is "work"
  6. Write-back of the result, commit

Steps 1–4 and 6 use far more energy and area than step 5. The CPU is designed on the assumption that "it does not know what comes next," and the cost of preparing for that uncertainty is the overhead.

But deep learning does know what comes next

Matrix multiplication has no data-dependent branches, its access pattern is fixed statically, and the same operation repeats billions of times. With no uncertainty, the whole cost of preparing for it can be removed. That is the entire reason accelerators exist.

Overhead item CPU GPU TPU/ASIC
Instruction fetch and decode For scalars, every operation; with SIMD and AMX, amortized per vector or tile Amortized per warp Almost none (fixed dataflow)
Branch prediction Present (expensive) Minimal None
Out-of-order execution Present None None
Cache hierarchy Large and complex Small, can be controlled explicitly Scratchpad (software-managed)
Share of area for control logic Very large Medium Very small

Steps 1–6 above describe a single scalar instruction. Real CPUs also load several operations onto one instruction. A SIMD instruction processes a whole vector, and Intel AMX goes all the way to matrices. According to Intel's AMX code-sample article, AMX consists of tiles, which are two-dimensional registers, and TMUL, an accelerator that multiplies tiles as matrices. In the palette 1 configuration there are 8 tile registers totaling 8 KB, and one tile is at most 16 rows × 64 bytes. The same article names 4th Gen Xeon Scalable processors and the Xeon Max series as the processors it applies to. So the description of a CPU handling operations one at a time is an introductory shorthand. The conclusion does not change, though. The CPU still carries the control machinery it needs for generality, so it cannot amortize the same work as deeply as an accelerator.

In short: going from CPU to GPU to ASIC, you "sell flexibility to buy efficiency." The terms of that trade are the ASIC economics of section 5.

3. What a GPU really is — what one line of matmul does in hardware

The SIMT execution model

A GPU runs threads in bundles of 32 (a warp), and the 32 threads of a warp execute the same instruction at the same time. The cost of fetching and decoding an instruction is spread over 32 operations, so the overhead becomes 1/32.

Readers who have written GPU code will know the performance traps that come from this.

  • Warp divergence: if threads in the same warp take different branches, the two paths run one after the other, and threads that do not belong to the path being run sit idle. If the threads split half and half between two paths of equal length, throughput halves; the size of the loss depends on the path lengths and the split ratio. → This is what the advice "avoid if on the GPU" really means.
  • Memory coalescing: global memory is read in 32-byte transactions. If the 32 threads of a warp each read one consecutive 4-byte value, that is 128 bytes in all and takes four transactions; if the addresses are scattered 32 bytes or more apart, it takes one per thread, 32 in all. → This is why tensor layout (NCHW vs NHWC) decides performance.
  • Occupancy: the GPU hides memory waits by running other warps, so the number of warps that can be resident at once matters. GPUs have L1 and L2 caches and shared memory too, but caches smaller than a CPU's cannot remove all of the latency, so much of the latency is hidden by parallelism.

Tensor cores — amortization taken to the limit

A tensor core performs the multiply-accumulate of small matrix blocks, D=A×B+C, as one instruction. For a 16×16 block product, say, one instruction covers thousands of MACs, so the instruction overhead effectively goes to 0.

One line of torch.matmul, seen as a hierarchy:

torch.matmul(A, B)
  └─ cuBLAS/cuBLASLt kernel selection (tile size, split strategy)
       └─ grid/block decomposition: split the output matrix into tiles
            └─ load tiles from global memory (HBM) → shared memory (SRAM)
                 └─ shared memory → register fragments
                      └─ tensor core MMA instructions (block multiply-accumulate)
                           └─ accumulated results passed back up

The key point: this whole hierarchy exists for one purpose, "reuse each tile fetched from HBM as many times as possible." A block product with tile size T reads O(T2) bytes and performs O(T3) operations, so the arithmetic intensity grows as O(T). Tiling is the software way of raising the roofline's I.

The precision ladder

AI accelerators gain throughput roughly by multiples as precision drops (FP32 → TF32 → BF16/FP16 → FP8 → FP4). There are two reasons.

  1. Arithmetic-unit area: the area of a multiplier is roughly proportional to the square of its bit width, so halving the bits lets you fit about 4 times as many in the same area.
  2. Memory traffic: half the data means half the bandwidth demand. The real gain from quantization comes from bandwidth, not computation. This is why quantization matters so much in inference.

4. TPUs and systolic arrays — building reuse into the hardware

Structure

A systolic array lays out processing elements (PEs) in a grid and streams data through it, with each PE passing values on to its neighbor. The name comes from the way data flows in a regular rhythm, like blood pushed out by the heart (systole).

In an N×N array, one input element is reused N times as it passes through the array. That is, each piece of data read once from memory is used for O(N) operations. The arithmetic intensity is guaranteed by the wiring, not by software.

Google's TPU v1 arranged 256×256 = 65,536 8-bit MAC units this way. Data moving inside the array travels over short wires between neighboring PEs, so the energy is extremely low.

The figure below shows the fourth beat when one token (M=1, decoding) is streamed through a 4×4 array whose weights sit in the PEs. In the screen edition you can step through the beats one at a time, or change the number of tokens M and the matrix size, and count how many PEs are working at each beat.

GPU vs. systolic array — what was given up and what was gained

GPU Systolic array
Guarantee of reuse Software (tiling, kernels) is responsible Guaranteed by the hardware structure
Flexibility Can run arbitrary kernels Best for matrix-multiplication shapes, inefficient for anything else
Programming Mature ecosystem such as CUDA Very heavy dependence on the compiler
Utilization Depends heavily on kernel quality Drops sharply when the matrix size does not fit the array

The weakness of the systolic array: if the matrix size is not a multiple of the array dimension, the PEs at the edges sit idle. When the batch is small or the matrix is long and thin (decoding!), utilization falls a long way. This is why designs dedicated to inference take a different form from those for training.

Counted in beats, it looks like this. With the weights fixed in the PEs, streaming M tokens through one K×N tile takes M+K+N−2 beats to fill and drain. At TPU v1 size (K=N=256), with M=1 the PEs are working only 0.2% of the time on average over 511 beats; with M=4,096 that rises to about 89%. Real chips feed the next tile in right behind the current one to overlap the fill and drain time, and loading the weights into the PEs takes time of its own. Still, when M is small each weight is used only M times and then discarded, so overlapping gains little. There are also several dataflows besides weight-stationary, such as output-stationary (the textbook by Sze et al. in section 11).

5. NPUs and ASICs — the economics of specialization

NPU

A neural-network accelerator for mobile and edge devices. Its objective function is different.

  • What it optimizes is not absolute performance but TOPS/W (performance per watt)
  • Centered on low precision (INT8/INT4), under battery and heat constraints
  • Integrated in an SoC with the CPU, GPU and ISP, sharing memory (LPDDR)
  • Use is intermittent, so latency and wake-up overhead matter

The fundamental difference from server accelerators: a server spends power to get throughput, whereas at the edge the power budget is fixed and you squeeze out the most performance inside it. Both are "AI chips," but their design goals are close to opposite.

Calculating the ASIC break-even point (exercise)

Whether to build a dedicated chip or buy one can be quantified.

  • CNRE : non-recurring engineering cost (design staff, EDA licenses, IP licenses, mask set, verification and prototypes). At leading-edge nodes the mask set alone runs to tens of millions of dollars, and total NRE can reach hundreds of millions of dollars.
  • cA : ASIC unit cost (wafer cost ÷ number of good dies + packaging + test)
  • cG : unit acquisition cost of the alternative (a commercial GPU)
  • N : expected volume

Here we assume that one ASIC does the work of one GPU at the same throughput, latency and quality (1:1 replacement). Only then does the same volume N mean the same demand.

Comparing total costs: CNRE+NcA<NcG

N*=CNREcG−cA

If the ASIC's throughput is r times the GPU's, the same demand needs N/r ASICs. In that case put cA/r in place of cA (if r<1, the break-even volume grows).

But this formula is only half right. In practice three more terms have to go in.

  1. The time axis: developing a chip takes 2–3 years, and model architectures change faster than that. When the chip is finished, will that workload still dominate?
  2. Electricity: in a data center, several years of electricity bills can exceed a chip's acquisition price in its total cost of ownership (TCO). Put operating costs into c and the dedicated chip looks far better. Counted per unit, however, what decides the break-even count is mostly the difference in acquisition price; the difference in electricity costs is only a few percent (solution to Exercise 4). Electricity becomes a large sum only in totals at the scale of tens of thousands of units running for several years.
  3. Bargaining power: having your own chip gives you option value in price negotiations with commercial GPU vendors. Even if you never use it, its existence is worth something.

Try it yourself: with these three terms added, explain "why hyperscalers build their own chips and most startups do not." The heart of the answer is the difference in scale of N and CNRE, and whether the workload is stable.

The flexibility-efficiency spectrum

The FPGA is an interesting middle point. Its hardware can be reconfigured, so it needs no mask set, but it implements the same function with far more area and power than an ASIC. It suits low-volume, high-mix products and early stages when the algorithm is still in flux.

6. The roofline model — the shared tool of this book

Definition

The performance ceiling is the minimum of two constraints.

Pattainable(I)=min(Ppeak,B×I)

  • Ppeak : the chip's peak compute rate [FLOP/s]
  • B : memory bandwidth [byte/s]
  • I : arithmetic intensity [FLOP/byte] = (operations performed) / (bytes moved from memory)

Plotted on log-log axes, a line of slope 1 (the bandwidth limit) meets a horizontal line (the compute limit) to form the shape of a roof. The point where it bends is the ridge point, I*=Ppeak/B.

Ridge points of real chips

Chip Ppeak (BF16 dense) B I*
NVIDIA H100 SXM 989 TFLOP/s 3.35 TB/s (HBM3, 80 GB) ≈ 295 FLOP/byte
NVIDIA B200 2,250 TFLOP/s 7.7 TB/s (HBM3E; chip's published maximum 192 GB · 180 GB per GPU in the DGX B200) ≈ 292 FLOP/byte

Caution: vendor material also lists a figure twice as high with structured sparsity. The values above are dense. Always check which one you are looking at on a spec sheet.

Capacity also differs between chip and system. NVIDIA's Blackwell Architecture Technical Brief (V2.1) gives "Up to 192 GB" as the GPU memory of the HGX B200. The user guide and datasheet for the DGX B200, the finished server, give 1,440 GB in total for 8 GPUs, which works out to 180 GB per GPU. When you plug capacity into a calculation, state whether it is the chip's published value or a system specification. Bandwidth also varies by document. Technical Brief V2.1 gives the bandwidth of the same HGX B200 GPU as 7.7 TB/s, and the DGX B200 datasheet gives 64 TB/s in total for 8 GPUs (8.0 TB/s per GPU by calculation). The tables and figures in this book use the chip values from the Technical Brief (192 GB, 7.7 TB/s), the same source as the capacity. Calculated with 8.0 TB/s, I*≈281, so the conclusion below, that it sits near 300, holds either way. The compute figure of 2,250 TFLOP/s is half of the sparse 4.5 PFLOPS in the same table (the table's dense column gives 2.2).

What to notice: from one generation to the next, I* barely moves from around 300. When compute grew 2.3 times, bandwidth was also raised 2.3 times, which means the balance was only just kept. Getting that bandwidth took enormous spending, from HBM3 to HBM3E and on to HBM4. That is the subject of Session 3.

Placing LLM workloads on the roofline

(a) Training / prefill

The tokens of sequence length S and batch Bsz are processed all at once, so this becomes a large GEMM. When a weight matrix W∈ℝn×n is applied to M tokens:

  • Computation ≈ 2Mn2 FLOP
  • Memory traffic ≈ 2n2 bytes (fp16 weights loaded once)
  • Arithmetic intensity I≈M (when activation traffic is left out of the count)

Leaving out the activations is an approximation. If the M×n input is read from HBM and an output of the same size is written back, the traffic becomes 2n2+4Mn bytes and I=Mn/(n+2M). This value cannot exceed the smaller of M and n/2. So I≈M holds when n is much larger than M, or when kernel fusion keeps the activations on chip. In LLMs n is in the thousands or more (n=8,192 and M=4,096 give I=2,048), so whichever way you count, I≫I* → compute-bound. The GPU's compute units are well filled.

(b) Inference / decode

Tokens are generated one at a time. Even if a batch of Bsz sequences is processed together, each step handles one token per sequence.

  • Computation ≈ 2Bszn2 FLOP
  • Memory traffic ≈ 2n2 bytes (the weights must be read again in full)
  • Arithmetic intensity I≈Bsz

With fp16 weights, a batch below 300 is memory-bound. If you serve with a batch of 32, I≈32, so you use only about 32/295≈11% of the theoretical performance. The other 89% of the compute units sit idle waiting for memory.

The figure below shows where the workload falls under the roof when decoding runs on an H100 with fp16 weights and a batch of 32. In the screen edition you can change the chip, phase, batch, weight precision and model size and see when the point crosses the ridge point.

The ceiling on decoding speed — a rule of thumb counted in bandwidth

For a model with P weights (parameters) at b bytes per parameter, the maximum number of tokens generated per second is set by bandwidth alone.

tokens/s≲BP·b×Bsz

Example: to run a 70B model in fp16 (b=2) on one H100 with a batch of 1, the weights alone are 140 GB and do not fit in 80 GB. Split across 2 cards, the total bandwidth is 6.7 TB/s, so the theoretical ceiling is 6.7e12/(1.4e11)≈48 tokens/s. This rule of thumb assumes that when the weights are spread over N chips, each chip reads its share at the same time, so the bandwidth adds up N times. Quantized to INT8 (b=1), the weights are 70 GB and only just fit on one card. Drop to one card and the bandwidth also falls to 3.35 TB/s, so the ceiling stays at about 48 tokens/s; keep both cards and it doubles to about 96 tokens/s.

This formula counts only the bandwidth side, so it holds only when the arithmetic intensity I is below the ridge point I*. If only the weights are read at b bytes and the computation runs at the BF16 peak, then I=2Bsz/b, and the batch at which you cross into compute-bound is Bsz=(b/2)I*. For the H100 that is about 295 in fp16, about 148 in INT8 and about 74 in INT4. If the computation also runs at the same low precision and the peak rises with it, the boundary moves back to around the BF16 I* (solution to Exercise 3). When compute-bound, the ceiling is set by the 2P FLOP that one token takes (for the whole batch, tokens/s≲NPpeak/(2P), where Ppeak is the peak at the precision actually used). The traffic from reading the KV cache at every step is also left out, so the longer the context, the further real speed falls below this ceiling. Translated into a metric users feel, for a single sequence this formula gives a lower bound P·b/B on the time between output tokens (TPOT). The time to the first token (TTFT) is set not by this formula but by prefill ("Conditions for a fair comparison" at the end of section 8).

What this one rule of thumb explains: why quantization is essential in inference, why you try to grow the batch, why "do the weights all fit in memory?" is decisive, and why the HBF (high-capacity memory) of Session 3 is being discussed.

Every way to raise arithmetic intensity (summary)

Method Where How it raises I
Tiling / blocking Software Reuses tiles loaded on chip many times
Kernel fusion (e.g., FlashAttention) Software Keeps intermediate results on chip instead of writing them to HBM
Larger batches Serving policy Processes more sequences with the same weights
Quantization Model Fewer bytes moved, so a smaller denominator
MoE / sparsity Model structure Not a way to raise I. Only the weights one token uses are read and computed, so computation and traffic fall together and I stays the same; fewer bytes per token raise the decoding ceiling. With MoE, when the tokens in a batch scatter across many experts, fewer tokens reuse each expert and I actually falls (and routing overhead is added)
Systolic array Hardware Reuse guaranteed by structure
Large on-chip SRAM Hardware Cuts the number of off-chip accesses itself
More HBM bandwidth Hardware Raises B, not I (→ Session 3)
PIM Hardware Moves computation toward the memory (→ Session 3)

Worth pinning down: in this list, the software items all raise I, and half of the hardware items raise B. Once you see the picture of two camps attacking different terms of the same inequality, papers and articles become much easier to read.

7. Software lock-in — a moat outside the technology

Even when hardware performance is similar, software decides what actually gets adopted.

  • The CUDA ecosystem: optimized kernels built up over many years, such as cuDNN, cuBLAS, NCCL and TensorRT, and extensive library support.
  • The alternatives: AMD ROCm, Intel oneAPI, Google XLA/JAX, OpenAI Triton, the compiler stack of PyTorch 2.x. Attempts like Triton to describe kernels in a hardware-neutral way could weaken lock-in. A compiler stack captures the model as a computation graph, lifts it into an intermediate representation (IR), and then lowers it step by step into representations closer to the hardware to produce kernels. According to the PyTorch 2.14 documentation, in torch.compile TorchDynamo captures the graph from Python code, and the default compiler, TorchInductor, generates code for a range of accelerators and backends. On NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs, TorchInductor builds its kernels on OpenAI Triton.
  • Why hyperscalers can build their own chips: they control their own workloads, so they only have to fit the compiler stack to their own models. Not needing to build a general-purpose software ecosystem is their decisive advantage.

Operator coverage and fallback

Here is a common reason why the hardware is good but the model is slow. Accelerator libraries do not cover every operator. When the runtime meets an operator it does not support, it hands just that node to the CPU (fallback). The input then has to be moved down from device memory to host memory, and the result the CPU computes has to be moved back up to the device; before and after each transfer, device and host wait for each other. Even if the operation itself is small, this round trip adds to the latency of the whole graph.

Two widely used runtimes document this behavior. ONNX Runtime takes a list of execution providers in order of priority. Given ['CUDAExecutionProvider', 'CPUExecutionProvider'], it runs on CUDA the nodes CUDA can handle and runs the rest on the CPU. PyTorch's Apple GPU backend (MPS) sends operations that MPS does not support to the CPU when the environment variable PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK is set to 1 (PyTorch 2.14 documentation).

How expensive the round trip is becomes clear when you set the widths of the two paths side by side. The NVIDIA H100 spec sheet lists PCIe Gen5 for the H100 SXM at 128 GB/s and GPU memory bandwidth at 3.35 TB/s. The H100 white paper states that 128 GB/s is the total for both directions, 64 GB/s each way. Dividing the official figures gives about 26 times; counting one direction, about 52 times. A single fallback moves data that would have stayed inside HBM twice through a path more than an order of magnitude narrower. The claim that lock-in really consists of accumulated kernels (appendix B, question 4) takes a concrete shape here. A new chip with a short operator list can be slowed by fallback even if its arithmetic units are fast.

Case — DeepSeek-V3, hiding communication behind computation

The DeepSeek-V3 technical report (arXiv:2412.19437) gives an example of software making up for hardware constraints. According to the report, the model was trained on a cluster of 2,048 H800s, and full training (2,664K GPU hours for pre-training, 119K for context-length extension, 5K for post-training) took 2.788M H800 GPU hours. The report assumes a rental price of USD 2 per GPU hour to arrive at USD 5.576 million, and in the same paragraph states that this figure covers only the official training and excludes the costs of prior research and ablation experiments on architecture, algorithms and data. So the figure must not be read as the cost of developing the model.

What matters technically is how communication was handled. The report designed DualPipe, an algorithm that overlaps the computation and communication phases of the forward and backward passes in pipeline parallelism, and set aside 20 of the H800's 132 SMs to handle cross-node expert (MoE) communication. That works out to about 15% of the compute units. The report itself notes that this approach limits computational throughput, and it suggests to chip designers that communication be moved off the SMs onto dedicated hardware. It is a case of hiding cross-node communication, an item outside the roofline (appendix B, question 1), behind computation by scheduling, and of giving up part of the compute units in return.

8. Common misconceptions

Misconception 1: "High FLOPS means a fast chip" → If the workload's arithmetic intensity is below the ridge point, FLOPS mean nothing. In LLM inference, the bandwidth figure is the better predictor.

Misconception 2: "You can compare TOPS/TFLOPS figures as they are" → They differ by 4–8 times depending on precision (FP32/BF16/FP8/INT8/INT4) and on whether sparsity is applied. Match the conditions before comparing. Even matching precision and sparsity is not enough — see "Conditions for a fair comparison" at the end of this section.

Misconception 3: "GPU utilization at 90% means it is well used" → The utilization reported by nvidia-smi is "the share of time a kernel is running," not a sign that the compute units are full. A kernel spinning while it waits for memory also shows as 100%. The real metric is achieved FLOPS against theoretical FLOPS, such as MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization). When kernels are very short there is a trap on the other side, too. The overhead of launching a kernel and waiting for it becomes larger than its run time, and the GPU sits idle between kernels (the CUDA Graphs example in appendix B, question 1).

Misconception 4: "Quantization makes computation faster" → The throughput of the arithmetic units does rise, but in inference most of the gain you notice comes from less memory traffic.

Misconception 5: "An ASIC is always more efficient than a GPU" → Only when the workload is fixed. When matrices that do not fit the array size or new operators (for example, a new attention variant) come in, utilization drops sharply.

Misconception 6: "NPUs and GPUs are the same thing at different sizes" → Their objective functions differ (throughput vs. performance per watt). There are many points where design decisions go in opposite directions.

Conditions for a fair comparison — what to match besides precision

The speed of an inference service cannot be captured in one number. The latency a user feels splits into three. TTFT (time to first token) is the time from sending the request until the first token comes out, and it is governed by prefill, which processes the whole input at once. TPOT (time per output token) is the average interval between output tokens, governed by the decoding ceiling of section 6. P99 is the tail latency below which 99% of requests finish. Even with a good average, a long tail means the service-quality promise cannot be kept.

That is why MLPerf Inference, the industry-standard benchmark, ties several conditions together when it compares chips. In the data-center Llama2-70B task of the MLCommons inference rules (the master version checked on October 8, 2026, last modified August 20, 2026), the Closed division requires the same model and preprocessing as the reference implementation (quantization calibration is allowed, retraining is not) and fixes the dataset as OpenOrca. Accuracy must be at least 99.9% of the FP32 reference ROUGE scores, and the latency constraints are TTFT 2,000 ms and TPOT 200 ms in the Conversational category, TTFT 450 ms and TPOT 40 ms in the Interactive category. In the Server and Interactive scenarios, where requests arrive at random following a Poisson distribution, latency is measured at the 99th percentile. A chip that raised its throughput with lower precision also has to clear the accuracy floor and the latency constraints for its result to count. One line of a TOPS table tells you none of this. The rules change with every round, so when you cite them, state the version.

9. Quantitative exercises

Exercise 1 — Computing the ridge point Pick any accelerator from a spec sheet, find the dense Ppeak and B, and compute I*. Compare three generations and look at the trend in I*.

Exercise 2 — The decoding ceiling For 7B / 70B / 405B models served in fp16, INT8 and INT4, compute the theoretical maximum tokens/s at a batch of 1 on a given accelerator. Which combinations meet a real service latency requirement (for example, 30 tokens/s)?

Exercise 3 — The KV cache budget With sequence length S, layers L, total KV head dimension d (number of heads storing K and V × dimension per head; query heads are not counted) and batch Bsz, the size of an fp16 KV cache is roughly 2·L·S·d·Bsz·2 bytes. Find the largest batch possible for a given memory capacity, and place the arithmetic intensity at that batch on the roofline. How the capacity constraint limits bandwidth efficiency comes out.

Exercise 4 — ASIC break-even Using assumed values (NRE USD 100 million, ASIC unit price USD 3,000, GPU unit price USD 30,000, 3 years of electricity included), find N* and discuss whether it is achievable if the model's life is 2 years.

10. Discussion questions

  1. What does the roofline model fail to explain? (Latency, the cache hierarchy, communication, kernel launch overhead and so on. Knowing a model's limits is half of knowing the model.)
  2. Is it chance or design that the ridge point stays near 300 across generations? What happens if it moves away in either direction?
  3. What effect does MoE (mixture of experts) have from the roofline's point of view? How should we assess a structure in which total parameters grow but active parameters shrink?
  4. How long can software lock-in last? What changes as intermediate layers such as Triton and XLA mature?
  5. If you were designing a new chip only for inference, what would you do differently from a training chip? (Hint: where would you put the ridge point?)

11. Further study

  • The roofline original: Williams, Waterman & Patterson, "Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures", CACM 52(4), 2009 — DOI 10.1145/1498765.1498785
  • The source of the energy figures: Horowitz, "Computing's Energy Problem (and what we can do about it)", ISSCC 2014 keynote — DOI 10.1109/ISSCC.2014.6757323. The two 32-bit memory values in the section 1 table come from Figure 1 of Han, Pool, Tran & Dally, "Learning both Weights and Connections for Efficient Neural Networks", NIPS 2015 — arXiv:1506.02626
  • TPU architecture: Jouppi et al., "In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit", ISCA 2017 — the paper that sets out the design rationale of TPU v1 directly. If you read only one paper alongside this session, make it this one. arXiv:1704.04760
  • Accelerator design textbook: Sze, Chen, Yang & Emer, "Efficient Processing of Deep Neural Networks" (Synthesis Lectures, 2020) — the standard treatment of the dataflow taxonomy (weight stationary / output stationary and so on). DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-01766-7
  • Kernel-level optimization: Dao et al., the "FlashAttention" series — the leading example of raising I through kernel fusion. The first paper is arXiv:2205.14135
  • GPU architecture: NVIDIA architecture white papers (H100 white paper, Blackwell Architecture Technical Brief) and the memory-hierarchy chapters of the CUDA Programming Guide
  • Kernel launch overhead: NVIDIA technical blog, "Getting Started with CUDA Graphs" (2019) — an example that measures how batching short kernels into one launch works and what it gains
  • The rules of comparison: MLCommons MLPerf Inference rules — accuracy floors and TTFT/TPOT constraints for each task

Self-study appendix A — solutions to the quantitative exercises

These are the solutions to the exercises in section 9. Solve them yourself first, then open them. The numbers come from public spec sheets, and all are dense (no sparsity) values.

Solution to Exercise 1 — Computing the ridge point

SolutionSolution

Plug three generations into I*=Ppeak/B.

Chip Ppeak (BF16 dense) B I*
A100 80GB SXM 312 TFLOP/s 2.04 TB/s 153 FLOP/byte
H100 SXM 989 TFLOP/s 3.35 TB/s 295 FLOP/byte
B200 2,250 TFLOP/s 7.7 TB/s 292 FLOP/byte

Calculation: 312/2.04=153, 989/3.35=295, 2250/7.7=292.

Seen as growth rates from generation to generation, it is much clearer.

Step Compute Bandwidth I*
A100 → H100 ×3.17 ×1.64 ×1.93 (worse)
H100 → B200 ×2.28 ×2.30 ×0.99 (almost unchanged)

How to read it: in the A100→H100 generation, compute grew much faster than bandwidth, and the ridge point nearly doubled. That is, it became easier to end up memory-bound. From H100 to B200, HBM3E was attached to raise bandwidth at almost the same rate as compute, and the ridge point stayed where it was.

Implication: I* staying near 300 is no accident. It means bandwidth is only just keeping up with compute, and the price of that "only just" is the cost of HBM and advanced packaging. The reason Session 3 and Session 6 exist is contained in this one table.

A caution when reading spec sheets: vendor material also lists values with sparsity applied, and using them inflates I* twofold. Always check that a figure is dense.

Solution to Exercise 2 — The decoding ceiling

SolutionSolution

tokens/s≲BP·b×Bsz

The calculation is for one H100 SXM (B=3.35 TB/s, capacity 80 GB) at a batch of 1. P·b is the total number of bytes in the weights.

Model Precision Weight size Cards needed Total B Theoretical ceiling
7B fp16 (b=2) 14 GB 1 3.35 TB/s 239 tok/s
7B INT8 7 GB 1 3.35 479
7B INT4 3.5 GB 1 3.35 957
70B fp16 140 GB 2 (exceeds capacity) 6.7 48 tok/s
70B INT8 70 GB 1 (tight) 3.35 48
70B INT4 35 GB 1 3.35 96
405B fp16 810 GB 11 36.85 45
405B INT8 405 GB 6 20.1 50
405B INT4 202.5 GB 3 10.05 50

Worked example: 70B fp16 on 2 cards → 6.7×1012/(1.4×1011)=47.9 tok/s. Total B is the number of cards × 3.35 TB/s, and the ceilings were computed from unrounded values.

Combinations that meet the 30 tok/s requirement: in the table above, all of them. But note that these are theoretical ceilings. In practice, bandwidth utilization reaches only 60–80% (an assumed value in this book), and tensor-parallel communication and kernel launch overhead come on top. Utilization alone takes 70B fp16 on 2 cards from 48 to about 29–38 tok/s, and with overhead added it can fall below 30, which makes it a close call.

Three insights

  1. On the same equipment, model size and speed are inversely proportional. P sits in the denominator of the formula, so with the number of cards and the precision fixed, the ceiling drops 10 times going from 7B to 70B. In the table above, fp16 7B (1 card, 239) and 70B (2 cards, 48) differ by 5 times because 70B uses twice as many cards and so has twice the total bandwidth. The decision "let's use a bigger model" is a decision to run that much slower on the same equipment, or to buy that many more chips for the same speed.
  2. Quantization wins twice. Each time the weight bytes are halved, the ceiling doubles on the same number of cards, or the same ceiling is reached with half the cards. Switching 70B from fp16 to INT4 gets you both. 48 tok/s on 2 cards becomes 96 tok/s on 1, and the equipment cost halves.
  3. If you load a model onto just enough cards to hold it, the batch-1 ceiling becomes almost independent of model size. 70B fp16 on 2 cards (48), 70B INT8 on 1 (48), 405B fp16 on 11 (45) and 405B INT4 on 3 (50) are all similar. Each chip reads, once per token, weights that nearly fill its own memory, so the ceiling clusters just above one chip's "capacity ÷ bandwidth" (for the H100, 80 GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s ≈ 24 ms, about 42 tok/s). For the same model and precision, adding chips raises this rule of thumb's ceiling in proportion to the number of cards (405B fp16, 11 cards 45 → 12 cards 50). In reality, tensor-parallel communication between chips is added, so it does not rise that much. This communication cost lies outside the rule of thumb (appendix B, question 1).

Solution to Exercise 3 — The KV cache budget

SolutionSolution

The size of an fp16 KV cache is 4·L·S·d bytes per sequence (×2 for K and V, ×2 for fp16).

Setup: a 70B-class model, L=80 layers, with GQA d=8 heads×128=1,024, S=4,096, one H100 80GB.

KV per sequence =4×80×4096×1024=1.34×109 bytes = 1.34 GB

Precision Weights Remaining capacity Largest batch Arithmetic intensity I=2Bsz/b I* at that precision Utilization I/I*
INT8 70 GB 10 GB 7 14 590 2.4%
INT4 35 GB 45 GB 33 132 1,181 11.2%

(I* here takes the H100 BF16 dense value of 295 and assumes the compute peak doubles for INT8 and quadruples for INT4. The doubling for INT8 matches the INT8 tensor core figure on the H100 spec sheet; the quadrupling for INT4 is an assumption that extends the same ratio. In practice, activation buffers and fragmentation leave even less room, so these values are optimistic ceilings. On the other hand, assuming every sequence fills up to S is a conservative assumption. With schemes such as PagedAttention, which reserve space only as it is used, the average length is what counts.)

There are two precision assumptions. The table above is an approximation that assumes the computation runs at the same precision as the weights. Then arithmetic intensity and the ridge point both grow by a factor of 2/b, and utilization comes out as Bsz/295, just as in fp16 (this is the "Bsz/I*" used by the KV figure for Exercise 3). The roofline figure of section 6 (screen edition) is the case where only the weights are read at low precision and the computation runs in BF16. Arithmetic intensity is the same 2Bsz/b, but the ridge point is set at the BF16 value of 295, so utilization comes out 2/b times higher. Calculated, the INT8 batch of 7 in the table above becomes about 4.7% and the INT4 batch of 33 about 45%. The two values differ not because of an error but because the assumptions differ.

What comes out — the heart of this exercise

The capacity constraint holds down the batch, a held-down batch holds down arithmetic intensity, and held-down arithmetic intensity leaves 97% of the compute units, the most expensive part, idle. The bandwidth constraint and the capacity constraint look like separate things, but capacity governs bandwidth efficiency through the batch.

One step further — without GQA

With Multi-Head Attention, d=64×128=8,192, 8 times as large, and the KV per sequence is 10.7 GB. In INT8, not even a batch of 1 fits. Why GQA and MQA are a necessity, not an option, lies in this one-line calculation.

Priorities among the means of raising throughput (they follow naturally from this calculation)

  1. KV cache quantization (INT8) → KV halves, batch doubles
  2. Weight quantization → remaining capacity jumps, batch jumps
  3. Removing fragmentation with PagedAttention and similar → recovers effective capacity
  4. Limiting sequence length → linear in S

The figure below shows how memory is divided when a 70B-class model is loaded onto one H100 80GB with INT8 weights, an fp16 KV cache and GQA, at S=4,096. In the screen edition you can change the chip, sequence length, weight and KV cache precision, attention scheme and reserve ratio, and watch how the largest batch and compute-unit utilization move.

Solution to Exercise 4 — ASIC break-even

SolutionSolution

N*=CNRE(cG+oG)−(cA+oA)

Assumptions: NRE USD 100 million, ASIC unit price USD 3,000, GPU unit price USD 30,000. One ASIC replaces one GPU 1:1 (section 5). Electricity over 3 years is set up as follows: GPU 700W, ASIC 300W, PUE 1.3, 80% utilization (here, the share of time the chip draws its rated power), electricity at USD 0.08/kWh.

  • GPU energy =0.7×1.3×8760×3×0.8=19,132 kWh → oG≈ USD 1,531
  • ASIC energy =0.3×1.3×8760×3×0.8=8,199 kWh → oA≈ USD 656

N*=108(30,000+1,531)−(3,000+656)=10827,875≈3,590 units

What if the model's life is 2 years? Electricity costs fall to 2/3, the denominator becomes 27,583 → N*≈3,630 units (3,625.4 by division). It barely changes.

Where to measure power — chip, server, facility. The 700 W above is the value the NVIDIA H100 spec sheet gives as the maximum TDP of the H100 SXM ("Up to 700W (configurable)"). It is the ceiling on the heat one chip can produce, not its average draw during work, and still less the power of the whole server. Power grows as the boundary widens.

Boundary Value Basis
Chip Up to 700 W (H100 SXM TDP) H100 spec sheet
Server Up to 10.2 kW (DGX H100, 8 GPUs) → about 1.28 kW per GPU Power specifications in the DGX H100/H200 User Guide. By calculation, 10.2÷8=1.275 kW
Facility Server power × PUE This exercise's assumed PUE of 1.3

Counted again at the server boundary with the same assumptions (PUE 1.3, utilization 0.8, USD 0.08/kWh, 3 years):

  • GPU energy =1.275×1.3×8760×3×0.8≈34,847 kWh → oG≈ USD 2,788 (about 1.8 times the chip boundary)
  • For fairness the ASIC has to be raised to the same boundary. There is no basis for specifying an ASIC server, so raise it by the same ratio as the GPU (1.275/0.7≈1.82 times) to about 0.546 kW (0.3×1.275/0.7=0.54643…). Then energy ≈14,935 kWh (computed without rounding the ratio) → oA≈ USD 1,195

N*=108(30,000+2,788)−(3,000+1,195)=10828,593≈3,500 units

If only the GPU is raised to the server boundary and the ASIC is left at its chip value of 300 W, the denominator becomes USD 29,132 and N*≈3,430 units, tilting toward the ASIC. Moving the boundary on one side only skews the comparison. Whichever way you count, N* stays at 3,400–3,600 units, and at the server boundary the electricity difference of USD 1,593 is about 6% of the denominator, so the conclusion (acquisition cost dominates) stands. One more example at the same boundary: for the Blackwell generation, the DGX B200 datasheet gives the maximum power of the 8-GPU system as about 14.3 kW (about 1.79 kW per GPU by calculation). Unit prices, electricity rates, PUE and utilization are still illustrative assumed values; only the power ceilings of the chip and the server come from manufacturer specifications.

What this exercise really teaches — the result runs against intuition

  1. The break-even volume is surprisingly small. 3,600 units is a few weeks' deployment for a hyperscaler. On pure accounting, an in-house chip wins by a wide margin.
  2. Electricity is not decisive. Of the USD 27,875 denominator, the electricity difference is USD 875, a mere 3% (about 6% even at the server boundary). What dominates is the USD 27,000 difference in acquisition cost. The common explanation "they build their own chips to save on electricity" does not fit these numbers.
  3. Then why do most not do it? Because N* is not the answer. The real constraint is time. Development takes 2–3 years, and at completion the computation pattern the chip was aimed at must still dominate. The probability that a design decision made 2 years ago gets today's model structures right (MoE, long contexts, new attention variants) is the real decision variable.

So the hyperscalers' real advantage lies not in volume but in "controlling their own workloads." If, instead of fitting the chip to the model, they can fit the model to the chip, the part of the time risk above that comes from "the design failing to anticipate the model structure" shrinks a great deal. Risks such as whether demand arrives as expected, or where the performance that competing models require will move, remain. The software lock-in discussion of section 7 is completed here.

In section 5 of Session 4, cA is computed directly from the yield equation to refine this formula.

The figure below counts the assumed values of Exercise 4 (NRE USD 100 million, ASIC USD 3,000, GPU USD 30,000, PUE 1.3, 80% utilization, USD 0.08/kWh, 3 years) at the chip boundary (GPU 700 W, ASIC 300 W). In the screen edition you can switch the power boundary among chip, server (both sides) and server (GPU only), and move the unit prices, power, PUE, utilization, electricity rate and period to see how N*, the crossing point of the two total-cost lines, and the electricity share of the denominator change.

Self-study appendix B — leads for the discussion questions

Question Key axis Leads
1. Limits of the roofline The steady-state assumption The roofline is the ceiling for "a kernel that runs long enough." It captures none of the following: latency (time to the first token), the cache hierarchy (flattened into a single B), cross-node communication, kernel launch and synchronization overhead, and clock throttling from power limits. The decoding example in section 6 assumed that only the weights are read, so the traffic from reading the KV cache is also missing, and with a long context the real arithmetic intensity is lower still (Exercise 3). The peaks of low-precision arithmetic units were also simplified. The roofline figure of section 6 keeps Ppeak at the BF16 dense value even for INT8 and INT4 weights; if the computation runs at the same precision, the peak and the arithmetic intensity grow together and utilization ends up similar to fp16 (solution to Exercise 3). For the size of launch overhead, the example NVIDIA measured in its 2019 CUDA Graphs post on a V100 with CUDA 10.1 gives a feel. Launching a short kernel that runs in 2.9 μs and synchronizing after each one took 9.6 μs per kernel; cutting synchronization to once per step brought it to 3.8 μs; launching 20 kernels bundled into one CUDA Graph brought it to 3.4 μs. These are not figures for current GPUs but an example of scale. When kernels get as short as microseconds, the time to launch and wait can exceed the run time. It is a model that gives a ceiling, not a predictive model
2. Is I*≈300 a coincidence? Design intent No coincidence. If bandwidth cannot be raised to keep up, the chip ends up with idle compute units, so vendors keep the balance. Move above it (too much compute) and real-world efficiency falls; move below it (too much bandwidth) and HBM costs eat into profit
3. MoE on the roofline Weights read vs. weights held Total parameters grow, so capacity pressure rises; active parameters shrink, so the decoding ceiling rises. It is a structure that trades a capacity constraint for a bandwidth constraint. But routing creates irregular access that lowers effective bandwidth utilization, and when experts scatter within a batch the gain is halved
4. How long software lock-in lasts Who writes the kernels What lock-in really consists of is not the language but the accumulation of optimized kernels. If Triton and XLA lower the cost of writing kernels, that accumulation is worth less. Conversely, the more specialized the hardware becomes (dedicated instructions, special memory hierarchies), the harder it is for compilers to absorb, and lock-in grows stronger
5. Designing an inference-only chip Where to put the ridge point Decoding is low at I≈Bsz, so it is rational to cut compute, put the budget into bandwidth and capacity, and design I* low. Fix precision mainly at INT8/INT4 and spend the area that frees up on on-chip SRAM. This is the direction actual inference-specialized chips have taken

Self-study appendix C — key terms

Term One-line definition
Roofline model A model that expresses the performance ceiling as the minimum of the compute limit and the bandwidth limit
Ridge point The arithmetic intensity I*=Ppeak/B at which compute-bound and memory-bound divide
Compute-bound A state in which the compute units are the limit (I>I*)
Memory-bound A state in which memory transfer is the limit (I<I*)
GEMM (general matrix multiply) General matrix-matrix multiplication
Prefill / decode The phase that processes the whole input at once / the phase that generates tokens one at a time
Batch size The number of sequences processed at once
Tiling / blocking An optimization that cuts data into pieces small enough to load on chip and reuses them
Kernel fusion An optimization that merges several operations so that intermediate results are not written to memory
FlashAttention The leading kernel that fuses attention to cut round trips to HBM
MoE (mixture of experts) A sparse model structure that activates only some experts for each token
GQA / MQA (grouped / multi-query attention) Attention variants that reduce the number of KV heads to shrink the KV cache
Systolic array A compute structure that streams data through a grid and repeats multiply-accumulate operations
Structured sparsity A technique that sets some weights to 0 to cut computation. The main culprit in inflated spec-sheet figures
NRE (non-recurring engineering) The one-time cost of developing a chip
Tensor parallelism A scheme that splits the matrices of one layer across several accelerators
TTFT (time to first token) The time from the request to the first token. Governed by prefill
TPOT (time per output token) The average interval between output tokens. Governed by decoding
P99 (99th percentile latency) The latency below which 99% of requests finish. A measure of tail latency
Fallback Handing an operation the accelerator does not support to the CPU to run. A device-host round trip is added

Self-study appendix D — self-assessment

  • ☐ I can write Pattainable=min(Ppeak,B×I) without looking and say what each term is → section 6 ★
  • ☐ Given any chip's spec sheet, I can compute I* within 30 seconds → Exercise 1 ★
  • ☐ I can explain why prefill is compute-bound and decoding memory-bound, using the I of each → section 6
  • ☐ Using the decoding-ceiling formula, I can give two reasons why "70B fp16 on one H100" is impossible → Exercise 2
  • ☐ I can explain why quantization improves both the ceiling and capacity → Exercise 2
  • ☐ I can set up the KV cache size formula and explain how capacity limits bandwidth efficiency → Exercise 3 ★
  • ☐ I can tell ways of raising arithmetic intensity from ways of raising bandwidth and name three of each → the last table in section 6
  • ☐ I can show by calculation that in ASIC break-even acquisition cost, not electricity, dominates → Exercise 4
  • ☐ I can name three things the roofline cannot explain → appendix B

If you do not pass the three ★ items, do not move on to Session 3. All of Session 3 is the answer to "so how do we raise B?"

Before the next session

The conclusion of this session fits in one sentence. For work whose arithmetic intensity falls short of the ridge point, small-batch decoding above all, performance is set by bandwidth, not by compute. Work with high arithmetic intensity, such as prefill and training, is still compute-bound.

That leads naturally to the next questions.

Question this session leaves The answer in Session 3
What does it take to raise B? Widen the bus or raise the pin speed, and why the former was chosen
Why is that so expensive? Stacking, TSVs, KGD screening, bonding, and the cruel arithmetic of stack yield
How is the capacity constraint (Exercise 3) solved? HBF and memory tiering
