Session 3

AI Memory — DRAM · HBM · HBF

Key takeaway

HBM's odd-looking shape (vertical stacking + a 2,048-bit ultra-wide bus + a silicon interposer) is not a design choice. It follows inevitably from physical constraints. There are only two ways to raise bandwidth: "send each signal faster" or "add more wires." The first ran into walls of signal integrity and power. So the industry pushed the second to the extreme, and pulling out thousands of wires means placing the parts physically very close together, which made TSVs and interposers indispensable. That is why the memory problem became a packaging problem. HBM is expensive because yields multiply (a 12-high stack = die yield to the 12th power). HBF appeared because, apart from bandwidth, capacity is a bottleneck of its own.

Primary sources

Semiconductor Network, "The Evolution of Memory Semiconductors in the AI Era… from Flash, SRAM and DRAM to HBM" (in Korean) · Rambus, "High Bandwidth Memory (HBM): Everything You Need to Know" · HyperAccel, "Understanding HBF" (in Korean) · ETRI, Electronics and Telecommunications Trends vol. 41 no. 3, "Key Technologies and Market Trends in Artificial Intelligence (AI) Memory Semiconductors" (in Korean) · JEDEC JESD270-4 (HBM4) press release · Samsung Electronics press release on shipping HBM4 in volume (2026-02-12) · SK hynix, first HBF standard specifications (2026-08-04) · Micron 16Gb DDR4 data sheet Rev. H

Learning objectives

  1. Explain why the different device structures of SRAM, DRAM and NAND produce their characteristic speed, capacity and cost.
  2. Explain why DRAM latency has barely improved in 20 years.
  3. Reconstruct the structure of HBM from the question "why does it look like this?"
  4. Calculate the multiplicative structure of stack yield and explain the cost structure of HBM.
  5. Distinguish the bottleneck HBF targets from the one HBM targets.

0. Self-study guide — for readers working alone

This session is the answer to Session 2

Session 2 ended with "in small-batch decoding, bandwidth sets performance." Then why not just raise the bandwidth? This session shows why that "just raise it" is a problem that shakes the whole industry. Work through the stack-yield arithmetic (Exercise 1) and the price of HBM shows up in numbers.

What carries over from the previous session

From Session 2 In this session
I*=Ppeak/B How B is physically built
"Decoding is memory-bound" Hence the need for HBM
The capacity constraint in Exercise 3 Hence the discussion of HBF (high capacity)

Prerequisite check

Concept One-line answer
DRAM cell Stores a 0 or 1 as charge in a single capacitor. The charge leaks away, so it is rewritten periodically (refresh)
NAND flash Traps charge inside an insulating layer, so data survives power-off. In exchange it is slow and has a limited write life
Bus width / transfer rate How many lanes carry data at once / how many times per second one lane sends. Bandwidth = the product of the two
TSV Through-silicon via. An electrical path that runs vertically through the silicon
pJ/bit The energy needed to move 1 bit. The real currency of the bandwidth era

Reading order (110 minutes in total recommended)

Step Section Time Note
1 Memory hierarchy, DRAM basics 25 min Background
2 Two ways to build bandwidth 20 min Much faster if read together with Exercise 2
3 HBM structure and stack yield 30 min Read closely. Do Exercise 1 right here
4 Section 6, HBF 20 min Capacity, a different axis
5 Section 7, PIM/PNM + appendices 15 min

The one sentence that runs through this session

Bandwidth and capacity are different constraints, and different technologies solve them. Bandwidth: HBM (close and wide). Capacity: HBF and tiering (farther away but large). Mix the two up and this session will confuse you throughout.

A common sticking point — why "wide and slow"?

Intuitively, raising pin speed looks easier. Isn't making one lane twice as fast simpler than planting 1,024 pins?

No. Raising the transfer rate makes energy per bit grow nonlinearly (equalization circuits, clock recovery, driver strength), and signal-integrity problems get sharply worse. Build 4 TB/s of bandwidth from 1,024 pins at 32 Gbps and the interface alone can eat close to 100W per stack (96W at 3 pJ/bit). With 8 stacks on one accelerator, the memory interface alone takes about 770W, a second heat source on par with the GPU's own power (700–1,000W). How much the temperature actually rises depends on the area over which that heat spreads and on the cooling, but it is hard to give the memory side a power budget of that size. So HBM chose to use very many slow pins, and the price was that it needed room to plant them, which brought in stacking, TSVs and interposers. Exercise 2 checks this logic with numbers.

1. Getting the intuition — the memory hierarchy is a map of physical compromises

Readers who have studied computer architecture will know the hierarchy "registers → L1 → L2 → L3 → DRAM → SSD." Such courses usually do not cover why the hierarchy splits into those sizes and speeds. The answer lies in the device structure.

Level Device structure Transistors per cell Result
SRAM (cache) Cross-coupled inverter latch 6 (6T) Fast, not nonvolatile, large area → small capacity and expensive
DRAM (main memory) 1 transistor + 1 capacitor 1 (1T1C) Small cell, so dense and cheap; in exchange slower and needs refresh
NAND (storage) Transistor with a charge-storage layer, stacked vertically 1, but 3–4 bits per cell (TLC, QLC) Ultra-dense and nonvolatile; in exchange erased block by block, slow, finite endurance

One-sentence summary: the number of devices it takes to hold one bit sets the character of the whole hierarchy. As transistors per bit fall from 6 for SRAM → 1 for DRAM (plus one capacitor) → 1/3–1/4 for NAND (3–4 bits per cell), memory gets cheaper and denser but slower and harder to handle. NAND then stacks cells vertically in hundreds of layers, multiplying the bits held in the same area once more. Cutting the device count and stacking layers are separate sources of density.

The hierarchy as seen from an AI accelerator (as of October 2026)

Inside an AI server the same devices sit in the order below. The higher the level, the shorter the latency; the lower, the larger and cheaper. Looking at stack bandwidth alone, HBF can exceed host DRAM, but NAND's long read latency puts it a level below DRAM. In its keynote at FMS in August 2026, SK hynix presented the memory hierarchy as four levels: HBM, DRAM, NAND (HBF) and SSD. This table adds on-chip SRAM on top of that order.

Level Medium Where it sits What it does
On-chip SRAM SRAM Inside the accelerator die The tile currently being computed
HBM Stacked DRAM Right beside the accelerator (on the interposer) Weights and KV cache read for every token
DRAM DDR, LPDDR (including CXL expansion memory) Memory slots on the CPU side, expansion devices Host memory, overflow KV cache
HBF Stacked NAND Connected to the processor over UCIe (section 6) Large data that rarely changes (proposal stage)
SSD NAND The server's storage devices Model files, datasets

The order is by speed and capacity, not by physical distance. HBF sits below DRAM, yet it is meant to be placed close to the accelerator as HBM is. As an analogy, SRAM is the top of your desk, HBM the bookshelf within arm's reach, DRAM the stacks in the same room, and SSD the basement archive. HBF is a large new set of shelves placed next to the desk: close by, but slower to pull a book from than the stacks. The analogy captures only distance, retrieval speed and size. NAND's wear with every write and the fact that it can be erased only block by block have no counterpart in the book analogy.

2. The physics of DRAM — why it is slow and why it does not get faster

What a read actually does

A DRAM cell stores 1 bit as the presence or absence of charge on a very small capacitor. To read it:

  1. Wordline activation — turn on the access transistors of the row
  2. Charge sharing — the charge on the cell capacitor flows out onto the bitline and shifts the bitline voltage very slightly. Cell capacitance is far smaller than bitline capacitance, so the change is only on the order of tens of mV
  3. Sense amplification — compare against a reference voltage and amplify that tiny difference to full swing
  4. Reading = destroying — the charge has left, so the original value must be written back (restore)
  5. Precharge — return the bitline to the midpoint voltage for the next access

What the timing parameters mean

This procedure is exactly what DRAM timing is made of.

Parameter Physical process it corresponds to
tRCD (RAS to CAS delay) Wordline activation → sense amplification complete
tCL (CAS latency) Column address → data out
tRP (row precharge) Time to complete precharge
tRAS (row active time) Minimum time a row stays open, including restore
tREFI / tRFC Refresh interval / time a refresh takes

The key fact: these are analog physical processes governed by charge and capacitance, so process scaling does not speed them up much. If anything, smaller cells store less charge and sensing gets harder.

Twenty years of asymmetry: DRAM bandwidth has grown dozens of times over, but latency has stayed nearly the same. Bandwidth can be raised through parallelism and interface speed, but latency is set by the physical process in a single cell. This asymmetry pushed all of computer architecture toward "hiding latency" (prefetching, multiple banks, the massive thread parallelism of GPUs).

The refresh tax

Charge leaks, so cells must be read and rewritten periodically. During refresh the bank cannot be accessed, which eats into bandwidth and power. The burden grows with capacity, making it a standing problem in high-capacity DRAM design.

It is easy to confuse this with step 4 above (restore after a read). Restore is caused by an access; refresh is caused by time. Even a cell nobody reads must be refilled once within a fixed period.

Worked example — how large is the tax? Take the Micron 16Gb DDR4 data sheet (Rev. H, 2021). At or below 85°C, 8,192 REFRESH commands must be issued within 64ms, so the command interval tREFI is 7.8μs (64ms ÷ 8,192 = 7.8125μs). Between 85 and 95°C it is 8,192 within 32ms, so tREFI halves to 3.9μs. The time one command ties up the chip, tRFC1, depends on density. The fraction of time the chip is tied up in refresh is roughly tRFC/tREFI.

Die density tRFC1 At or below 85°C (tREFI 7.8μs) 85–95°C (tREFI 3.9μs)
2Gb 160 ns 2.0% 4.1%
4Gb 260 ns 3.3% 6.7%
8Gb 350 ns 4.5% 9.0%

While density quadrupled, the tax more than doubled, and it doubles again when the chip runs hot. These ratios divide tRFC1 by 7.8125μs and 3.90625μs. It is a simple calculation that assumes the whole chip can do nothing else during refresh.

3. Two ways to raise bandwidth, and the dead end

Memory bandwidth is approximately

B=(bus width)×(transfer rate per pin)

So there are only two methods.

Think of a road: bus width is the number of lanes, and the per-pin transfer rate is how fast the cars go. To get more cars past per hour, you add lanes or make the cars go faster. The analogy misses something. On a road, faster cars do not make sending one car steeply more expensive, but a memory pin spends steeply more energy per bit (pJ/bit) the faster it sends. That cost is why the two paths below part ways.

Path ①: raise the per-pin transfer rate (the GDDR path)

  • Toggle the signal faster. GDDR6X and GDDR7 go as far as multilevel signaling (PAM3/PAM4).
  • How fast has it become? The JEDEC GDDR7 standard (JESD239, published 2024-03-05) uses PAM3, which sends 3 bits in 2 cycles using three voltage levels, and reaches up to 192 GB/s per device. For a 32-bit device that works out to 48 Gbps per pin, 6 times the HBM4 standard pin speed of 8 Gbps. HBM does not use slow pins because pin speed cannot be raised.
  • The limit: raising the frequency makes signal integrity deteriorate sharply. Loss, reflection and crosstalk in board traces all worsen with frequency, and the equalization and serialization circuits that compensate eat power. The decisive problem is that energy per transferred bit (pJ/bit) goes up.
  • At data-center scale that power is both operating cost and heat, so this path alone cannot get there.

Path ②: widen the bus (the HBM path)

  • A DDR5 channel is 64 bits and GDDR is 32 bits per device, while an HBM stack is 1,024 bits (through HBM3), and HBM4 is 2,048 bits.
  • The same bandwidth can be had at a much lower frequency, so pJ/bit falls substantially.
  • The limit: to pull out thousands of wires, the wires need somewhere to go. An ordinary PCB substrate cannot reach that wiring density, and a package does not have enough pins either.
  • A caveat — there is also a standard that mixes the two paths. SPHBM4 (JESD330-4), published by JEDEC on July 13, 2026, uses the same DRAM dies as HBM4 but changes the base die, cutting the data signals from 2,048 to 512 and using 4:1 serialization to reach the same aggregate bandwidth. With fewer pins the bump pitch can be relaxed, so the stack can be mounted on an ordinary organic substrate instead of a silicon interposer, and the memory can sit farther from the SoC. "A wide bus requires an interposer" holds when all 2,048 signals are used; pay the price of running each signal four times faster and you can move partway back toward path ①. What that price is in pJ/bit is not in the press release.

The answer that emerged

  1. To pull out a very large number of wires → you need a medium that allows extremely dense wiring → a silicon interposer
  2. To connect several dies inside a stack → TSVs (through-silicon vias)
  3. Shorter distance means less power and latency → attach it right beside the GPU (2.5D packaging)

At that moment the memory problem became a packaging problem. That is why Session 6 is the most important session in this book.

4. HBM structure in detail

Physical layout

What each element does

  • Stacked DRAM dies: capacity comes from height rather than area. 8-high, 12-high, 16-high.
  • TSVs: vertical wiring that runs through each die. They bind the whole stack into one wide bus.
  • Base die: a layer made in a logic process, not a DRAM process. It holds the PHY (physical-layer interface), test circuits and control logic. With HBM4, making this base die in a foundry logic process has become reality. Samsung Electronics used a 1c DRAM core and a 4nm logic process in the HBM4 it began shipping in volume in February 2026, and its May 2026 press release on HBM4E samples stated that the base die is "Samsung Foundry's 4nm logic base die" and that HBM4E uses "the same combination of core and base die" as HBM4. This is where the line between memory makers and foundries blurs.
  • Die-to-die bonding — microbumps and what comes next: HBM in volume production today joins dies with microbumps and fills the gaps between them. SK hynix used MR-MUF (pouring a liquid protective material between the stacked chips and curing it) for HBM4 (announced 2025-09), and Samsung Electronics used TC-NCF (laying a non-conductive film on each layer and thermocompression bonding it) for its 12-high HBM3E (announced 2024-02). Hybrid bonding, which joins copper to copper directly without bumps, is under development as the next candidate for taller stacks; as of October 2026 we found no manufacturer announcement of volume production of HBM using it. Hybrid bonding itself is covered in Session 6.
  • Interposer: the silicon plate that actually draws the thousands of wires between the GPU and the HBM.

Specifications by generation

Generation Interface width Channels Stack bandwidth — per standard Stack bandwidth — volume product (announcement date)
HBM2E 1,024 bits 8 ~0.4–0.5 TB/s (approximate)
HBM3 1,024 bits 16 ~0.8 TB/s (approximate)
HBM3E 1,024 bits 16 Pin up to 9.6 Gbps → about 1.2 TB/s by calculation (comparison value in Samsung's HBM4 press release, 2026-02-12). Samsung's HBM3E 12H press release (2024-02-27) gives up to 1,280 GB/s
HBM4 2,048 bits 32 (2 pseudo-channels per channel) 8 Gbps → up to about 2 TB/s (JESD270-4, 2025-04-16) Pin 11.7 Gbps (up to 13 Gbps), up to 3.3 TB/s per stack (Samsung, volume shipment 2026-02-12)
HBM4E Pin 14 Gbps (up to 16 Gbps), up to 3.6 TB/s per stack, 12-high 48 GB (Samsung, sample shipment 2026-05-29)

The standard column gives what the pin speed set by the JEDEC standard can deliver; the product column gives values the manufacturers announced. As of October 2026, volume HBM4 exceeds the standard pin speed.

  • SK hynix announced on September 12, 2025, that it had completed HBM4 development and readied mass production: 2,048 I/O, over 10 Gbps per pin (above the JEDEC standard of 8 Gbps), 1b DRAM (the fifth generation of the 10nm class), and the Advanced MR-MUF process.
  • Samsung Electronics announced volume shipments of HBM4 on February 12, 2026. It runs at 11.7 Gbps per pin, can be pushed to 13 Gbps, and comes as a 12-high stack of 24–36 GB. Multiply 11.7 Gbps by 2,048 bits and you get about 3.0 TB/s; at 13 Gbps, about 3.3 TB/s. The press release's "maximum of 3.3 terabytes-per-second (TB/s)" per stack is the 13 Gbps figure.
  • The same company's 12-high HBM4E samples (2026-05-29): assume 2,048 bits as for HBM4 and multiply by 14 Gbps, and you get about 3.6 TB/s, matching the press release (which does not state the interface width).
  • The standard-column values for HBM2E and HBM3 and the HBM3E row are rough ranges, because pin speed differs by vendor and product. Blank cells were not confirmed from a primary source for this edition.

Main changes in HBM4

  • Interface width 1,024 → 2,048 bits (2 times)
  • Independent channels 16 → 32, each with 2 pseudo-channels
  • Backward compatibility with HBM3 controllers — the interface is defined so that a single controller can handle both HBM3 and HBM4
  • DRFM (directed refresh management) introduced — row-hammer mitigation and better reliability (RAS)
  • Supports 4- to 16-high stacks, die density 24Gb or 32Gb → 32Gb at 16-high gives 64 GB per cube
  • Lower core voltage (1.1V in HBM3/3E → 1.0/1.05V); VDDQ chosen by the vendor from 0.7–0.9V

Note: HBM4 doubled the width instead of raising the frequency sharply. That means it chose "path ②" from section 3 once again. Power efficiency is why this path keeps being chosen.

Why each GPU carries several HBM stacks

Because one stack is short on both bandwidth and capacity. The latest accelerators arrange 6–8 HBM stacks around the GPU die. As one example, NVIDIA said the Rubin GPU, with 12-high HBM4 stacks, delivers up to 288 GB and up to 22 TB/s per GPU (technical blog, 2026-07-21; 2.8 times Blackwell's bandwidth). The post does not give the number of stacks. Assuming 36 GB stacks, there are 8, which gives 2.75 TB/s per stack and about 10.7 Gbps per pin — an estimate worked backward, nothing more. But adding stacks:

  • enlarges the interposer → the interposer, too, is limited by the lithography exposure field → extension methods such as CoWoS-L are needed
  • makes the package bigger and raises heat density
  • makes packaging capacity the ceiling on AI chip shipments (what the supply-chain bottleneck in Session 1 actually is)

5. Why HBM is expensive — yields multiply

For readers trained in statistics, this is the most intuitive section.

The basic calculation

Let y be the yield of one DRAM die, and stack n of them. If dies are simply picked at random and stacked, the probability that the whole stack works is

Ystack=yn×∏i=1n−1ybond,i

where ybond is the yield of each bonding step.

Numerical example (y=0.99, bonding yield 0.995)

Stack height Die term yn Bonding term Stack yield
4-high 0.961 0.985 0.946
8-high 0.923 0.966 0.891
12-high 0.886 0.946 0.839
16-high 0.851 0.928 0.790

The stack-yield column multiplies the unrounded values, so multiplying the two printed columns may differ in the last digit.

Even with an excellent 99% per die, a 16-high stack throws away 1 stack in 5. And when a stack is thrown away, its good dies go with it. If one die is bad, the other 15 good dies are discarded; if all 16 dies are good but one bond fails, all 16 are discarded. This is the heart of HBM's price structure.

Countermeasures

  1. KGD (known good die) screening — test each die fully before stacking and use only good ones. This pushes y in the formula above toward 1. But a full test at wafer level needs separate test structures and time, and that is itself a cost.
  2. Redundancy — provide spare rows, columns and TSVs to replace defects. DRAM has traditionally been good at repair.
  3. Better bonding yield — one of the reasons hybrid bonding is being considered as the next candidate.

The cost structure in brief

HBM costs several times as much as ordinary DRAM of the same capacity because of a combination of (a) low stack yield, (b) extra steps such as TSV formation, thinning and bonding, (c) the cost of the interposer and advanced packaging, and (d) a market in which supply is limited to three companies.

For discussion: which of these terms improves over time, and which remains structurally?

6. HBF (high bandwidth flash) — capacity, another bottleneck

Why it appeared

Look again at the decoding ceiling from Session 2.

tokens/s≲BP·b×Bsz

Raising the batch size Bsz raises throughput, but a larger batch needs memory capacity to hold the KV cache. And as the model itself grows, it needs capacity to hold the weights. Bandwidth and capacity are separate constraints.

HBM is optimized for bandwidth, but its capacity is expensive (around 24–32Gb per die). NAND, by contrast, is overwhelmingly denser. "What if we stacked NAND like HBM and gave it a wide bus?" is the idea behind HBF.

Status and specifications

  • On August 6, 2025, Sandisk and SK hynix announced a collaboration (memorandum of understanding) to standardize HBF.
  • On February 25, 2026, the two companies began standardization work as a dedicated workstream within the OCP (Open Compute Project).
  • On August 4, 2026, the two companies released the first HBF standard specification through the OCP (SK hynix announcement). Two configurations, 8-high and 16-high, give up to 512 GB per stack; bandwidth comes in three grades (Grade 1–3) of about 0.4–3.0 TB/s; the connection to the processor is UCIe, the chiplet interconnect standard. Google and Tenstorrent have joined the consortium. The value for the middle grade could not be confirmed from public material.
  • Sandisk's earlier first-generation product target (July 2025 material) was 256Gb (gigabits) per die, a 16-high stack of 512 GB, and 1.6 TB/s read bandwidth, aiming at a footprint, power profile and stack height close to HBM4's. 256Gb is 32 GB, so 16-high gives 512 GB. The 1.6 TB/s is the target for one product, within the grade range of the standard above.
  • Schedule: in August 2025, Sandisk set targets of first HBF samples in the second half of 2026 and samples of HBF-equipped AI inference devices in early 2027. Its investor day presentation of August 2026 (Sandisk Investor Day 2026, HBF presentation PDF) put the tape-out of the first HBF memory die and 2027 samples of the first HBF inference product on its roadmap, and did not repeat the target of memory samples in the second half of 2026.
  • Technology base: Sandisk's BiCS NAND and CBA (CMOS directly Bonded to Array, a structure that bonds the CMOS circuit wafer directly to the cell-array wafer) + SK hynix's HBM packaging and 3D stacking capabilities.

The structure of the trade — what you give and what you get

Item HBM4 (for reference) HBF (specification released 2026-08)
Stack capacity Tens of GB (volume 12-high 24–36 GB, standard maximum 64 GB) Up to 512 GB (8-high, 16-high)
Read bandwidth About 2 TB/s by the standard, up to 3.3 TB/s in volume products Three grades, about 0.4–3.0 TB/s
Write behavior Symmetric, unrestricted Asymmetric — slow writes, block erase required
Endurance Effectively unlimited Finite P/E cycles
Latency Low High
Use Training and inference in general Mainly keeping weights resident during inference

The key point: HBF is not something that replaces HBM; it adds one level to the memory hierarchy. The intended arrangement keeps large data that rarely changes (model weights, inactive MoE experts, long-context caches) in HBF and keeps actively updated data in HBM.

Mixing the two levels — a simple model

Suppose that in one decoding step a fraction f of the bytes read comes from HBF and the remaining 1−f from HBM. If the two are read one after the other, the time taken is the sum of the two shares, so the effective bandwidth is

Beff=1(1−f)/BHBM+f/BHBF

and the capacity available is the sum of the two levels, CHBM+CHBF.

Worked example. Pair one HBM4 stack (up to 3.3 TB/s as announced by Samsung, 12-high 36 GB) with one HBF stack (512 GB). For HBF bandwidth, use the bottom of the published specification range, 0.4 TB/s, as an assumed value. If only 10% of the bytes read come from HBF (f=0.1),

Beff=10.9/3.3+0.1/0.4≈1.91 TB/s

which is 58% of reading from HBM alone. At the same f, assuming the top grade of 3.0 TB/s for HBF gives about 3.27 TB/s, almost no loss. Capacity is 36 + 512 = 548 GB either way. Let the share read from the slow level grow even a little and that level sets the overall speed. So HBF's place is data for which f can be kept small — for example, in MoE, the expert weights not used in the current step: mostly just held, read only now and then (Exercise 4).

This model assumes the two levels are read in sequence. It leaves out reading both at once so the reads overlap, and moving needed data into HBM ahead of time (prefetching), and it folds NAND's long latency into a single bandwidth number. All bandwidth values are announced or assumed values for a single stack.

The figure below shows the worked example above: f=0.1, HBM4 at 3.3 TB/s and 36 GB, HBF at 0.4 TB/s (assumed) and 512 GB. In the screen edition you can change f, HBM bandwidth and capacity, and HBF bandwidth (within the published range of 0.4–3.0 TB/s).

Open questions — what has not yet been verified

  • NAND read latency is far longer than DRAM's. How many real workloads can offset it with bandwidth?
  • How will write endurance (wear leveling) be managed at the accelerator level?
  • Will the software stack (the policies that decide which data goes on which level) mature?
  • How standardization proceeds and whether the technology is actually adopted — as of October 2026 the first standard specification has been released but there are no volume products, and the performance figures are specification ranges and targets. Treat this as "an attempt in progress," not "an established fact." Intel Optane (3D XPoint), an earlier attempt to fill the gap between DRAM and NAND, began winding down in the second quarter of 2022. A candidate for a new level does not necessarily take hold (appendix B).

Another answer on the capacity axis — CXL

If HBF is the path that attaches capacity close to the accelerator, CXL (Compute Express Link) is the path that adds memory on the server side. CXL is an open standard that borrows the physical and electrical interface of PCIe while keeping cache coherence between the CPU's memory space and the memory of attached devices. It is used to add memory to a single server (expansion) or to let several servers share a pool of memory (pooling). The CXL Consortium released CXL 4.0 on November 18, 2025, doubling the transfer rate from 64 GT/s to 128 GT/s. At FMS 2026, SK hynix demonstrated several servers moving and reusing KV cache through CXL pooled memory. In the hierarchy table of section 1, CXL memory belongs to the DRAM level. One x16 link works out to about 256 GB/s in one direction (128 GT/s × 16 ÷ 8, ignoring encoding overhead), around one-tenth of a single HBM4 stack. So it is a place not for data read on every token but for data fetched now and then, such as overflow KV cache.

7. PIM / PNM — taking computation to the memory

In the roofline formula P=min(Ppeak,B×I), the approaches so far have raised I (software) or raised B (HBM). A third approach is not to move the data in the first place.

  • PIM (processing-in-memory): put simple compute units inside the memory die. Place a multiply-accumulate unit in each DRAM bank and the internal bandwidth (not limited by external pins) can be used directly. Samsung's HBM-PIM and SK hynix's AiM are among the attempts.
  • PNM (processing-near-memory): put compute units near the memory (for example, on the base die or a buffer chip).

Why it is not yet mainstream

  • A DRAM process is not a logic process. Putting complex logic on the same die worsens cost and yield.
  • There is no programming model. The compilers and runtimes that decide which operations to send down to memory are immature.
  • It is not general-purpose; the gain is large only for particular operations (for example, embedding lookup and GEMV).

Why it still deserves attention: the move to make the base die in a foundry logic process, as in Samsung's HBM4 (section 4), is a change that opens the door to PNM. The boundary between memory and compute is physically blurring.

8. Common misconceptions

Misconception 1: "HBM is just fast DRAM" → The cells themselves are not very different from ordinary DRAM. What differs is the interface width and the packaging. HBM is closer to a packaging technology than to a memory technology.

Misconception 2: "HBM is always better than GDDR" → It wins on absolute bandwidth and power efficiency, but it costs far more, its capacity is harder to scale, and it is in short supply. There is a reason gaming GPUs still use GDDR.

Misconception 3: "Increase HBM capacity and the memory problem is solved" → Capacity and bandwidth are different problems. And raising bandwidth does not settle things either. If Ppeak stays the same and B grows, the ridge point I*=Ppeak/B comes down (for example, the H100 from Session 2, 989 TFLOP/s ÷ 3.35 TB/s ≈ 295 FLOP/byte, becomes about 148 FLOP/byte if B doubles). When the ridge point comes down, workloads with lower arithmetic intensity also cross over to the compute-bound side, but a workload like decoding, whose arithmetic intensity is below even the new ridge point, stays bound by bandwidth.

Misconception 4: "DRAM keeps getting faster as it scales" → Bandwidth grows, but latency does not improve. If anything, there is pressure in the other direction: cell capacitors shrink and sensing becomes harder.

Misconception 5: "HBF will replace HBM" → Because of its write behavior and endurance, it adds a level rather than replacing one. And as of October 2026 only the first standard specification has been released; there are no volume products.

Misconception 6: "More layers increase capacity at linear cost" → The capacity of one good stack is proportional to its height (die capacity × number of dies). What is not proportional is the cost of getting that stack. Stack without screening and stack yield falls as yn, so the dies needed for one good stack, n/yn, grow faster than the height. Taller stacks also tighten the constraints of heat removal and stack height (package standards).

Misconception 7: "An HBM channel is like a mainframe I/O channel" → Only the name is shared. A mainframe I/O channel is a dedicated processor that handles input and output on the CPU's behalf. An HBM channel is a unit into which the stack's wide bus is divided, each part operating independently. Bus width = number of channels × channel width, so HBM3 is 16 channels × 64 bits = 1,024 bits and HBM4 is 32 channels × 64 bits = 2,048 bits (the channel width is the bus width the standard states divided by the channel count). GDDR has the same structure; in GDDR7, JEDEC increased the independent channels from 2 in GDDR6 to 4.

Misconception 8: "Refresh refills the charge that leaves during a read" → That is restore. Restore is caused by an access (the read); refresh is caused by time. Even cells that are not read must be refilled within a fixed period because of leakage. For DDR4, at or below 85°C, 8,192 REFRESH commands must be issued within 64ms (section 2).

Misconception 9: "Pin speed is stuck at a physical limit and cannot go higher" → It is not that signals cannot be sent faster; it is that sending them faster is expensive. The GDDR7 standard already provides 48 Gbps per pin (192 GB/s per device divided by 32 bits). What holds speed back is not an absolute limit but the channel loss that grows with speed, the pJ/bit driven up by the equalization circuits that compensate for it, and the shorter distance a signal can travel (section 3).

9. Quantitative exercises

Exercise 1 — Stack yield Vary die yield y over 0.95 / 0.98 / 0.995, calculate the stack yield for 8-, 12- and 16-high stacks, and find the number of good dies discarded without KGD screening. The answer to "why do HBM makers invest so much in testing?" comes out in numbers.

Exercise 2 — Bandwidth design To reach a target bandwidth of 4 TB/s with (a) a 1,024-bit bus and (b) a 2,048-bit bus, what must the per-pin transfer rate be? Discuss qualitatively how the difference in pJ/bit between the two affects system power.

Exercise 3 — Allocating the memory budget When serving a given model, how should the available memory be split between weights and KV cache to maximize throughput? A larger batch grows the KV cache; quantization shrinks the weights. Set it up as a problem of finding the optimum.

Exercise 4 — Judging fitness for HBF Set up criteria for judging which workloads would benefit from HBF. (Hint: read/write ratio, reuse distance, latency sensitivity.)

10. Discussion questions

  1. Reconstruct the shape of HBM from its physical constraints. If there had been no signal-integrity problem, would HBM exist?
  2. How might the move to make HBM4's base die in a logic foundry process (Samsung has done it with its own foundry's 4nm process) change the competitive structure of the memory industry?
  3. If the memory hierarchy is subdivided further into SRAM–HBM–DRAM–HBF–SSD, what does software have to do? Can that decision be automated?
  4. What must be solved first for PIM to become practical? Is it a hardware problem or a software problem?
  5. If the bandwidth race keeps depending on pJ/bit improvements, where is the physical limit? Could optical interconnect be the answer? (Continued in Session 7.)

11. Further study

  • Memory systems textbook: Jacob, Ng & Wang, Memory Systems: Cache, DRAM, Disk (Morgan Kaufmann, 2007) — the standard reference on DRAM timing and structure
  • DRAM research: lecture materials and papers from the home page of Prof. Onur Mutlu (ETH Zürich) and the SAFARI Research Group — the most systematic body of work on DRAM latency, refresh and PIM, with lecture videos available online. Recommended for readers who want to go deeper into DRAM
  • HBM standards: JEDEC JESD235 (HBM), JEDEC JESD270-4 (HBM4) — the standard documents themselves (as of October 2026 the HBM4 standard page carries the revision JESD270-4A). For summaries, the technical blogs of Rambus and Synopsys are accessible
  • The signal-speed standard: JEDEC JESD239 (GDDR7) — the current form of path ①, raising pin speed with PAM3
  • HBF: Sandisk press release on collaborating with SK hynix on standardization (2025-08-06), SK hynix, first HBF standard specifications (2026-08-04), IEEE Spectrum, "The Memory in Your Thumb Drive Could Fix AI's Big Problem" (2026-07-14), OCP workstream documents
  • PIM: ISSCC and Hot Chips presentations on Samsung's HBM-PIM and SK hynix's AiM
  • Korean technology trends: ETRI, Electronics and Telecommunications Trends vol. 41 no. 3, "Key Technologies and Market Trends in Artificial Intelligence (AI) Memory Semiconductors" (in Korean)

Self-study appendix A — solutions to the quantitative exercises

Solution to Exercise 1 — Stack yield

SolutionSolution

Set bonding yield to 1 and look only at die yield: Ystack=yn.

Die yield y 8-high 12-high 16-high
0.95 66.3% 54.0% 44.0%
0.98 85.1% 78.5% 72.4%
0.995 96.1% 94.2% 92.3%

Stop here and you have seen only half. The real question is "if you stack without screening, how many perfectly good dies are thrown away with the bad ones?"

The expected number of good dies in one failed stack is

E[good dies∣stack fails]=ny−nyn1−yn

Substituting n=12, y=0.95:

12(0.95)−12(0.5404)1−0.5404=11.40−6.4850.4596=10.7 dies

Applying the same formula to all nine combinations gives the following. In each cell, the first value is the expected number of good dies in one failed stack, and the value in parentheses is the expected number of good dies discarded when making 1,000 stacks, 1,000(ny−nyn).

Die yield y 8-high 12-high 16-high
0.95 6.8 (2,293) 10.7 (4,916) 14.6 (8,158)
0.98 6.9 (1,034) 10.9 (2,343) 14.8 (4,099)
0.995 7.0 (274) 11.0 (641) 15.0 (1,153)

As die yield rises, the total number of good dies discarded (in parentheses) drops sharply, but the number of good dies in one failed stack actually approaches n−1. The rarer defects become, the more a failed stack is one with "only one bad die."

Suppose you make 1,000 12-high stacks.

  • 12,000 dies go in, of which 11,400 are good
  • 540.4 stacks (about 540) come out whole → 6,484.3 good dies survive (about 6,484)
  • 4,915.7 good dies (about 4,916) are discarded — 43% of the good dies are wasted

(Fractions remain because these are expected values. They multiply the unrounded stack yield 0.54036.)

What these numbers explain

  1. Why so much is invested in KGD (known good die) screening. Perfect screening brings that 43% to 0. It recovers about 4,916 good dies per 1,000 stacks, so if one die is worth c, screening wins when its extra test cost is less than about 4,916c (include the stacking and bonding costs spent on discarded stacks and the threshold rises further). Real test costs and die prices are not part of this exercise.
  2. Why it is so hard to raise the number of HBM layers. Going from 8-high to 16-high drops yield from 66% → 44% at y=0.95. To double the height while keeping the same stack yield, die yield has to be pushed from 0.95 to around 0.975.
  3. Why HBM supply does not grow quickly even when more money is offered. Section 4 showed that packaging capacity sets the ceiling on shipments. This calculation adds a different constraint on top of that: the yield learning curve. With low yield, the same capacity turns out fewer good stacks, and yield is hard to pull forward with money the way equipment can be bought. This calculation has no capacity or expansion period as an input, so it cannot tell which of the two binds harder right now. This is what the movement of the bottleneck seen in Session 1 actually looks like.

Add bonding yield and it gets worse. Even with ybond=0.999, a 12-high stack has 11 bonds, so 0.99911=0.989 is multiplied in.

What this calculation leaves out

  • Die defects are treated as independent. Real defects tend to cluster on the wafer.
  • "Perfect screening" is the extreme in which the KGD test misses no defect at all. Test cost and the miss rate are not included.
  • The effect of repairing defects with redundancy is taken to be already included in the die yield y.

The figure below shows a sample of 100 stacks made without screening at die yield y=0.95, 12-high. In the screen edition you can change die yield, stack height, bonding yield and whether dies are screened before stacking.

Solution to Exercise 2 — Bandwidth design

SolutionSolution

B=(bus width)×(transfer rate per pin). Target 4 TB/s =3.2×1013 bit/s.

Bus width Required per-pin transfer rate How it is done
(a) 1,024 bit 3.2×1013/1024= 31.25 Gbps SerDes territory. Equalization and CDR circuits required
(b) 2,048 bit 15.6 Gbps Possible with a parallel interface

The pJ/bit difference and power

As the transfer rate rises, energy per bit grows not linearly but steeply, because equalization, clock and data recovery (CDR), driver strength and termination losses all pile on. As a rough sense:

Approach Rough pJ/bit Power at 4 TB/s
High-speed SerDes (30 Gbps class) 3–5 96–160 W
Wide parallel (15 Gbps class) 0.5–1 16–32 W

3.2×1013 bit/s×3 pJ/bit=96 W. That is for one stack.

Conclusion: with 8 stacks on one accelerator, (a) at the low end of the range, 3 pJ/bit, takes about 770W (96W × 8) for memory alone, approaching 800W; at the high end, 5 pJ/bit, it is 1,280W. (b) at 0.5–1 pJ/bit takes about 130–260W. When the accelerator itself draws 700–1,000W, this difference changes the system design. Power is why HBM uses "very many slow pins."

The price: 2,048 pins cannot be planted along the edges of a die; they need an area array → microbumps → interposer → CoWoS. In Exercise 5 of Session 6 you count these wires yourself. This holds when all 2,048 pins are used, though. Like SPHBM4 at the end of section 3, cutting the signals to 512 and running each four times faster lets the stack sit on an organic substrate. Four times the HBM4 standard of 8 Gbps is 32 Gbps per signal, a speed similar to (a) in this exercise. It is a choice to avoid the interposer at the cost of carrying (a)'s pJ/bit burden (SPHBM4's actual power figures are not in the JEDEC press release).

What this calculation leaves out: the pJ/bit ranges are a rough sense, not vendor measurements. The relationship between pin speed and pJ/bit has not been turned into a formula either — real values differ by circuit and process.

The figure below assumes a target of 4 TB/s per stack, 8 stacks per accelerator, (a) 3 pJ/bit and (b) 0.75 pJ/bit. In the screen edition you can change the target bandwidth, the number of stacks and the pJ/bit of the two approaches.

Solution to Exercise 3 — Allocating the memory budget

SolutionSolution

Set the problem up as a formula. With total memory M, weights P·b and KV cache per sequence k: the weights must fit first (M≥P·b, or the model cannot be served), so the batch is the number of sequences that fit in the remaining capacity, rounded down to an integer.

Bsz=⌊M−P·bk⌋,throughput≲BP·b×Bsz≤B(M−Pb)Pbk

The rightmost expression is the continuous ceiling without the rounding. The properties below are read from that continuous ceiling; the batches in the table are rounded down.

Look at it in terms of b: the numerator grows and the denominator shrinks — a double gain. That is why quantization has a far larger effect than intuition suggests.

Numerical check (70B, M=80 GB, k=1.34 GB, B=3.35 TB/s)

Precision Weights Batch Throughput ceiling Multiple
fp16 140 GB — Does not fit —
INT8 70 GB 7 335 tok/s ×1
INT4 35 GB 33 3,159 tok/s ×9.4

Halving the precision raised throughput not 2 times but 9.4 times. The doubling of the ceiling is multiplied by a 4.7-times larger batch, because the spare capacity grows from 10 GB → 45 GB.

Properties as an optimization problem

  • b is not a free variable. It is the smallest value you can choose under the constraint of accuracy loss.
  • Quantizing the KV cache separately shrinks k for a further gain. KV quantization is often more forgiving of accuracy than weight quantization, so in practice it is applied first.
  • With longer sequences, k∝S, so the batch collapses. This term is why long-context services are expensive.

What to take away: whenever someone says "add memory," always ask whether they mean bandwidth or capacity. Here it was capacity that governed throughput.

The same calculation can be tried in the figure at the end of the solution to Exercise 3 in Session 2. In the screen edition, change the sequence length and precision and watch how the maximum batch changes.

Solution to Exercise 4 — Judging fitness for HBF

SolutionSolution

For NAND-based high-capacity memory to pay off, the workload must not touch NAND's weak points. Set up the criteria on four axes.

Axis Favors HBF Works against HBF
Read/write ratio Read-dominated (almost no writes) Frequent writes — NAND is weak on write endurance and latency
Reuse distance Long — not covered by an HBM cache Short — it stays in HBM anyway
Access granularity Large and sequential Small and random
Latency sensitivity Low, or known in advance so it can be prefetched High and unpredictable

Good fits

  • MoE expert weights — most are inactive and read-only. But the router chooses experts only after seeing the hidden state that enters that layer, so the decision for the same layer cannot be known in advance. For prefetching to work you need either to predict the next layer's experts from the previous layer's hidden state and read them early (reading that much later when the prediction misses) or a schedule that overlaps the computation of several layers and tokens to hide the read time. Given such mechanisms, this is counted as HBF's most promising use.
  • The less-read parts of a very long KV cache — with dense attention, which looks at every earlier position, each new token reads the K and V of all earlier positions, so older tokens are not read less just because they are old. Access frequency actually falls when sliding-window or sparse attention is used, or a policy that reads only selected important positions, or when the KV cache belongs to a conversation that is waiting rather than being decoded now. Under those conditions it becomes a candidate for tiering.
  • RAG vector indexes and embedding tables — large, read-only, batched access.
  • Offline batch inference — there is no latency requirement at all.

Poor fits

  • Optimizer state during training — writes happen at every step. NAND endurance becomes a problem immediately.
  • The hot path of interactive decoding — the active weights needed for every token. Latency shows directly to the user.
  • Workloads dominated by small, random accesses — amplification is severe on NAND, which is accessed page by page.

The one-line rule: "Is it read-only, is it large, and can you know in advance when it will be needed?" If all three hold, HBF; if any one fails, keep it in HBM.

Self-study appendix B — leads for the discussion questions

Type of question Where it divides Leads
Will the HBM oligopoly last? The nature of the entry barrier If the barrier is patents, they expire; if it is capacity, money loosens it; but if it is the yield learning curve, only time loosens it. What Exercise 1 shows is the weight of the third type — where yields multiply, a small difference in die yield opens into a large difference in stack yield, and a latecomer can hardly skip the leader's accumulated learning with money. This calculation cannot tell which of the three barriers is largest right now
Will HBF replace HBM? Replacement vs. an added level It is more accurate to see it not as replacement but as one more level. Historically, memory hierarchy levels have never disappeared; they have only been added (registers → cache → DRAM → SSD). HBF is a candidate to fill the gap between DRAM and SSD in the order HBM–DRAM–HBF–SSD. But new levels have not always taken hold. Intel Optane (3D XPoint), which aimed at the same gap, began winding down in the second quarter of 2022. HBF faces the same test
Why doesn't PIM work yet? Ecosystem vs. device The barrier has two layers. One is hardware: putting logic into a DRAM process worsens cost and yield (section 7). The other, emphasized here, is the programming model. Sending computation to memory requires compilers, frameworks and kernels all to change, and the lock-in in section 7 of Session 2 operates exactly here. It is also why hyperscalers can try PIM in their in-house chips
Are memory prices normal? Cycle vs. structural change The same question as discussion question 5 in Session 1. Here, though, there is one more piece of evidence — HBM eats into ordinary DRAM capacity, so a path exists by which AI demand reduces the supply of ordinary memory. This is a structure that past cycles did not have

Self-study appendix C — key terms

Term One-line definition
Bandwidth / capacity The amount moved per second / the amount held. The two axes to keep apart throughout this session
HBM (high bandwidth memory) Memory that stacks DRAM dies vertically and connects them through a wide bus
HBF (high bandwidth flash) A proposal to stack NAND the same way to reach high capacity. First standard specification released in August 2026; no volume products yet
CXL (Compute Express Link) An interconnect standard that keeps cache coherence between the CPU and devices on top of the PCIe physical layer. Used for server memory expansion and pooling
TSV (through-silicon via) Vertical wiring that runs through silicon
KGD (known good die) A good die verified before stacking
Microbump A tiny solder bump that joins one die to another
Hybrid bonding Joining copper to copper directly without bumps. Better in both pitch and thermal resistance. For HBM, as of October 2026, a candidate for the next generation
MR-MUF / TC-NCF (mass reflow molded underfill / thermal compression non-conductive film) The stacking methods of volume HBM. Fill and cure a liquid protective material all at once after stacking (SK hynix) vs. lay a film on each layer and thermocompression bond it (Samsung)
Interposer An intermediate substrate on which several dies sit and through which they are connected
Refresh Rewriting DRAM capacitors at a set interval before their charge leaks away. Caused by time, and different from the restore right after a read
Bank A group of cell arrays inside a DRAM die that can be opened and closed separately. The unit of internal parallel access
Channel A unit into which a memory interface is divided, each part operating independently. Bus width = number of channels × channel width (HBM4: 32 × 64 bits). Not the same thing as a mainframe I/O channel
pJ/bit (picojoule per bit) Energy to transfer 1 bit. The practical constraint on bandwidth design
PIM / PNM (processing in / near memory) Placing compute units inside / beside the memory
Stack yield The probability that the whole stack works. Falls steeply as yn
Memory tiering Placing data on different media according to access frequency

Session 4

Fabless, Foundry and the Value Chain

Key takeaway

The division of labor in the semiconductor industry (fabless, foundry, IDM, OSAT) is not a matter of taste but a consequence of its cost structure. As the cost of building a fab grew exponentially, manufacturing became an oligopoly of a few firms governed by economies of scale, while design became an asset-light field with many competitors. And nearly every economic judgment in this industry comes down to one formula: yield Y=e−AD0 — as die area grows, yield falls exponentially. This formula is the case for splitting chips into chiplets, the basis of how foundries price their work, and the reason advanced packaging exists (Session 6). "3nm process" is a marketing name, not a physical dimension. What you should compare is transistor density and cell structure.

Learning objectives

  1. Distinguish the roles of fabless companies, foundries, IDMs, OSATs and IP vendors, and how each makes money.
  2. Explain the whole chip-design pipeline by mapping it onto the software development process.
  3. Set up the Poisson yield model and calculate the number of good dies per wafer for different die sizes.
  4. Know which metrics you actually need to check behind the label "3nm."
  5. Decide quantitatively whether to develop an ASIC.

0. Self-study guide — for readers working alone

This session builds the second shared tool

If Session 2 built the roofline, this session builds the yield formula. The single line Y=e−AD0 governs all of Session 5 (why every process step has to be six sigma), Session 6 (why chiplets) and Session 7 (why supply does not grow). Do Exercises 1 and 2 by hand. Reading a table and putting numbers into the exponential yourself leave different things behind.

Prerequisite check

Concept One-line answer Needed for

If you have a statistics background: section 5 of this session is a rare case where the first chapter of an undergraduate probability course becomes an industry's cost structure as it stands. Exercise 3 (Poisson vs. negative binomial) reduces to one line of Jensen's inequality — see the solution in the appendix.

Reading order (110 minutes recommended)

Step Section Time Note

2 Section 5, the economics of yield 35 min The heart of this session. Do Exercises 1 and 2 right here

Never skip: the table "Getting a feel for the numbers" in section 5. Looking at that table, you should be able to explain from the properties of the exponential function why yield halves when area grows 16-fold.

A common sticking point — why the GDPW formula looks the way it does

GDPW≈πd2/4A−πd2A

There is nothing to fear here. Read the two terms separately.

  • First term = wafer area ÷ die area. Simply "how many fit."
  • Second term = a correction for edge loss. When you fill a disc with squares, some dies straddle the rim and get cut off. The second term estimates their number as wafer circumference ÷ die diagonal. If a square die has side A, its diagonal is 2A, which gives πd/2A. Take the side A as the denominator instead and the loss grows by a factor of 2; that one constant changes the result visibly (table below).

In short, "divide by area, then subtract what is thrown away at the rim" is all there is to it. The larger the die, the greater the weight of the second term — a big chip loses twice, once on yield and once at the rim.

This formula is an approximation too. Count directly and the difference shows. The conditions are a 300 mm wafer, square dies, zero edge exclusion and zero scribe-line width. Lay a grid of dies over the wafer and count only the dies whose four corners all fall inside the circle of radius 150 mm. We shifted the origin of the grid horizontally and vertically in steps of 1/20 of a side, counted at 400 positions, and took the mean and range. The result:

Die area Counted directly: mean (min–max) 2A formula A formula
100 mm² 647.8 (640–657) 640.2 (−1.2%) 612.6 (−5.4%)
400 mm² 147.8 (144–151) 143.4 (−3.0%) 129.6 (−12.3%)
800 mm² 68.2 (66–71) 64.8 (−5.0%) 55.0 (−19.3%)

The percentages in parentheses are differences from the directly counted mean. The 2A formula comes out 1–5% below the mean; the A formula, 5–19% below. The error grows with die size, and the count also depends on where the grid is placed (66 versus 71 at 800 mm²). Align one die corner with the wafer center and you get 648, 148 and 68 dies at 100, 400 and 800 mm², almost the same as the mean. A real wafer has edge exclusion and scribe lines, so even the directly counted values shrink below these. For a comparison of several approximation formulas, see de Vries (2005), doi:10.1109/TSM.2004.836656.

1. Getting the intuition — why design and manufacturing split apart

The explosion of fixed costs

The cost of making a chip comes in two lumps.

  • Fixed costs (NRE, non-recurring engineering): design labor, EDA tool licenses, IP licenses, the cost of making the mask set, verification and prototypes. Paid once, regardless of volume.
  • Variable costs: wafers, packaging, test. Paid per unit.

On top of these sits a far larger fixed cost: building the fab. One state-of-the-art fab costs tens of billions of dollars. To recover a fixed cost of that size, the fab has to run 24 hours a day with enormous volumes flowing through it.

Conclusion: no company can fill a fab with its own chips alone. So two paths emerged.

  1. IDM (integrated device manufacturer): when a company's own product volume is large enough (as with memory, standard products made in bulk). Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, Micron, Intel.
  2. The foundry–fabless division of labor: gather the designs of many companies and fill one fab with them. TSMC established this model.

Economics frame: an industry with large fixed costs and low marginal costs tends toward natural monopoly. Semiconductor manufacturing adds a learning curve (yield rises as cumulative output grows) on top, so the leader keeps gaining ground. What keeps latecomers from catching up is capital, and beyond capital, accumulated experience.

2. The players and their roles

Type What it does Representative firms Characteristics
Fabless Design only; manufacturing is outsourced NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Qualcomm, Apple, MediaTek Asset-light, high margins, fierce competition
Foundry Manufacturing only; no design TSMC, Samsung Foundry, Intel Foundry, GlobalFoundries, UMC, SMIC Extremely high fixed costs; keeping customer secrets is everything
Design house (design services) Implements and verifies a fabless company's logical design physically for a particular foundry process; sometimes also handles manufacturing, assembly and test on the client's behalf Each foundry has an accredited partner network. TSMC has the DCA (Design Center Alliance, chip implementation services) and the VCA (Value Chain Alliance) inside OIP; Samsung has the Design Service Alliance (DSP, VDP) inside SAFE™ Works to the process and IP of the foundry it partners with. The route by which system companies and start-ups reach volume production
IDM Design + manufacturing Samsung, SK hynix, Micron, Intel, TI Common in memory and analog
OSAT Outsourced packaging and test ASE, Amkor, JCET, PTI Traditionally low value-added, but rising in standing with advanced packaging
IP vendor Licenses design blocks Arm, Synopsys, Cadence, Imagination Royalty model
EDA Design automation tools Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens EDA Three-firm oligopoly, extremely high barriers to entry
Equipment Manufacturing tools ASML, Applied Materials, Lam Research, TEL, KLA Effectively an oligopoly or monopoly in each process
Materials Wafers, gases, photoresist and more Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, JSR, TOK, Linde Large share held by Japanese firms

Where the boundaries blur (2026)

  • Memory makers need logic processes — the HBM4 base die is made on a logic foundry process. In April 2024, when SK hynix signed a memorandum of understanding with TSMC on HBM4, it announced that it "plans to adopt TSMC's advanced logic process for HBM4's base die" and that the two companies "will first focus on improving the performance of the base die." Collaboration between memory makers and foundries becomes a necessity.
  • Foundries expand into packaging — TSMC's CoWoS and SoIC. Foundries are absorbing territory that traditionally belonged to OSATs. The reason is plain: advanced packaging decides performance, so it has to be optimized together with the front end.
  • Hyperscalers become fabless companies — Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft design their own chips. Most of them, though, work with design partners such as Broadcom and Marvell.
  • IDMs open foundries — Intel Foundry, Samsung Foundry. The question of trust (can you hand your design to a competitor?) is a structural problem.

3. The chip-design pipeline — mapped onto software development

Mapping table

Chip-design stage Software counterpart What it does What physically exists at that stage
Specification (architecture) System design Sets performance, power and area (PPA) targets Documents
RTL design (Verilog/VHDL) Writing source code Describes behavior at the register-transfer level Code files
Functional verification (simulation, formal) Testing, CI Checks that the logic is correct Simulation result files
Logic synthesis Compiling RTL → gate-level netlist of standard cells Netlist file
Place and route (P&R) Linking + layout optimization Puts cells in real positions and wires them Layout data
Timing/power/signal verification (STA etc.) Profiling, optimization Does each signal arrive within the clock period? Verification reports
DRC / LVS Lint + static analysis Checks for manufacturing-rule violations and layout-versus-schematic agreement Layout data that has passed verification
Tape-out Release (irreversible) Hands the data over for mask making One set of layout files. Still nothing but data
Mask making Producing distribution media A mask set for a leading-edge node costs on the order of tens of millions of dollars and takes weeks The first physical object — a bundle of photomasks for the process layers (the mask set)
Wafer fabrication Running the build Takes months Wafers with the circuits patterned on them
Wafer test (EDS/probe) Integration testing Pass/fail judgment per die, repair A wafer with pass/fail recorded for each die (wafer map)
Packaging and final test Packaging, deployment Session 6 Cut dies → chips in packages

Read the fourth column from top to bottom: until tape-out, the chip exists only as files. What goes to the foundry at tape-out is a layout file, and the long-standing format is the GDSII stream. SEMI has standardized OASIS (SEMI P39) as its successor format. This column is why the software analogy ends at tape-out. Below that line, fixing anything means making the object again.

Two ways it differs decisively from software

  1. There are no hotfixes. If a bug turns up after tape-out, you remake the masks (a respin) and spend months and tens of millions of dollars again. That is why verification takes more than half of the total development effort. "The cost of one bug" differs from software by orders of magnitude.
  2. Physics intervenes. The same RTL can perform very differently depending on the result of place and route. Timing closure (making every path meet the clock period) is the main pain of late development.

There is one more place where the "RTL = source code" analogy breaks. RTL statements are not instructions executed from top to bottom; they describe circuits that exist at the same time. Three assign statements do not add three times; they place three adders side by side, and an if is not a branch but becomes a multiplexer that picks one of two inputs. What people coming from software most often get wrong is the nonblocking assignment (<=).

always @(posedge clk) begin
  q1 <= d;
  q2 <= q1;
end

Suppose that just before the clock edge d = 1, q1 = 0 and q2 = 0. Read as top-to-bottom execution, q1 and q2 should both be 1 after the clock. In fact q1 = 1 and q2 = 0. A nonblocking assignment reads all the right-hand values first at the clock instant and then updates the left-hand sides together (the nonblocking procedural assignment provisions of IEEE Std 1364-2005; that standard has since been superseded by IEEE Std 1800, SystemVerilog). Swapping the two lines gives the same result. This code is not two instructions but a picture of a two-stage shift register made of two flip-flops in a row.

PDKs and standard cells — the abstraction layer

The foundry supplies a PDK (process design kit). It contains the design rules (DRC rules), device models (SPICE parameters) and a standard-cell library (the layouts and timing characteristics of basic blocks such as NAND gates and flip-flops).

Why this is decisive: thanks to the PDK, a fabless company can design without knowing semiconductor physics. It plays exactly the role of an API/ABI in software. And as with an API, a design made for one PDK does not carry over to another foundry as it is. The standard cells and design rules change, so everything from synthesis through place and route, timing closure and DRC/LVS has to be run again, and a new mask set has to be made. This porting cost is the real barrier to switching foundries, and it is where TSMC's ecosystem advantage comes from.

This ecosystem is a named institution. TSMC groups its partners into alliances under OIP (Open Innovation Platform®). When the Cloud Alliance was added as the fifth in October 2018, the lineup was EDA, IP, Design Center, VCA (then called Value Chain Aggregator, now Value Chain Alliance) and Cloud; in October 2022 the 3DFabric Alliance (advanced packaging and 3D IC) was formed as the sixth. Samsung Foundry does the same thing through its SAFE™ program. It bundles certified PDKs, design methodologies and IP, and runs IP, EDA, Cloud, Design Service, Multi-Die Integration (MDI) and OSAT alliances (checked October 2026). From the customer's side, choosing a foundry is not choosing one process but choosing this whole partner network.

4. The truth about "3nm" — how to read node names

What it is not

Node names once referred to a real physical dimension such as gate length. Since FinFET they have become marketing names that correspond to no physical dimension at all. Different companies' "3nm" processes differ in density and performance, and even across generations at the same company the name does not track the performance gain directly.

Then what should you look at?

Metric Meaning
Transistor density (MTr/mm²) Millions of transistors per square millimeter. The most direct comparison metric, though it varies with the logic/SRAM mix
CPP (contacted poly pitch) Spacing between gates
MMP (minimum metal pitch) Minimum wiring pitch
Cell height (number of tracks) The height of a standard cell counted in the horizontal routing tracks that run through it (in units of the minimum metal pitch). The T in 6T and 5T stands for track. It is a different word from the T in the 6T SRAM of Session 3 (six transistors)
PPA improvement Gains in performance, power and area over the previous node. Always check the conditions behind vendor figures
SRAM cell area Especially important lately. SRAM does not scale as well as logic, so chips with large caches gain little from a new node

What matters more for AI accelerators: AI chip performance depends more on memory bandwidth and packaging than on the node. Attaching one more HBM stack can affect performance more than being one node generation ahead.

Foundry Node Transistor structure Backside power delivery Status

Production was planned for 2026 at the time of the April 2024 announcement; according to a TSMC executive's remarks reported from the April 2026 technology symposium, volume production is expected to begin in 2027. checked 2026-10-22) Volume production began in Q4 2025.
