The contrast to watch: Intel chose the aggressive strategy of introducing GAA and backside power delivery at the same time; TSMC chose the conservative one of stabilizing GAA first and pushing backside power delivery to the next node. This is not a difference in technical superiority but a difference in risk-budgeting strategy. It makes a good discussion topic.

5. The economics of yield — this book's second key tool

The Poisson model

Assume that defects land on the wafer at random (spatially independent and uniform). If the average density of killer defects per unit area is D0 [defects/cm²] and the die area is A [cm²], the number of defects landing on one die follows a Poisson distribution with mean λ=AD0. The probability of no defect at all, that is, the yield, is

Y=P(X=0)=e−AD0

For statistics majors: this is just the P(X=0) of a Poisson distribution. One of the pleasures of this field is that semiconductor yield theory starts from the first chapter of undergraduate probability.

Where the formula comes from — cutting the die into cells. Divide the die into n small cells of equal area, and let the probability of a defect landing in each cell be p=λ/n. If the cells are independent, the probability that the die is clean is the probability that every cell is clean, and as you cut the cells ever finer this becomes the high-school limit limn→∞(1+x/n)n=ex with x=−λ.

P(0 defects)=(1−λn)n⟶e−λ(n→∞)

Calculating, for λ=0.8 you get 0.4344 at n=10, 0.4479 at n=100 and 0.4492 at n=1,000, while the limit e−0.8 is 0.4493. Splitting into just ten cells already reaches 97% of the answer.

Show

General k — the limit of the binomial. The probability that defects land in exactly k of the n cells is binomial. Write it as four factors.

P(X=k)=(nk)(λn)k(1−λn)n−k=λkk!·n(n−1)⋯(n−k+1)nk·(1−λn)n·(1−λn)−k

Fix k and let n→∞; the last three factors go to 1, e−λ and 1. What remains is P(X=k)=e−λλk/k!, the Poisson distribution. This result, that the count of a rare event spread over very many opportunities follows a Poisson distribution, is called the law of rare events. With k=0 the first, second and fourth factors all become 1, and only the third is left, which is the formula in the text.

Numerically, for λ=0.8 and k=1 the binomial probability is 0.3777 at n=10, 0.3612 at n=100 and 0.3596 at n=1,000, and the Poisson value is 0.3595 (calculated).

Getting a feel for the numbers

With D0=0.1 defects/cm² (an illustrative value at the level of a mature process):

Die area λ=AD0 Yield e−λ
50 mm² (0.5 cm²) 0.05 95.1%
100 mm² 0.10 90.5%
200 mm² 0.20 81.9%
400 mm² 0.40 67.0%
600 mm² 0.60 54.9%
800 mm² (near the reticle limit) 0.80 44.9%

When area grows 16-fold, yield falls below half. And because a large die also fits fewer times on a wafer, the number of good dies falls much more steeply.

Good dies per wafer

The area of a 300mm wafer is about π×152=706 cm². There are several approximation formulas for gross die per wafer that account for edge loss; a common one is

GDPW≈πd2/4A−πd2A

(d = wafer diameter, A = die area. The second term is the edge-loss correction: the wafer circumference divided by the die diagonal 2A. The comparison showing that this formula comes out 1–5% below the directly counted number for 100–800 mm² dies is in "A common sticking point" in section 0.)

Good dies = GDPW × Y, and cost per die = wafer price / number of good dies.

Exercise: with the price of one wafer as W, find the ratio of cost per die for die areas of 100 mm² and 800 mm². The area ratio is 8, but the cost ratio comes out much larger.

Why the Poisson model is wrong — defect clustering

Real defects do not scatter independently; they cluster (particle contamination, tool faults, wafer-edge effects). With clustering, the Poisson model underestimates yield, because when defects crowd onto a few dies, the remaining dies stay clean.

Alternative models

Model Formula Assumption
Poisson Y=e−AD0 Completely random
Murphy Y=(1−e−AD0AD0)2 Defect density has a triangular distribution
Exponential (Seeds) Y=11+AD0 Defect density has an exponential distribution
Negative binomial Y=(1+AD0α)−α Defect density has a gamma distribution → reflects clustering

In the negative binomial model, α is the clustering parameter: as α→∞ it converges to Poisson, and the smaller α, the heavier the clustering. That a gamma–Poisson mixture becomes a negative binomial is a familiar result in statistics, and the semiconductor yield model has exactly that structure. If the defect density D follows a gamma distribution with mean D0, its variance is D02/α. α=1 means the standard deviation of the defect density equals its mean (the integral is in the solution to Exercise 3). The memory yield model IBM published in 1980 was also a mixture model that shook the Poisson mean (Stapper et al., 1980).

Going deeper: this section is where someone trained in statistics can most comfortably dig deeper. In real fabs, spatial statistics and machine learning are applied to wafer-map data (which dies at which positions failed) to classify defect patterns and trace them back to the tool that caused them. This connects to the inspection and metrology section of Session 5.

A is not the whole die area — critical area. Not every defect that lands causes a failure. A particle that falls between two wires does not short them unless it is big enough to touch both, and one that lands where there is no circuit does nothing. So strictly, the A in λ=AD0 is not the die area but the critical area: the area of the places where a defect of that size would break the circuit. On the same die, the larger the defect, the larger the critical area, and densely wired blocks have more of it. IBM's memory yield model (Stapper et al., 1980) described the product by this critical area and the process by the defect density, separately. When this book calls D0 the "killer defect density" and uses the die area as it is, that is a simplification that absorbs the effect of critical area into the density.

What yield explains

  1. Why chiplets — making four 200 mm² dies (82% each) separately, testing them, and binding only the good ones (KGD) is far better than one 800 mm² die (45% yield). Bind the four without sorting and the finished-product yield is (e−0.2)4=e−0.8≈45%, the same as the single die (the multiplicative yield of Session 3). The gain comes not from cutting the die smaller but from throwing out the bad ones before assembly so that only good silicon is used. The cost of joining them and the assembly yield are added, however. That profit-and-loss calculation is the core of Session 6.
  2. Why foundries sell by the wafer — it is a question of who bears the yield risk. Under a per-wafer contract the fabless company bears it; under a per-good-die contract the foundry does. The newer the node, the more the foundry prefers per-wafer terms.
  3. Why new nodes are expensive — early on, D0 is high. Over time it comes down along the learning curve (yield learning). This is the structural advantage of the front-runner.
  4. Why binning is done — binning comes in two kinds.
    • Defect binning. Some defects leave the chip usable if the affected core is disabled. Selling an 8-core design as a 6-core product is a strategy for recovering yield. Defects can also be repaired. Memory keeps spare rows and columns and swaps the defective lines for spares (repair), and chips that work only in part are sometimes sold separately. IBM, reporting the yield trend of its 64K-bit RAM, also presented the yield gains it obtained from redundant circuits and partially good products (Stapper et al., 1982). The redundant circuits of HBM in Session 3 work on the same principle.
    • Speed and power binning. Even among defect-free dies, process variation makes the maximum operating frequency and power differ. So each die is tested for its maximum frequency and graded. This is a matter of parametric yield, which e−AD0, a formula that counts defects, cannot explain. Where defect binning deals with "how many are alive," speed binning deals with "how fast the living ones are."

6. ASIC, FPGA or general-purpose processor — a quantitative choice

Break-even (a refinement of the formula from Session 2)

N*=CNRE(cG+oG)−(cA+oA)

  • c: unit acquisition cost; o: present value of lifetime operating cost (mainly electricity)
  • As in Session 2, assume one ASIC replaces the work of one GPU 1:1. If throughput differs, N has to be converted into the number of units that handle the same demand
  • cA is calculated from the cost per die in section 5 above + packaging + test

Trade-offs on five axes

Development time NRE Unit cost Power efficiency Flexibility
General-purpose CPU/GPU 0 (purchase) 0 High Low Highest
FPGA Months Low Very high Low to medium Reconfigurable
Structured ASIC About 1 year Medium Medium Medium Limited
Full-custom ASIC 2–3 years Very high Low Highest None

The trap on the time axis

Even with enough volume to clear N*, it is no use if the period over which that chip handles that volume is short. If model architectures change substantially every two years and chip development takes two to three years, the computation pattern the chip targeted must still dominate when it is finished.

Why hyperscalers can take this risk

  1. Their volume N is overwhelming.
  2. They control their own workloads. Being able to design the model to fit the chip is decisive.
  3. The total savings on electricity are large (at data center scale). Per unit, it is mainly the difference in acquisition price that decides the break-even count, and the difference in electricity cost amounts to only a few percent to a dozen-odd percent (solution to Exercise 4 in Session 2, solution to Exercise 5 in this session); but run tens of thousands of units for several years and that share also becomes a large sum.
  4. There is option value in bargaining power with vendors.
  5. They have the capital to absorb a failure.

Why most companies do not: none of the five holds for them.

7. Common misconceptions

Misconception 1: "TSMC also designs chips" → The core of the pure-play foundry model is the trust that it does not compete with its customers. It offers IP blocks and packaging services but does not design finished chips. This neutrality is a large part of TSMC's success.

Misconception 2: "A more advanced node makes a faster chip" → For AI accelerators, memory and packaging can matter more. And the node name itself is not a comparable metric.

Misconception 3: "Yield converges to 100% as a process matures" → Inside the Poisson formula, that is right. Whatever the area, e−AD0→1 as D0→0. The trouble is that D0 never goes all the way to 0. At the same D0, yield falls exponentially with die size, so even on a mature process a large die stays at a lower yield than a small one (an 800 mm² die is at 67.0% even with D0=0.05). On top of that, parametric losses that are not counted as defects (speed and power binning in section 5) remain outside the formula. And a new node always starts again from low yield.

Misconception 4: "A fabless company doesn't need to know manufacturing" → The PDK abstracts it away, but high-performance design has to take process characteristics (variability, electromigration, heat) deeply into account. That is why DFM (design for manufacturability) exists as a field of its own.

Misconception 5: "An OSAT is a low-value-added subcontractor" → Its standing has risen sharply now that advanced packaging decides performance. The leading edge, however, is being absorbed by foundries, so the OSAT's position is in flux.

Misconception 6: "EDA is just CAD software" → Place and route and timing optimization are large-scale combinatorial optimization problems, and reinforcement learning and graph neural networks are now actually being applied to them. This is the most direct point of entry for people trained in CS and AI.

8. Quantitative exercises

Exercise 1 — Yield curves For each of D0=0.05,0.1,0.2, plot the yield curve over die areas of 50–800 mm². From what area does yield drop sharply?

Exercise 2 — Cost per die With the price of a 300mm wafer as W, find the cost per die for die areas of 100 / 400 / 800 mm² as multiples of W. Apply both the GDPW approximation and the yield.

Exercise 3 — Poisson vs. negative binomial For the same AD0, compare the yields of the Poisson model and the negative binomial (α=1,2,5). Confirm that the heavier the clustering, the more the actual yield exceeds the Poisson prediction, and explain why in probabilistic terms.

Exercise 4 — Chiplet profit and loss (preview of Session 6) Compare a single 800 mm² die with four 200 mm² chiplets. On the chiplet side, include (a) a 10% area overhead for the interface circuits between chiplets, (b) an assembly yield of 95% and (c) the added cost of the interposer and assembly. Take (c) as the cost loaded onto one finished product (including the share of failed assembly attempts). Which side wins? Is there a point where changing D0 reverses the conclusion?

Exercise 5 — The ASIC decision Assumptions: NRE USD 150 million, ASIC unit cost USD 4,000, commercial GPU unit cost USD 30,000, three-year electricity cost USD 2,000 for the ASIC and USD 6,000 for the GPU. Find N*, and discuss which organizations could realistically reach that volume.

9. Discussion questions

  1. Can the foundry–fabless division of labor be reversed? Which direction does each of Intel's IDM 2.0 strategy and hyperscalers' vertical integration point in?
  2. Between the risk-budgeting strategies of Intel (GAA and backside power at once) and TSMC (GAA first, backside power later), which is rational? Under what conditions is each right?
  3. Yield data are trade secrets. What observable proxies could be used to estimate yield from outside? (Prices, lead times, product lineups, binning structure, etc.)
  4. Why does the three-firm EDA oligopoly not break? Could open-source EDA (OpenROAD and others) and open PDKs change that?
  5. Now that node names have lost their physical meaning, why does the industry keep using that naming scheme? Is there an alternative?

10. Further study

  • Standard VLSI design textbook: Weste & Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective — sets out models of yield, area and power
  • Yield theory: Stapper's papers on the IBM yield model — Stapper, McLaren, Dreckmann, "Yield Model for Productivity Optimization of VLSI Memory Chips with Redundancy and Partially Good Product," IBM J. Res. Dev. 24(3):398–409 (1980), doi:10.1147/rd.243.0398 · Stapper et al., "Evolution and Accomplishments of VLSI Yield Management at IBM," IBM J. Res. Dev. 26(5):532–545 (1982), doi:10.1147/rd.265.0532. For a comparison of several yield models, Cunningham, "The Use and Evaluation of Yield Models in Integrated Circuit Manufacturing," IEEE Trans. Semiconductor Manufacturing 3(2):60–71 (1990), doi:10.1109/66.53188
  • GDPW approximations: de Vries, "Investigation of Gross Die Per Wafer Formulas," IEEE Trans. Semiconductor Manufacturing 18(1):136–139 (2005), doi:10.1109/TSM.2004.836656 — worth reading after you have worked out the table in section 0 yourself
  • Try it yourself: Tiny Tapeout — a project that lets you put your own design on a real chip for a small fee. The best way for someone with a CS background to feel the tape-out pipeline firsthand
  • Open toolchain: OpenLane / OpenROAD + SkyWater 130nm open PDK — lets you run from RTL to GDS for free
  • AI × EDA: Mirhoseini et al., "A graph placement methodology for fast chip design," Nature 594 (2021), doi:10.1038/s41586-021-03544-w — placement based on reinforcement learning. The paper's reproducibility was disputed, so read the later rebuttals and replies along with it
  • Industry structure: IR materials and technology-symposium presentations from TSMC, Intel and Samsung — TSMC quarterly results · Intel press releases

Self-study appendix A — solutions to the quantitative exercises

Solutions to the exercises in section 8. All areas are converted to cm² before being plugged in (100 mm² = 1 cm²).

Solution to Exercise 1 — Yield curves

SolutionSolution

Y=e−AD0.

Die area D0=0.05 D0=0.1 D0=0.2
50 mm² 97.5% 95.1% 90.5%
100 mm² 95.1% 90.5% 81.9%
200 mm² 90.5% 81.9% 67.0%
400 mm² 81.9% 67.0% 44.9%
600 mm² 74.1% 54.9% 30.1%
800 mm² 67.0% 44.9% 20.2%

How to answer "from what area does it drop sharply"

An exponential has no separate knee. Fix a reference line instead, and a clean formula comes out. The area at which yield is 50% is

Y=0.5⇒A50=ln2D0=0.693D0 cm2

D0 A50
0.05 1,386 mm² (larger than the reticle limit — by the 50% criterion, the exposure area blocks you first. Even at the reticle limit of 858 mm², yield is 65.1%, so the effect on cost remains)
0.1 693 mm²
0.2 347 mm²

How to read it: when D0 doubles, the die area allowed at the same target yield (here 50%) halves. 50% is only a reference line chosen for the explanation; chips larger than this area can still be made. Their cost simply rises as yield falls. A high D0 early in a new node means it is hard to make large chips at an affordable cost, and this is both the structural advantage of the leading foundry and one of the reasons large AI accelerators cannot move to the newest node right away. The largest size that can actually be made is set not by yield but by the reticle limit.

Solution to Exercise 2 — Cost per die

SolutionSolution

Set d=30 cm and D0=0.1, and apply both GDPW and yield.

GDPW≈π·900/4A−π·302A=706.9A−94.252A

Die area GDPW Yield Good dies Cost per die
100 mm² (1 cm²) 640.2 0.905 579.3 0.00173W
400 mm² (4 cm²) 143.4 0.670 96.1 0.01040W
800 mm² (8 cm²) 64.8 0.449 29.1 0.03435W

Worked example (800 mm²): 706.9/8=88.36, 94.25/16=23.56, GDPW =64.80. Good dies =64.80×0.4493=29.1. Cost =W/29.1.

Key result

0.034350.00173≈19.9×

The area is 8 times larger, but the cost is 20 times larger. It is the product of three things — 8 times from area, 2.0 times from yield and 1.2 times from edge loss.

Implications

  • The silicon cost of one 800 mm²-class AI accelerator equals that of twenty 100 mm²-class chips. The accurate statement is not "big chips are expensive" but "chips get superlinearly more expensive with area."
  • This superlinearity is the economic driver of chiplets. If the same total area can be split into small pieces, cost drops sharply. Exercise 4 calculates this.
  • Here you can actually fill in the cA of Exercise 4 in Session 2. Put one wafer at USD 15,000 and the silicon cost alone of an 800 mm² die is about USD 515, with HBM, packaging and test on top.

The figure below shows a die area of 800 mm², defect density D0=0.1, and a layout with a die corner aligned to the wafer center. In the screen edition you can change the die area, grid position, D0, wafer price and defect model and watch how the directly counted number, the two approximation formulas, the yield and the cost per die move. The defect dots in the figure are one random sample; the yield and cost in the readout are calculated from the formulas.

Solution to Exercise 3 — Poisson vs. negative binomial

SolutionSolution

Fix λ=AD0=0.8 (800 mm², D0=0.1) and compare.

Model Formula Yield
Poisson e−0.8 44.93%
Negative binomial α=5 (1+0.16)−5 47.61%
Negative binomial α=2 (1+0.40)−2 51.02%
Negative binomial α=1 (1+0.80)−1 55.56%

The heavier the clustering (the smaller α), the higher the yield, even though the total expected number of defects is exactly the same.

The probabilistic explanation — one line of Jensen's inequality

Suppose the defect density itself varies from wafer to wafer. That is, Λ is a random variable with E[Λ]=λ. The yield is the average of the conditional Poisson P(X=0), so

Y=E[e−Λ]≥e−E[Λ]=e−λ

Because e−x is a convex function, Jensen's inequality always holds in this direction. The more defects cluster (the larger the variance), the higher the yield must be relative to the Poisson prediction.

Set Λ~Gamma(α,λ/α) and the expectation above is exactly the moment-generating function of the gamma distribution, whose value is (1+λ/α)−α — the negative binomial yield formula. As α→∞ the variance goes to 0 and it converges to Poisson.

Writing out the integral. Let the defect density D follow a gamma distribution with mean D0 and shape parameter α, and average the conditional yield e−AD over its density.

Y=∫0∞e−AD(α/D0)αΓ(α)Dα−1e−αD/D0dD=(α/D0)α(A+α/D0)α=(1+AD0α)−α

The middle step plugs c=A+α/D0 into the definition of the gamma function, ∫0∞Dα−1e−cDdD=Γ(α)/cα. The variance of this gamma distribution is as follows.

Var(D)=D02α

With this formula you can read α as a number rather than under the name "clustering parameter." At α=1 the standard deviation of the defect density equals its mean; at α=5 it is about 45% of the mean (1/5).

Checking numerically (calculated): at D0=0.1 and A=8, the numerical value of the integral above and the closed form agree at 0.555556, 0.510204 and 0.476113 for α=1,2,5, and the variances are 0.01, 0.005 and 0.002, equal to D02/α. These are the negative binomial yields in the table above.

Intuition: if 100 defects are spread evenly over the whole wafer, almost every die gets hit once. If the same 100 crowd onto 10 dies, all the rest are clean. Yield is a question not of "how many defects there are" but of "how many dies are contaminated."

Practical implication: using Poisson estimates yield conservatively (low). That is why fabs estimate α from actual wafer-map data, and the classification of those wafer-map patterns is where machine learning comes in, in the inspection and metrology section of Session 5.

The figure below shows a die split into 10 cells at λ=0.8, and a comparison of Poisson and negative binomial (α=2) for an 800 mm² die at D0=0.1. In the screen edition you can change the number of cells, λ, the die area, D0 and α. The two small grids on the right are a sample with the same number of defects scattered evenly and a sample scattered according to a density shaken by a gamma.

Solution to Exercise 4 — Chiplet profit and loss (preview of Session 6)

SolutionSolution

A single 800 mm² die vs. four 200 mm² chiplets. D0=0.1, interface overhead 10%, assembly yield 95%.

Single die: 0.03435W from Exercise 2 above

Chiplets: 10% overhead on each 200 mm² → 220 mm² = 2.2 cm²

  • GDPW =706.9/2.2−94.25/4.4=321.3−44.93=276.4
  • Yield =e−0.22=0.8025 → good dies =221.8
  • Per chiplet W/221.8=0.004509W; for four, 0.018035W (the KGD assumption that only good chiplets are used. Dividing by the number of good dies to get the cost means exactly that)
  • Dividing by the assembly yield of 0.95 gives 0.018984W

Savings =0.03435−0.018984=0.01536W

Verdict: the chiplets win if the added interposer and assembly cost per finished product is less than about 1.5% of the price of a wafer (0.01536 W). With a wafer at USD 15,000, that means a margin of about USD 230 per system.

If the added cost is incurred at every assembly attempt, the share of failed attempts is also divided by 0.95, and the cost of a finished product becomes (4c+C)/0.95. The threshold is then C<0.95×0.03435−0.018035=0.01459W, about USD 219 per attempt, slightly lower. Whichever basis you use, the direction of the conclusion is the same.

Where the conclusion flips — changing D0

D0 Single Four chiplets Savings Verdict
0.02 0.01811W 0.01592W 0.0022W Reverses once assembly cost exceeds just 0.22% of the wafer price
0.1 0.03435W 0.01898W 0.0154W Chiplets ahead

What to read from this example: the cost advantage of chiplets is larger the worse the yield. Under the conditions of the same wafer price, the same D0, a four-way split, 10% overhead and 95% assembly yield, the advantage shrinks quickly as the process matures and D0 falls. This fits the fact that chiplets were adopted first for the newest nodes and large-area chips. But the reasons for using chiplets also include area beyond the reticle limit, heterogeneous integration that uses a different process for each block, and design reuse (Session 6), so this one calculation cannot settle where chiplets are and are not used.

In Exercise 1 of Session 6, the number of pieces n becomes a free variable and the optimum is found. To give away the result — the optimal number of pieces shifts with D0.

The same calculation can be done with this exercise's assumptions in the figure at the end of the solution to Exercise 1 in Session 6 (screen edition).

Solution to Exercise 5 — The ASIC decision

SolutionSolution

NRE USD 150 million, ASIC USD 4,000, GPU USD 30,000, three-year electricity cost USD 2,000 and USD 6,000 respectively.

N*=1.5×108(30,000+6,000)−(4,000+2,000)=1.5×10830,000=5,000 units

Organizations for which this volume is realistic

Type of organization Units deployed over 3 years Verdict
Hyperscaler Hundreds of thousands Far above — an in-house chip is rational
Large AI lab Tens of thousands Above — but the risk of workload change is large
In-house AI infrastructure at a large company Hundreds to thousands Borderline. Usually below
Ordinary companies, research institutes Dozens Clearly below

The structural implication for the industry

A threshold of 5,000 units is lower than you might expect. So operators that are "almost hyperscaler-class" can consider custom silicon even if they are not hyperscalers, and the businesses that take on this demand are custom-ASIC design services such as Broadcom and Marvell. The structural reason for their recent rapid rise lies in this calculation.

But the warning from Exercise 4 in Session 2 applies in full. N* is only a necessary condition. The sufficient condition is that the workload still be alive two to three years later, after development, and the only organizations that can guarantee this are those that control their own models.

The figure below uses the assumed values of Exercise 5 (NRE USD 150 million, ASIC USD 4,000, GPU USD 30,000, three-year electricity USD 2,000 / USD 6,000). In the screen edition you can change the five values and see which organization size in the table above N* falls into. Section 6 defined o as the present value of operating cost but did not fix a discount rate, so the figure uses the three-year electricity cost undiscounted. The boundaries of the organization bands translate the table's "dozens, hundreds to thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of units" into orders of magnitude.

Self-study appendix B — leads for the discussion questions

Question Key axis Leads
1. Can the division of labor be reversed? Capital intensity The division happened because fab investment exceeded the demand of any single company. Reversing it would require one company's demand to be large enough to fill a fab — and hyperscalers' AI demand is actually approaching that scale. This is the basis for the return of vertical integration, and its logic runs in a different direction from Intel's IDM 2.0
2. Risk budgeting for GAA and backside power Serial vs. parallel risk What can be observed: introduce two changes at once, and when something goes wrong it is hard to tell which one caused it, and a delay in either one pushes back the whole schedule. Doing them in sequence keeps that risk small but takes more time. A hypothesis for discussion: the one behind has an incentive to go simultaneous to catch up, and the one ahead has an incentive to go sequential to hold its place. Whether the hypothesis is right has to be weighed against the probability of success of each choice, the losses a delay causes and the reward for the leading position, and those values are not set here
3. Observable proxies for yield Prices carry information Lead times, binning structure (a large share of lower SKUs signals low yield), the speed of price cuts, early volumes of new products, the form of the foundry contract (per wafer or per good die — see section 5). The form of the contract is the most honest signal
4. Why the EDA oligopoly does not break The value of what has been proven The cost of switching tools is not the price of the tool but the cost of re-verification. Would you print a mask set worth tens of millions of dollars on the strength of a new tool's verification results alone? Open-source EDA cannot skip this accumulation of trust
5. Why keep using node names? The name as a coordination device Though they have no physical meaning, they still work as a common coordinate for naming generations. The alternatives (density metrics, performance and power metrics) are more accurate but do not compress into a single number, which makes them hard to use in marketing and contract negotiations

Self-study appendix C — key terms

Term One-line definition
Defect density D0 Number of killer defects per unit area [defects/cm²]
Critical area The area of the places where a defect of a given size would break the circuit. Larger for larger defects
Die One chip cut from a wafer
GDPW (gross die per wafer) The total number of dies from one wafer (before yield is applied)
Good die A die that works correctly. GDPW × yield
Poisson yield model Y=e−AD0. Assumes defects are completely random
Negative binomial (yield model) Y=(1+AD0/α)−α. Reflects clustering
Clustering parameter α The smaller it is, the more defects cluster. Poisson at ∞
Yield learning The process by which D0 comes down over time
Binning Sorting dies into grades for sale. There is defect binning, which disables bad cores and sells the die as a lower product, and speed and power binning, which grades dies by maximum frequency and power
Chiplet Making a large chip as several small dies and joining them
Reticle limit The largest area a lithography tool exposes in one shot (about 26×33 mm)
NRE (non-recurring engineering) One-time cost of development
Structured ASIC An intermediate form that customizes only some layers to lower NRE
IDM (integrated device manufacturer) A semiconductor company that both designs and manufactures
PDK (process design kit) The bundle of process-specific design rules and models a foundry supplies
Track The slot for one horizontal wire running through a standard cell. Cell height is counted in tracks (6T and 5T cells). Not the same T (transistor) as in 6T SRAM

Session 5

Front-End Processing

Key takeaway

The eight major front-end processes are not a list to memorize but a single repeating loop: "draw a pattern → add or remove material → planarize → inspect." Repeated layer after layer, this loop becomes hundreds of steps. Lithography sits at its center, and lithography comes down to one equation, the Rayleigh criterion CD=k1λ/NA. Shorten the wavelength, enlarge the numerical aperture, or shrink the process factor. The whole history of semiconductor scaling is the history of attacking these three terms. Why transistors went from planar to FinFET to GAA also fits in one sentence: as channels grew shorter, the gate lost its grip, and the only remedy was to increase the area over which the gate wraps the channel.

Primary sources

Samsung Semiconductor Newsroom, "Eight Major Semiconductor Processes, Part 1: The Wafer" (in Korean) · Samsung Semiconductor, "Eight Major Semiconductor Processes, Part 2: Oxidation, Which Protects the Wafer Surface" (in Korean) · Samsung Semiconductor Newsroom, "Eight Major Semiconductor Processes, Part 6: Deposition and Ion Implantation" (in Korean) · ETRI, Electronics and Telecommunications Trends vol. 38 no. 6, "Complementary FET—The Future of the Semiconductor Transistor" (in Korean) · ScienceON JAKO202509150403114, "EUV lithography Technology Process Trends and Research Prospects" (in Korean) · ScienceON JAKO201326940561717, "Atomic Layer Deposition: Overview and Applications" (in Korean) · ASML, "5 things you should know about High NA EUV lithography" (2024) · van Schoot et al. (ASML, ZEISS), "High-NA EUV lithography enabling Moore's law in the next decade," EUVL Workshop 2017 · TSMC press release (2019-10-07), N7+ EUV in volume production · Deal & Grove (1965), doi:10.1063/1.1713945

Learning objectives

  1. Recast the eight major front-end processes not as a list of separate items but as one repeating loop.
  2. Explain the three terms of the Rayleigh criterion and describe how the industry attacked each one.
  3. Explain why the moves to FinFET and GAA were physically unavoidable.
  4. Explain the physical difficulties of EUV (reflective optics, the light source, stochastic defects).
  5. Tell apart which physical quantity each process controls.

0. Self-study guide — for readers working alone

This is the longest and most physical session

If the four sessions before it were about "how much," this one is about "how." Do not be put off by the length. The only genuinely hard part is section 4 (lithography); the rest either prepares you for section 4 or follows from it. If time is short, reading sections 3 and 4 alone gets you 80 percent of this session.

What you bring from earlier sessions

From earlier sessions In this session
Session 4 Y=e−AD0 The roughly 1,000 process steps that produce that D0
Session 4 reticle limit Where that limit comes from: the exposure field
Session 3 "Why is HBM expensive?" Here, why logic chips are expensive

Prerequisite check — what you can skip and what you must know

Concept One-line answer Need
MOSFET A switch: apply a voltage to the gate and a current path (the channel) opens between source and drain ★ Required
Doping Si has 4 outer electrons and pairs up neatly with its 4 neighbors. Mix in phosphorus (P) or arsenic (As), which have 5, and one electron is left over: n-type. Mix in boron (B), which has 3, and a vacancy (a hole) appears: p-type. Picture a restaurant whose tables for 4 are all full. A party of 5 arrives and one person ends up standing and wandering about; a party of 3 arrives and the guests shuffle along one seat at a time to fill the empty place. Pure Si is not an insulator either; it is a semiconductor with low conductivity ☆ Concept only (section 7)
Wavelength and frequency The shorter light's wavelength, the more energy each photon carries. E=hc/λ ★ Required (Exercise 3)
Numerical aperture NA How wide an angle of light a lens gathers. The larger it is, the better the resolution ★ Required
Diffraction limit The narrowest line light can draw is proportional to the wavelength and inversely proportional to NA (k1λ/NA). Techniques that shrink the process factor k1 let you draw lines narrower than the wavelength: in Exercise 1, about 43 nm with 193 nm light ★ Required
Plasma A gas separated into electrons and ions. In etching it produces reactive ions ☆ Concept only
Annealing and diffusion Using heat to repair the crystal damaged by ion implantation and to seat the dopants on lattice sites (activation). Apply heat for long and the dopants spread out (diffusion) ☆ Concept only (section 7)

If you have a background in signal processing or communications, there is a shortcut. Read "Seen as signal processing" in section 4 first. Lithography is ultimately the problem of passing a signal through a low-pass filter and then recovering the original, and OPC (optical proximity correction) is pre-distortion. Once you have that mapping, all of section 4 reads in a familiar language.

Day 2
