Never skip

  1. The Rayleigh criterion in section 4 — Exercises 1, 2 and 5 all come from it.
  2. "The brutal physics of EUV" in section 4 — the background to Exercise 3, and the real reason EUV is so expensive.
  3. Exercise 4, step yield — it takes five minutes and sums up the difficulty of semiconductor manufacturing in one number.

A common sticking point — "Why does a larger NA make depth of focus worse with the square?"

Put the two equations side by side and the tension shows.

CD=k1λNA,DOF=k2λNA2

Intuitively it goes like this. A large NA means the light is gathered from a very wide angle. Light converging from a wide angle comes to a sharper point at focus (resolution ↑), but move a little away from focus and the rays arriving from different directions fall badly out of step (depth of focus ↓). At a distance z from focus, the path difference between an oblique ray at the edge and a ray arriving straight down is roughly z(1−cosθ)≈zsin2θ/2. In air sinθ=NA, so the path difference is proportional to the square of NA; once it exceeds a set fraction of the wavelength the image blurs, so the allowable z is proportional to λ/NA2. In the same medium, doubling NA halves the CD and cuts the depth of focus to 1/4.

As a photography analogy: open the aperture wide (NA ↑) and the image is sharp, but the depth that stays in focus becomes paper-thin. A DOF of a few tens of nanometers for High-NA EUV means that the unevenness of the wafer surface has to fit inside it, and that is why CMP (planarization) becomes a required process, not an option.

1. Getting the intuition — chipmaking is "printing and coating," not "sculpting"

The whole picture

If you think of making a chip as sculpting (carving away), you will get it wrong. It is closer to multilayer printing.

  1. Coat the silicon disc (the wafer) with a thin film (deposition)
  2. Apply a light-sensitive material and draw a pattern with light (lithography)
  3. Develop it to dissolve away the areas that were (or were not) exposed
  4. Cut away only the exposed parts (etching)
  5. Remove the remaining light-sensitive material
  6. Smooth the surface flat (CMP)
  7. Inspect (metrology and inspection)
  8. → Back to step 1 for the next layer

The loop is repeated dozens of times, and each pass contains many detailed steps, so the whole process exceeds 1,000 steps. From the time a wafer goes into the fab until the finished product comes out takes several months.

Why there are so many layers

A chip has two main parts.

  • FEOL (front-end of line): the part that builds transistors on the silicon surface. The device layer.
  • BEOL (back-end of line): the part that stacks many layers of wiring on top to connect the transistors. The latest chips have 15–20 wiring layers.

In a city analogy, FEOL is the buildings and BEOL the road network. And lately the road network is the bigger problem: as wires grow thinner their resistance rises steeply, until it dominates signal delay and power consumption. This is the background to techniques such as backside power delivery (BSPDN).

2. The wafer — the starting point

How it is made

  1. Refining polycrystalline silicon — metallurgical-grade silicon is obtained from quartzite and refined to ultra-high purity by the Siemens process or similar. A purity of around 11N (99.999999999%) is required, because a single impurity changes device characteristics.
  2. Growing a single crystal (the Czochralski method) — dip a seed crystal into molten silicon and draw it up slowly while rotating it; the atoms take on the seed's crystal orientation, and a huge single-crystal ingot grows.
  3. Slicing → lapping → etching → polishing — the ingot is cut into thin slices and the surface polished flat to the atomic level.
  4. Epitaxy (optional) — a high-quality silicon layer that continues the crystal orientation is grown on top of the wafer.

Why it stopped at 300 mm

The larger the wafer, the more dies you get at once and the lower the cost per die. So wafers grew from 150 to 200 to 300 mm. But the move to 450 mm ran aground.

The reasons were purely economic. Making the wafer diameter 1.5 times larger multiplies the area by 2.25, but every tool that handles the larger wafer has to be built anew (lithography tools, etchers, transport systems, all of them), and obtaining uniform process results across the whole wafer becomes much harder. The development cost exceeded the savings. Instead of larger wafers, the industry chose scaling and the third dimension (stacking).

General lesson: technology choices in the semiconductor industry are decided not by physical possibility but by cost-effectiveness. The failure of 450 mm is the classic example.

Names on the wafer

Look down on a wafer that has finished processing and you see the same square repeated like a checkerboard. Each part has a name.

  • Chip (die): one square of the checkerboard. It is the result of the lithography tool printing the same pattern square after square.
  • Scribe line: the narrow lanes between dies. When processing is done, the wafer is cut along these lines (back end, Session 6).
  • TEG (test element group): test devices and patterns placed in spare spots such as the scribe lines. They are used to measure whether line width, resistance and threshold voltage came out on target, and they do not go into the product.
  • Edge dies: lay squares on a round disc and incomplete squares appear around the rim. The second term of the dies-per-wafer formula in Session 4 is exactly this loss. The edge exclusion width written in wafer specifications (example from a 300 mm specification: 3 mm) is also an unusable band.
  • Orientation mark: a mark that tells the tools the crystal orientation and the angle at which the wafer sits. Suppliers' specifications show that wafers of 150 mm or less usually have a flat, an edge cut off in a straight line, while 200 and 300 mm wafers have a notch, a V-shaped groove. The notch in a 300 mm specification is 1.0 mm deep, with a 90° angle, in the <110> direction (the same specification gives a diameter of 300±0.1 mm and a thickness of 775±25 μm).

Thermal oxidation — the first film silicon grows from itself

It is missing from the loop in section 1, but many processes start here: oxidizing the silicon surface to grow a SiO₂ film. If deposition (section 6) piles a different material on top, thermal oxidation turns the silicon itself into an oxide film. As the film grows, the silicon underneath is consumed.

  • Conditions: usually done at high temperatures of 800–1,200 °C. Using oxygen (O₂) alone is dry oxidation; adding water vapor (H₂O) is wet. Dry oxidation grows slowly, but the film is dense with good electrical properties, so it is used for thin films. Wet oxidation grows several times thicker at the same temperature and time, at the price of lower density.
  • Uses: insulating films between devices, films that mask unwanted areas during ion implantation, films that protect the layer beneath during etching.

Thickness and time — the Deal–Grove equation. The oxidant diffuses through the oxide already grown and reacts at the interface with the silicon. Whichever of the two processes is slower sets the rate. Deal and Grove (1965) combined the two in one equation.

x2+Ax=B(t+τ)

x is the oxide thickness, t the oxidation time, and τ a correction that converts any film present from the start into time. A and B are coefficients set by the temperature and the oxidant (O₂ or H₂O). The original paper showed that oxidation data for both oxygen and water vapor at 700–1,300 °C fit this equation well.

The two limits of the equation are the two phases of growth.

  • When thin — ignore x2 and x≈(B/A)(t+τ). Thickness is proportional to time (the linear regime). The interface reaction sets the rate.
  • When thick — grow long enough that x2 dominates, and x2≈Bt, so x≈Bt. This is the parabolic regime, where diffusion through the film sets the rate. Doubling the thickness takes four times as long.

The actual values of A and B are set separately for each temperature and oxidant and used from tables. This book does not give them.

3. How the transistor structure evolved — from planar to FinFET and GAA

What a MOSFET does (a 30-second review)

A channel lies between source and drain; apply a voltage to the gate and charge is induced in the channel so current flows. The gate is a valve. A good transistor is one whose valve shuts tight (small off-state leakage) and opens fully (large on-state current).

The problem — the short-channel effect

When scaling shortens the channel, source and drain come closer together. Then the drain voltage begins to act directly on the channel. The drain, not the gate, ends up controlling the channel, and current leaks even with the gate turned off (DIBL, a lowering of the threshold voltage).

In the valve analogy: the pipe has become so short that even with the valve shut, pressure from the other side pushes straight through.

The remedy — wrap more of the channel with the gate

The gate's control is proportional to the area over which the gate faces the channel. So the structure evolved like this.

Structure Faces the gate wraps Period Features
Planar 1 face (top) –2011 Simple, vulnerable to the short-channel effect
FinFET 3 faces (top + both sides) 2011– The channel stands up like a fin and the gate wraps around it. Drive strength set by the number of fins (quantized)
GAA / nanosheet 4 faces (all around) 2022– The channel is made as horizontal sheets fully surrounded by the gate. Sheet width can be varied continuously for fine-tuning of drive strength
(Next generation) CFET 4 faces + n/p stacked vertically Research stage nFET and pFET stacked one above the other to save area

Two practical advantages of GAA

  1. Better electrostatic control — wrapping all 4 faces lets the gate win even in a short channel.
  2. Design flexibility — in FinFETs drive strength could be set only by the number of fins (an integer), so there was a quantization loss. GAA lets the width of the nanosheets vary continuously, so circuit designers get exactly the drive strength they want.

The price: to build a stack of several nanosheets, you grow a Si/SiGe superlattice, selectively remove only the SiGe so the sheets float free, and fill the gaps with the gate dielectric and metal. Atomic layer deposition (ALD), which coats narrow gaps evenly, is the key to this process (see section 6).

Backside power delivery (BSPDN) — the next branch point

Traditionally, power and signals shared the wiring layers on the front of the wafer. But power wires need to be thick (to prevent IR drop) while signal wires need to be dense, so they fight over space.

The remedy: move the power wiring to the back of the wafer. Flip the wafer, grind it thin, build a power network on the back, and connect it directly to the transistors with nano-TSVs.

The gain: relief of front-side wiring congestion (better area and performance) + more efficient power delivery (less IR drop). The price: wafer thinning, alignment, changed heat-dissipation paths and more; the difficulty rises sharply.

As of October 2026, Intel was first to apply it, under the name PowerVia, in 18A. The first 18A product (Core Ultra series 3) was announced in January 2026. TSMC is introducing it in A16 as Super Power Rail. When it announced A16 in April 2024, it planned production for 2026. At the April 2026 technology symposium a TSMC executive was reported as saying: "A16 will be ready for production in 2026. However, actual product ramp depends on customers, and we expect volume production to begin in 2027." This schedule does not appear in TSMC's press releases or earnings materials, and as of October 22, 2026 there is no official announcement that volume production has begun. This is the point where the data center power story of Session 7 comes down to the level of the transistor.

4. Lithography — the part we go deepest into

The Rayleigh criterion

The smallest resolvable line width (CD, critical dimension) is

CD=k1λNA

  • λ : wavelength of the light source
  • NA : numerical aperture = nsinθ. How wide an angle of light the lens gathers
  • k1 : process factor. Its theoretical lower bound for a single exposure is about 0.25

And the depth of focus (DOF) is

DOF=k2λNA2

The central tension: a larger NA improves resolution linearly but makes depth of focus worse with the square. If the surface is even slightly uneven, the pattern fails to form. This is why CMP (planarization) is a required process (section 7).

Seen as signal processing — a shortcut for readers with a statistics or computing background

Treat the lithography system as a low-pass filter in a linear shift-invariant system and everything falls into place.

  • The mask pattern is a signal in the spatial domain. Its Fourier transform gives its spatial-frequency components.
  • The lens (projection optics) is a low-pass filter with cutoff frequency fc∝NA/λ. Spatial frequencies above that cannot pass through the lens pupil and are lost.
  • The image formed on the wafer is therefore the low-pass-filtered mask pattern. Sharp corners (high-frequency components) are smeared.

Seen in this frame:

  • OPC (optical proximity correction): distorting the input (the mask) in advance to get the output you want. A textbook inverse problem, or deconvolution. Serifs are added to corners and line widths are fine-tuned.
  • ILT (inverse lithography technology): formulate the whole thing as an optimization problem and solve for the mask pattern. The objective function is "the difference between the pattern on the wafer and the target pattern"; the variables are the mask pixels. It is a large non-convex optimization problem, and today it is solved on GPU clusters.
  • Phase-shift mask (PSM): reverses the phase of adjacent openings by 180° to create destructive interference at the boundary and raise contrast. In other words, it controls phase as well as amplitude.
  • Source-mask optimization (SMO): optimizes the shape of the illumination (the illumination distribution in the pupil) together with the mask.

Going further: "computational lithography" is, as the name says, a large computing problem. It is a leading example of machine learning put to work in real industry, and one of the most natural entry points into the semiconductor industry for people trained in CS or AI.

A history of shortening the wavelength

Light source Wavelength Period
g-line (mercury lamp) 436 nm –early 1990s
i-line 365 nm 1990s
KrF excimer 248 nm late 1990s
ArF excimer 193 nm 2000s
ArF immersion 193 nm (about 134 nm in water) 2007–
EUV 13.5 nm 2019–

The immersion trick: in NA =nsinθ, n is the refractive index of the medium. Fill the space between lens and wafer with water (n≈1.44) instead of air (n≈1) and NA can be pushed past 1, up to 1.35. It was a clever way to enlarge NA without changing the light source, and it let 193 nm hold out for another ten years or so. The 134 nm in the table is the wavelength shortened in water, λ0/n=193/1.44. That effect is already contained in the n of NA =nsinθ, so the Rayleigh equation takes the vacuum wavelength of 193 nm and an NA of 1.35 (Exercise 1). Plug in 134 nm and you count the refractive index twice.

Reduction projection — the mask is larger than the wafer

A lithography tool does not print the pattern of the mask (reticle) at the same size; it prints it reduced. A 0.33 NA EUV tool (ASML NXE) reduces it 4 times in both directions, and 4 times is also the standard for today's ArF scanners. That means the pattern on the mask is drawn 4 times larger than the pattern to be drawn on the wafer.

Two things follow from this setup. First, pattern errors on the mask are also carried to the wafer at roughly 1/4 the size (in very fine patterns the mask error can be carried over amplified beyond that; this is called the mask error enhancement factor, MEEF). Dust on the patterned surface of the mask likewise prints small. Second, a defect on the mask is nonetheless repeated identically in every field printed with that mask. Unlike particles that fall at random on the wafer (the Poisson defects of Session 4), a single mask defect creates a defect at the same spot in every field on the wafer.

The field printed in one exposure is at most 26×33 mm on the wafer. Do the arithmetic: at 4× reduction the pattern area on the mask is 104×132 mm, and that fits inside a mask 6 inches (152.4 mm) on a side.

High-NA has different magnifications in the two directions. Raising NA to 0.55 makes the mirrors larger, which makes the angle at which light strikes the mask larger, and then the reflective mask can no longer reflect the pattern properly. Reducing 8 times in both directions solves the angle problem but forces a larger mask. ASML's answer is anamorphic optics, which reduce 4 times in one direction and 8 times in the other. Do the arithmetic: the 104×132 mm area on the mask stays the same, and only the field in the 8× direction becomes 132 ÷ 8 = 16.5 mm, so the field on the wafer is halved to 26×16.5 mm. The field is halved so that the same 6-inch mask can still be used.

Multi-patterning — a way around k1

Once you reach the lower bound of k1 for a single exposure (about 0.25), you print one layer in several exposures.

  • LELE (litho-etch-litho-etch): split the pattern between two masks and expose and etch twice
  • SADP / SAQP (self-aligned double / quadruple patterning): deposit spacers on the sidewalls of an existing pattern and remove the original pattern, and a pattern at half the pitch remains. Repeat to go down to 1/4

The price is high: the number of process steps doubles, cost and cycle time jump, and overlay error becomes a new yield variable. The real motive for adopting EUV was not "smaller" but "fewer multi-patterning steps, and so lower cost."

The brutal physics of EUV

A wavelength of 13.5nm goes beyond ultraviolet and is close to soft X-rays. Here everything gets hard.

① No lenses 13.5nm is absorbed by almost every material. Refractive lenses are impossible, so only reflective optics will do. Even the mirrors are not ordinary mirrors but multilayer Bragg reflectors, alternating molybdenum and silicon layers a few nanometers thick, stacked up to about 100 layers, and even so they reflect at most about 70% of the light. Pass through several mirrors and the losses multiply, so only a tiny fraction of the source's output reaches the wafer.

② A vacuum is required Air absorbs EUV too, so the whole light path must be in vacuum.

③ The light source is extremely hard Droplets of tin (Sn) are dropped tens of thousands of times a second, and each is hit twice by a high-power CO₂ laser (flattened by a pre-pulse, then hit by the main pulse) to make a plasma that emits 13.5nm light. The conversion efficiency from electricity to EUV is very low, so the tool consumes a lot of power. On top of that, spattered tin contaminates the collector mirror. The one number that became the threshold for volume production is source power. When TSMC announced its first EUV volume-production process in 2019, it said its EUV tools had "output power of greater than 250 watts for day-to-day operations" (the throughput calculation in Exercise 3 starts from this power).

④ The mask is reflective too Transmissive masks cannot be used, so reflective masks are used; because light strikes them at an angle, a new distortion called shadowing appears. And since a protective membrane over the mask (pellicle) absorbs EUV, developing pellicles was a long-standing problem.

⑤ Stochastic defects — statisticians, take note

This is EUV's most interesting problem.

  • Photon energy E=hc/λ is inversely proportional to wavelength, so a 13.5nm photon carries about 14 times the energy of a 193nm photon.
  • To deliver the same exposure energy (dose), you need correspondingly fewer photons.
  • Photon arrival is a Poisson process, so the relative fluctuation of the count N is σ/μ=1/N. When N is small, the fluctuation is large.
  • The result: some spots happen to receive fewer photons and develop too little; others receive more. Line edge/width roughness (LER/LWR), missing holes and bridge defects occur at random.

These are not defects that better processing can remove; they are a statistical inevitability. The countermeasure is to raise the dose (more photons), but then throughput falls. The three-way trade-off between resolution, throughput and stochastic defects is the fundamental constraint of the EUV process. New resists (metal-containing resists and others) are attempts to improve this balance.

Deeper, for statisticians: the problem is the tail of the defect probability. A chip has billions of features, so even if the failure probability of an individual feature is on the order of 10−12, it affects yield at the chip level. This is an industrial problem where extreme value theory is actually used.

High-NA EUV — still unfolding

  • The next generation of EUV, with NA raised from 0.33 to 0.55. ASML TWINSCAN EXE:5200.
  • As of October 2026: Intel was the first to install the second-generation EXE:5200B and passed acceptance testing, and in July 2026 ASML and Intel announced that Intel was producing and shipping in high volume some Core Ultra series 3 products with certain 18A layers printed by High-NA. Yields are said to be on par with those printed on the existing NXE. SK hynix brought a production EXE:5200B into its M16 fab in Icheon, Korea, in September 2025, and imec received an EXE:5200 in March 2026 and plans to complete qualification by the fourth quarter of 2026.
  • For now it is used on some layers only. Intel has said it will validate it on 18A and then extend it to 14A production. Which node other companies will start using High-NA at, and how many tools have been installed worldwide, could not be confirmed from official announcements as of October 2026.

Two prices of High-NA

  1. A steep drop in depth of focus — since DOF∝λ/NA2, raising NA from 0.33 to 0.55 cuts DOF to about (0.33/0.55)² ≈ 0.36 times. Flatness requirements become extreme.
  2. Anamorphic optics and a smaller field — High-NA uses anamorphic optics with different magnifications in the two directions (4× and 8×), and as a result the field that can be exposed at once is halved (26×16.5mm). The existing reticle limit of 858 mm² becomes 429 mm². Why it halves was worked out in "Reduction projection" above.

★ This is the link between Session 5 and Session 6: when the exposure field shrinks, a chip larger than the field cannot be printed in one exposure. There are two ways out: stitching, which prints two fields edge to edge, and chiplets, which build the chip in pieces and join them in the package (Exercise 5). Stitching pays for alignment error at the seam and for design constraints, so the more layers are printed with High-NA, the stronger the incentive to split large chips into chiplets. It continues in Session 6.

5. Etching — the subtractive process

Think of copperplate etching. Coat a copper plate with a film that acid will not dissolve, scratch a picture through it with a needle, and dip it in the etching bath: only the scratched, exposed places dissolve, leaving grooves. In semiconductors, the photoresist is that film, lithography and development are the needle, and etching is the bath.

Wet vs. dry

  • Wet etching: immersion in a chemical solution. It is isotropic (it eats in equally in all directions), so it is unsuited to fine patterns. Used for cleaning, removing sacrificial layers and the like.
  • Dry etching (plasma): reactive ions accelerated by an electric field strike vertically. It can achieve anisotropy, so it is the standard for fine patterns.

Two key measures

  1. Anisotropy: you must etch only straight down. Etch sideways (undercut) and the line width collapses. Plasma etching gets its verticality by combining ion bombardment (physical) with chemical reaction, and forms a protective film on the sidewalls (passivation) to stop sideways etching.
  2. Selectivity: the ratio of etch rates between the material to be removed and the material to be left. With low selectivity you punch through into the layer below. In the GAA process, removing only the SiGe while leaving the Si nanosheets is the textbook case demanding extreme selectivity.

Other factors managed are etch rate and uniformity. Etch rate is the depth removed per unit time, and it sets how many wafers one tool processes per hour. Uniformity is whether the center and the edge of the wafer are etched to the same depth. If uniformity is poor, then while the under-etched places are being finished off, the places that broke through first keep eating into the layer below, and correspondingly more has to rest on selectivity.

High-aspect-ratio (HAR) etching — the hardest of the hard

This is the job of drilling deep, narrow holes.

  • 3D NAND: channel holes running through hundreds of layers. The aspect ratio exceeds 100:1.
  • TSVs: vias running through the silicon wafer (Session 6).
  • DRAM capacitors: keeping the capacitance while shrinking the area means digging deep.

Why it is hard: the deeper you go, the harder it is for reaction products to get out; ions bounce off the sidewalls and lose their direction; and you get bowing, where the hole widens near the top first, and taper, where it narrows toward the bottom. So special techniques such as cryogenic etching and pulsed plasma are brought in.

6. Deposition — the additive process

Method Principle Features Uses
PVD (physical vapor deposition) Target material is sputtered or evaporated and flies onto the surface Fast, poor step coverage Metal wiring, barriers
CVD (chemical vapor deposition) Gaseous precursors react to form a film on the surface Good coverage, may need high temperatures Insulating films, polysilicon
ALD (atomic layer deposition) Self-limiting reactions repeated in alternation Thickness control at the atomic-layer level, excellent step coverage Gate dielectrics, barriers, nanosheet gates

Why ALD is the savior of scaling

ALD introduces precursor A and lets it react only until the surface is saturated (self-limiting), purges, then introduces precursor B to complete the reaction. Because the reaction stops once the surface is saturated, the thickness deposited per cycle (growth per cycle) is nearly constant. That value is set by the size of the precursor molecules, the surface condition and the temperature, and it is usually less than one atomic layer.

Two properties that result

  1. Thickness is controlled precisely by the number of cycles. With a constant growth per cycle, the repetition count can set thickness down to the ångström.
  2. Even complex shapes are coated evenly. Allow each cycle enough time for the precursor to reach inside holes and between gaps and for the leftover gas to be cleared out (purged), and the inside of a deep hole and the narrow gaps between nanosheets are coated to nearly the same thickness. The more complex the shape, the longer each cycle takes.

GAA relies on ALD. The gate dielectric and metal have to fill the gaps of a few nanometers between floating nanosheets uniformly, and ALD, which builds up one layer at a time with surface reactions that stop by themselves, is the best fit for coating such narrow gaps evenly.

High-k gate dielectrics — a case of quantum mechanics changing an industry

The thinner the gate dielectric (traditionally SiO₂), the better the gate's control, but below 1–2nm electrons pass through the dielectric by quantum tunneling and leakage current explodes.

The remedy: in the capacitance C=εA/d, instead of reducing d, use a material with a large ε (permittivity). With high permittivity you get the same capacitance from a physically thicker film, blocking tunneling while keeping control. Hafnium oxide (HfO₂)-based materials play this role, and polysilicon gates were also replaced by metal gates (HKMG: high-k metal gate, introduced around 2007).

Going further: this is a case where a textbook result of quantum mechanics, "the tunneling probability depends exponentially on the barrier thickness," forced an industrial transition worth billions of dollars.

7. Ion implantation, annealing and CMP

Ion implantation

Doping in practice is not elegant. Dopant ions (boron, phosphorus, arsenic and others) are accelerated to tens to hundreds of keV and physically driven into the silicon.

  • Depth control: set by the acceleration energy. The higher the energy, the deeper they go.
  • Concentration control: set by the ion beam current and time (dose).
  • Distribution: stopping depth is random, so the concentration profile is roughly Gaussian (strictly, a skewed distribution). It is predicted by Monte Carlo simulation — a tool familiar to statisticians, used as is.
  • Side effect: the ions break up the crystal lattice. So annealing is needed to restore the crystal and to seat the dopants on lattice sites, activating them electrically.
  • The tension: anneal for long and the crystal recovers well, but the dopants diffuse and the profile smears. In fine devices this is fatal, so annealing has moved to ever shorter and more intense forms such as rapid thermal annealing (RTA), millisecond annealing and laser annealing.

CMP (chemical mechanical polishing)

Why it is required: as section 4 showed, depth of focus is shallow. If the surface is uneven, the pattern will not form in the next layer's exposure. Unevenness accumulates as layers are stacked, so every layer has to be planarized.

How: a pad rubs the surface mechanically while a slurry that softens it chemically flows over it. It is a combination of chemistry and mechanics, hence the name CMP.

What is hard: materials polish at different rates, producing dishing (wide metal areas becoming concave) and erosion. So dummy fill patterns that even out pattern density are inserted at the design stage. This is a textbook case of design adapting to the manufacturing process (DFM).

Cleaning

It is easy to mention in passing, but in reality a substantial share of all process steps is cleaning. One particle is one defect, and one defect is yield lost (the D0 in Y=e−AD0!), so cleaning goes in between every process.

8. Inspection and metrology — the direct point of contact for CS and AI people

Inspection vs. metrology

  • Inspection: is there a defect? Where? (particles, bridges, missing features)
  • Metrology: are the dimensions on target? (line width, film thickness, overlay error)

Main techniques

Technique Principle Features
Optical inspection Scattered light, contrast Fast; limited in detecting defects below the wavelength
E-beam inspection Scanning electron beam High resolution, very slow
OCD / scatterometry Fits the diffracted-light spectrum to a model to back out the shape Nondestructive, solves an inverse problem
Overlay metrology Measures alignment marks Manages layer-to-layer alignment error
CD-SEM Measures line width directly with an electron microscope Accurate, slow, local

Why this is AI's main stage

  1. The data is overwhelming. Thousands of dies on one wafer, tens of thousands of wafers a day in a fab. Wafer maps, sensor logs and metrology values pile up in vast quantities.
  2. Defect classification is a classic classification problem. Telling defect types apart in SEM images is image classification itself.
  3. Wafer-map patterns point to causes. Spatial patterns such as rings, scratches and edge concentration correspond to particular tool or process problems. A spatial-statistics plus pattern-recognition problem.
  4. Virtual metrology. Not every wafer can be measured (slow and expensive). Tool sensor data are used to predict metrology values and cut down sampling. It is a regression problem, and uncertainty quantification really matters.
  5. Predictive maintenance. Predicting tool failures in advance.
  6. APC (advanced process control). A control loop that feeds metrology results back into the process conditions for the next wafer. Run-to-run control is a classic time-series control problem.

Going further: the place where AI is used most, and most for real, in the semiconductor industry is not inside the chip but in running the fab.

"If you can't measure it, you can't make it"

Metrology itself is becoming a bottleneck of scaling. Measuring structures a few nanometers across nondestructively, quickly and accurately keeps getting harder. 3D structures (GAA nanosheets, 3D NAND channels) are harder still because they cannot be seen from the surface.

9. Putting it all together — how one layer is made

Take one wiring layer (BEOL) as an example (the damascene process):

1. Deposit insulating film (CVD)
2. Coat photoresist → expose → develop      ← defines the pattern
3. Etch trenches/vias (plasma)
4. Strip photoresist + clean
5. Deposit barrier/seed layer (ALD/PVD)     ← prevents Cu diffusion
6. Fill with copper by electroplating
7. Remove excess copper + planarize by CMP  ← needed before the next layer can be exposed
8. Deposit cap layer
9. Inspect and measure
   ↓ repeat for the next layer (15–20 times)

The wiring material changed once in a big way. Until the 1990s, wiring was aluminum (Al). An aluminum film was laid down and etched so that only the wiring shapes remained, and the narrow contact holes connecting transistors to the wiring were filled with tungsten (W) (W plugs). Aluminum in direct contact with silicon intermixes with it at the boundary and ruins the junction, so a barrier metal was laid between them. As wires grew thinner, aluminum hit two walls. One was resistance; the other was electromigration (current gradually pushing metal atoms along until the wire breaks or bunches up). Copper has lower resistance and resists this effect, but its atoms leak into silicon and ruin the devices, and it is hard to etch cleanly. So copper came in not by etching it into shape but by the damascene method, which cuts grooves into the insulating film, fills them, and removes the excess with CMP. Filling the via and the wiring groove in one go is dual damascene, and the barrier in step 5 above stops copper from leaking out. IBM announced on September 22, 1997 that it would put copper-wired chips into volume production (first shipments in September 1998), and said that copper wires conduct electricity with about 40% less resistance than aluminum. In the 2000s copper became the industry standard for wiring.

The sense to take away

  • Even one layer has this many steps, and they repeat dozens of times.
  • If any single step fails, that wafer is (partly) lost. Even if each of 1,000 steps succeeds 99.99% of the time, the whole comes to 0.99991000≈90%. That tells you how extreme the yield required of each step is.
  • With cycle times of several months, feedback is slow even when a problem is found. This is why virtual metrology and in-line control matter.

Mask count and cost

The finer the node, the more masks (number of layers × the multi-patterning factor), the more process steps and the more tool time, and the wafer price rises. EUV is a tool for easing this increase by reducing multi-patterning. That is why "EUV is expensive" and "EUV cuts costs" can both be true.

10. Common misconceptions

Misconception 1: "Lithography is just printing, like taking a photograph" → It makes structures smaller than the wavelength, so physically it is a fight against the diffraction limit. The pattern on the mask looks completely different from the pattern on the wafer (OPC/ILT).

Misconception 2: "With EUV, multi-patterning is no longer needed" → EUV has its own single-exposure limit, so at the leading edge EUV multi-patterning is done. High-NA is an attempt to postpone it.

Misconception 3: "Scaling will soon end because of the laws of physics" → The economic limit arrives before the physical one: the point where you can make it but cannot sell it at that cost. The failure of the 450mm wafer is an example.

Misconception 4: "GAA is simply better than FinFET" → Process complexity and cost rise sharply. There is no reason for every product to move to GAA, and mature nodes will remain.

Misconception 5: "Defects can be eliminated by raising cleanliness" → True for particle defects, but defects that are a statistical inevitability, such as EUV's stochastic defects, are not solved by cleanliness.

Misconception 6: "The bigger the wafer, the better" → As the failure of 450mm shows, the cost of redeveloping the tools and the difficulty of achieving uniformity can exceed the savings.

Misconception 7: "Ion implantation is doping by chemistry" → The ions are physically driven in. That is why the lattice is damaged and annealing must always follow.

Misconception 8: "EUV is used only at the leading edge, 3 nm and below" → EUV volume production began at the 7 nm class. TSMC billed N7+ as "the industry's first commercially available Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography technology" and began volume production in the second quarter of 2019 (Samsung Electronics announced in October 2018 that it had begun wafer production on its 7LPP process using EUV), and in October of that year it announced that customer products were reaching the market in high volume. In the same announcement it said that its successor N6 would apply EUV more widely, for 18% higher logic density than N7, and ASML explains that its 0.33 NA tools are used to print the critical layers of the 7, 5 and 3 nm nodes. As section 4 showed, the motive for bringing in EUV lay less in "smaller" than in cutting multi-patterning steps.

11. Quantitative exercises

Exercise 1 — The Rayleigh criterion With k1=0.3, find the CD for (a) ArF immersion (λ=193nm, NA=1.35), (b) EUV (λ=13.5nm, NA=0.33) and (c) High-NA EUV (λ=13.5nm, NA=0.55). What is the improvement factor from one generation to the next?

Exercise 2 — The price in depth of focus Under the same conditions, find the DOF ratios (assume the same k2). How much stricter do flatness requirements become with High-NA?

Exercise 3 — Stochastic defects At the same exposure energy, find the ratio of photon counts at 193nm and 13.5nm (E=hc/λ), and calculate how many times larger the relative fluctuation 1/N becomes. By what factor must the dose rise to reach the same level of fluctuation? What happens to throughput then?

Exercise 4 — Step yield If the whole process has 800 steps, what must the average yield of each step be to reach a target line yield of 90%? And with 1,200 steps?

Exercise 5 — Exposure field and die size Find the largest die area that can be made with the existing reticle limit (about 26×33mm) and with the High-NA field (about 26×16.5mm), and compare the yields of the largest dies by applying the yield equation of Session 4. It becomes the starting point of the chiplet discussion in Session 6.

12. Discussion questions

  1. Of the three terms of the Rayleigh criterion, which has the most room for improvement from here? Are Hyper-NA or a new wavelength realistic?
  2. How does the field reduction of High-NA EUV change design methodology? Do chiplets become a requirement rather than an option?
  3. For defects that are statistically inevitable, such as stochastic defects, what strategy should the industry take? Which is more efficient: leaving a margin at the design level, or raising the dose in the process?
  4. If metrology is becoming a bottleneck of scaling, how far can methods of "control without measurement" (model-based control, virtual metrology) go? How is their reliability assured?
  5. If scaling runs into an economic limit, what is the next axis of performance improvement? (A preview of Session 6)

13. Further study

  • Standard textbooks: Plummer, Deal & Griffin, Silicon VLSI Technology — the standard text on process physics. May & Spanos, Fundamentals of Semiconductor Manufacturing and Process Control (Wiley, 2006, doi:10.1002/0471790281) — it covers statistical process control, so it suits readers with a statistics background especially well
  • The original paper on thermal oxidation: Deal & Grove, "General Relationship for the Thermal Oxidation of Silicon," J. Appl. Phys. 36(12):3770–3778 (1965), doi:10.1063/1.1713945 — shows what experimental data the equation in section 2 came from
  • Device physics: Sze & Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices (Wiley, 3rd ed. 2006, doi:10.1002/0470068329, a full-scale textbook), Taur & Ning, Fundamentals of Modern VLSI Devices (Cambridge, 2nd ed. 2009, doi:10.1017/CBO9781139195065, short-channel effects and scaling theory)
  • Lithography: Chris Mack, Fundamental Principles of Optical Lithography (Wiley, 2007, doi:10.1002/9780470723876) — written in terms of Fourier optics, so it reads very well if you have a signal-processing background. The author's website lithoguru.com has online lectures and basic explanations
  • EUV: Bakshi (ed.), EUV Lithography (SPIE, 2nd ed. 2018, doi:10.1117/3.2305675). For the anamorphic design of High-NA, van Schoot et al., EUVL Workshop 2017 presentation and ASML, "5 things you should know about High NA EUV lithography"
  • Latest developments: presentations at IEDM, the VLSI Symposium and SPIE Advanced Lithography; imec's published roadmap material
  • AI × semiconductor manufacturing: run a model yourself on WM-811K, the public dataset for wafer-map defect classification (Wu, Jang, Chen, IEEE Trans. Semiconductor Manufacturing 28(1) (2015), doi:10.1109/TSM.2014.2364237), and section 8 will come alive

Self-study appendix A — solutions to the quantitative exercises

Solution to Exercise 1 — The Rayleigh criterion

SolutionSolution

CD=k1λ/NA, with k1=0.3 held fixed.

Generation λ NA CD
(a) ArF immersion 193 nm 1.35 0.3×193/1.35= 42.9 nm
(b) EUV 13.5 nm 0.33 0.3×13.5/0.33= 12.3 nm
(c) High-NA EUV 13.5 nm 0.55 0.3×13.5/0.55= 7.4 nm

Improvement factors

Step Factor What contributed
(a) → (b) 3.49× Almost entirely the wavelength (193 → 13.5, 14.3×). NA actually got worse, 1.35 → 0.33
(b) → (c) 1.67× Entirely NA (0.33 → 0.55)

How to read it — this table tells you everything about the character of EUV

In moving to EUV, NA was given up. 13.5 nm is absorbed by every material, so refractive lenses cannot be used and only reflective optics are possible, and it is hard to build a large NA from mirrors. The wavelength gained 14.3 times and NA lost 4.1 times, for a net gain of 3.5 times.

And High-NA is the work of winning back exactly that lost NA. 0.33 → 0.55 is a mere 1.67 times, yet for it the whole optical system is redesigned and the field is halved (Exercise 5).

Caution: k1=0.3 is near the practical lower bound for a single exposure (theoretical lower bound 0.25). The 42.9 nm is actually a half-pitch, and finer patterns made with ArF immersion are printed in several exposures by multi-patterning — that is, k1 is bypassed, not lowered.

What about real tools? You can work k1 backward from the resolution the toolmaker states. ASML gives the resolution of its High-NA tool (EXE) as 8 nm. The arithmetic gives k1=8×0.55/13.5=0.326. With the 13 nm resolution of the 0.33 NA tool (NXE), k1=13×0.33/13.5=0.318. In other words, the k1=0.3 assumed in the table above is not far from real tool specifications.

Solution to Exercise 2 — The price in depth of focus

SolutionSolution

DOF=k2λ/NA2. Keep k2 the same and compare λ/NA2 alone.

Generation λ/NA2 Relative DOF With k2=0.5
(a) ArF immersion 193/1.8225=105.9 1.00 53 nm
(b) EUV 13.5/0.1089=124.0 1.17 62 nm
(c) High-NA EUV 13.5/0.3025=44.6 0.42 22 nm

One unexpected result: EUV (b) actually has 17% more depth of focus than ArF immersion (a), thanks to its lower NA. EUV's arrival did not suddenly raise flatness requirements.

The real problem is High-NA. DOF shrinks to 0.36 times (b) and 0.42 times (a), to about 22 nm.

What has to fit inside 22 nm

  • Local unevenness of the wafer surface (CMP's job)
  • Flatness and vibration of the wafer chuck
  • The thickness of the resist film itself — a 50 nm resist already exceeds the DOF

What follows in a chain

  1. CMP requirements become extremely strict. Planarization becomes a precondition of lithography (section 7).
  2. The resist must be thinner. But a thin resist has less etch resistance — it disappears before it has done its job as a mask.
  3. So hardmasks and multilayer resists are used, or new materials that hold up even when thin, such as metal-oxide resists.

What to take away: a single improvement in resolution pushes up requirements in a chain, through planarization, materials and etching. Why scaling is not "just a matter of changing the lithography tool" is all in this one exercise.

The figure below shows the case of EUV (13.5 nm, NA 0.33) with k1=0.3 and k2=0.5. In the screen edition you can change the light source and NA of the three generations, k1 and k2, and you can also work k1 backward from a tool's nominal resolution.

Solution to Exercise 3 — Stochastic defects

SolutionSolution

The energy of one photon is E=hc/λ, so it is inversely proportional to wavelength.

EEUVEArF=19313.5=14.3

An EUV photon carries 14.3 times the energy of an ArF photon (about 92 eV vs. 6.4 eV).

Photon count at the same dose (energy per unit area)

With the same energy and each photon 14.3 times larger, the number of photons is only 1/14.3 = 7%.

NEUV=NArF14.3

Relative fluctuation

In Poisson statistics the relative fluctuation of a count N is 1/N, so

σEUV/NEUVσArF/NArF=14.3=3.78 times

To reach the same level of fluctuation, the dose must rise 14.3 times. (N has to become 14.3 times larger.)

Throughput at that point

EUV source power directly sets the processing time per wafer. Other conditions being equal, such as the time to move and align the wafer, the time to expose one wafer is proportional to the dose divided by the source power.

texposure∝dosesource power,throughput=1T0+texposure

Here T0 is the fixed time that does not depend on dose, such as wafer transport and alignment. So throughput is not simply proportional to source power ÷ dose; as the exposure time gets shorter, it saturates against 1/T0.

The reference point is the day-to-day source power of more than 250 W seen in section 4 (TSMC's 2019 announcement). Keep that power and raise the dose 14.3 times, and the exposure time becomes 14.3 times longer. In the limit where exposure time dominates everything, wafers per hour collapse to 1/14.3. With a fixed time T0 the drop is smaller, and how much smaller depends on how large T0 is compared with the original exposure time t. Throughput becomes (T0+t)/(T0+14.3t) of the original, so it falls to 13% if T0=t, to 45% if T0=10t, and hardly at all if T0 is much longer than the exposure time. This exercise gives no T0, so read 1/14.3 as the worst case. In that limit the productivity of a tool costing hundreds of millions of dollars drops to 7%, which is economically impossible. Conversely, keeping throughput would require raising source power 14.3 times, from 250 W to about 3.6 kW by the arithmetic.

So what is actually done

Measure Content
Raise the dose only partly ASML rates EUV tool throughput at 30 mJ/cm² (NXE:3600D, 3800E) and 50 mJ/cm² (High-NA EXE:5000). The dose is not raised 14.3-fold to match the photon count; it stays in the tens of mJ/cm²
Improve resist sensitivity and chemistry So that one photon triggers more reactions (chemical amplification, metal-oxide resists)
Avoid stochastic defects by design Designs built mainly on regular one-dimensional patterns, avoidance of forbidden pitches
Catch them with metrology Stochastic defects are rare and scattered, so fast large-area inspection is needed → section 8

This is what "the brutal physics of EUV" amounts to. Shortening the wavelength bought resolution, but in exchange the photon count itself became scarce and statistical uncertainty grew. There is a trade-off in principle between resolution and stochastic defects, and it ties dose, throughput and yield together.

Connection: these stochastic defects add straight onto the D0 of Session 4. And as D0 rises, the die area allowed for the same target yield shrinks (A50=ln2/D0). The physics of lithography sets the size of the chip.

The figure below shows the case where the EUV dose is raised by 193/13.5, that is about 14.3 times, to match the fluctuation of ArF. In the screen edition you can vary the dose multiple and the reference source power and see the relative fluctuation, the exposure time, and the source power needed to keep the same exposure time. Because the fixed time T0 is unknown, throughput is shown only as its limiting value, where exposure time dominates everything.

Solution to Exercise 4 — Step yield

SolutionSolution

If the total yield is the product of the step yields, yn=Y, so y=Y1/n.

800 steps, target 90%

y=0.91/800=exp(ln0.9800)=exp(−0.10536800)=0.9998683

1−0.9998683=1.317×10−4, so the allowable defect rate per step is 131.7 ppm. If a single step slips just 132 times in a million, the target is missed.

1,200 steps, same target

y=exp(−0.105361200)=0.9999122⇒87.8 ppm per step

When the steps increase 1.5 times, the allowable defect rate shrinks to 2/3.

Seen the other way round, it is far more frightening

Yield per step Defect rate per step Line yield, 800 steps 1,200 steps
99.99% 100 ppm 0.9999800=92.3% 88.7%
99.9% 1,000 ppm 0.999800=44.9% 30.1%
99% 10,000 ppm 0.99800=0.03% Almost 0

The line yields in the table are yn calculated directly. When the defect rate p=1−y is small, yn=(1−p)n≈e−pn, so at 800 steps you can also approximate 99.99% as e−0.08, 99.9% as e−0.8 and 99% as e−8. At the number of digits shown in the table, the two calculations agree.

99% per step is by common sense an excellent figure, yet after 800 steps virtually nothing comes out.

What this exercise sums up

Here is why semiconductor manufacturing differs fundamentally from other manufacturing. Hundreds of steps multiply in series, so each step has to be perfect not "almost" but "to the ppm." So

  • six-sigma-level control is demanded of every single process
  • inspection and metrology go in at every step (section 8)
  • a decision to add steps (multi-patterning!) becomes not a simple cost increase but an increase in yield risk

The real cost of multi-patterning: section 4 said multi-patterning bypasses k1. This is its price — print one layer in 4 exposures and the steps increase, and by the table above the line yield is cut multiplicatively. When EUV is adopted despite its expense, the reason is often not resolution but the reduction in step count.

The figure below shows the case of a target line yield of 90% at 800 steps. In the screen edition you can change the number of steps and the target yield, and you can also go the other way and find the line yield from a yield per step.

Solution to Exercise 5 — Exposure field and die size

SolutionSolution
Exposure method Field size Largest die area
Existing (including 0.33 NA) 26 × 33 mm 858 mm²
High-NA EUV 26 × 16.5 mm 429 mm²

High-NA uses anamorphic optics (the reduction ratio differs in one direction only), so the field is halved.

Why exactly half? The calculation in "Reduction projection" in section 4 is the answer. Existing tools reduce 4 times in both directions, so 104×132 mm on the mask becomes 26×33 mm on the wafer. High-NA reduces 8 times in one direction while using the same 6-inch mask, so the field in that direction shrinks to 132 ÷ 8 = 16.5 mm. Only the direction whose magnification doubled is halved, exactly.

Applying the yield equation of Session 4 (D0=0.1)

Field Area λ=AD0 Yield
Largest die, existing 8.58 cm² 0.858 42.4%
Largest die, High-NA 4.29 cm² 0.429 65.1%

The dilemma shows clearly

High-NA lets you draw finer patterns but halves the area you can draw at once. Yield improves (42% → 65%), but the chips you can make get smaller.

Yet AI accelerators keep getting bigger. The direction is dies of around 800 mm² with 8 HBM stacks attached, and such a die cannot be printed in one exposure with the High-NA field.

There are two remedies

Remedy Content Problem
Stitching Join two fields to make one die Alignment error and defects at the seam, more steps
Chiplets Make small dies from the start and join them in the package Interface overhead, assembly yield

Conclusion: a die larger than the High-NA field must either pay the cost of stitching or be split into chiplets. Which is cheaper is decided by weighing the alignment and yield cost of the seam against the interface and assembly cost of chiplets, but the more layers are printed with High-NA, the stronger the incentive to lean toward chiplets. It amounts to adding the High-NA field constraint as one more cost item to the chiplet profit-and-loss calculated in Exercise 4 of Session 4. Session 6 continues that accounting.

The figure below shows what field the same pattern area on a 6-inch mask (104 × 132 mm) becomes on a 0.33 NA tool and on a High-NA tool, and the yield of the largest die when D0=0.1. In the screen edition you can change the optics and D0.

Self-study appendix B — leads for the discussion questions

The numbers are those of the discussion questions in section 12. Rows marked + add questions worth thinking about alongside them.

Question Core axis Leads
1. Which of the three terms has room left Room left vs. price k1 is close to the theoretical single-exposure lower bound of 0.25 (0.3 assumed in Exercise 1; 0.32–0.33 worked back from tool specifications). Push NA beyond 0.55 and depth of focus shrinks in inverse proportion to NA² (Exercise 2), while the field and mask problems grow again. Shorten the wavelength further and each photon carries more energy, so the photon count at the same dose falls further (Exercise 3). For any of the terms, the starting point is to calculate the price that comes with it before the gain that is left
2. Field reduction and design methodology Stitching vs. chiplets A die larger than the High-NA field (429 mm²) must be printed in joined fields by stitching or split into chiplets (Exercise 5). "Is it a requirement?" turns into a comparison of the alignment and yield cost of the seam against the interface and assembly cost of chiplets. Print even one layer with High-NA and the field constraint applies at that layer, so the number of layers printed with High-NA changes the answer
3. Stochastic defects — dose vs. design margin Throughput vs. area Raising the dose shrinks the relative fluctuation in proportion to 1/dose, but exposure time grows in proportion to the dose (Exercise 3). A design margin enlarges features or uses regular patterns to thin the tail of the failure probability, at the cost of area. Convert both into the same unit, "the cost of a good die from one wafer," and you can compare them with the cost-per-die formula of Session 4
4. Control without measurement Prediction vs. verification Virtual metrology predicts metrology values from tool sensors and shrinks the measurement sample (section 8). The way to find out whether a prediction was wrong is, in the end, measurement too, so rather than eliminating measurement it is used to concentrate measurement on the wafers whose predictions are most uncertain. Reliability comes from continually checking the distribution of prediction errors against real measurements
5. The next axis after scaling Which limit comes first There are three candidates: (i) physics (channels counted in atoms, stochastic defects), (ii) economics (gain relative to mask and tool cost), (iii) heat (power density). The ones reached first today are (ii) and (iii); (i) still has room. That is why the industry is shifting its axis from scaling to integration (packaging)
+ How far can you go without EUV Step count vs. resolution Multi-patterning can keep up on resolution itself. What breaks is economics — as Exercise 4 showed, more steps cut yield multiplicatively, and more masks and longer cycle times drive costs up steeply. The accurate statement is not "technically impossible" but "economically impossible"
+ What backside power delivery means Separating wiring from devices Dedicating the front to signals and the back to power is not a simple improvement but a change in the philosophy of layer placement. Exercise 4 (IR drop) in Session 7 checks quantitatively why it matters as much as GAA
+ The role of AI in inspection and metrology Detection vs. root-cause analysis Classification of defect images is already mature. The hard problem is tracing back from wafer-map patterns to the tool and step that caused them, and it ties directly to the clustering (α) of Session 4. Seen as a spatial-statistics plus causal-inference problem, it opens up
+ Where should localization start The hierarchy of substitutability As the three-layer structure of Session 1 showed, the less replaceable a layer, the harder it is to produce domestically. But difficulty and payoff are not proportional — materials and parts that are substitutable but whose supply is concentrated offer the most for the cost

Self-study appendix C — key terms

Term One-line definition
Front-end process (FEOL + BEOL) The whole of the wafer processing that builds transistors (FEOL) and the wiring layers above them (BEOL) on the wafer. Distinguished from the back end, which cuts and joins wafers
Thermal oxidation A process that grows a SiO₂ film by oxidizing silicon at high temperature. The thickness follows the Deal–Grove equation
Reduction projection Printing the mask pattern onto the wafer at reduced size. 4× is standard; High-NA is 4× and 8×
Dual damascene A wiring process that cuts vias and wiring grooves into the insulating film, fills them with copper in one go, and removes the excess by CMP
CD (critical dimension) The smallest line width that has to be made
Rayleigh criterion CD=k1λ/NA. The fundamental limit on resolution
Numerical aperture (NA) A measure of the angle over which a lens gathers light
Depth of focus (DOF) The range of depth over which focus holds. ∝λ/NA2
EUV (extreme ultraviolet) Lithography with extreme ultraviolet light of 13.5 nm wavelength
High-NA EUV The next generation of EUV, with NA raised from 0.33 to 0.55. The field is halved
Multi-patterning Printing one layer in several exposures to get around the resolution limit
Stochastic defect A random defect arising from a shortage of photons
OPC (optical proximity correction) Deforming the mask so as to cancel diffraction distortion in advance
Photoresist A light-sensitive film whose properties change when exposed to light
Etching The process of removing unwanted material
Anisotropy / selectivity The degree to which etching cuts only vertically / the degree to which only the intended material is cut
HAR etch (high aspect ratio etch) Etching that drills deep, narrow holes. A hard problem in 3D NAND and TSVs
Deposition The process of building up the needed films
ALD (atomic layer deposition) Deposition that builds up atomic layer by atomic layer for precise thickness control
High-k A gate dielectric with high permittivity. It stops leakage current
Ion implantation A process that drives impurity ions in to change electrical properties
CMP (chemical mechanical polishing) A process that planarizes the surface chemically and mechanically
GAA (gate-all-around) A transistor structure in which the gate surrounds the channel on all sides
CFET (complementary FET) A next-generation structure that stacks n-type and p-type vertically
BSPDN (backside power delivery network) Moving the power wiring to the back of the wafer
Inspection / metrology Looking for whether there are defects / measuring dimensions and thicknesses
