Session 6

Back-End Processing and Advanced Packaging

Key takeaway

If you want to understand AI semiconductors, this is the session that matters most. The back end, once a low-value finishing step of "cut, attach and wrap," has become the main stage for performance gains. The reason is that three pressures acted at once: ① yield — a large die makes yield collapse as Y=e−AD0; ② the exposure field limit — there is a ceiling on the area that can be printed in one shot, and High-NA halves it; ③ heterogeneous optimization — logic, SRAM, analog and I/O each have a different best process. All three point to "split it up and join the pieces." And the HBM problem of Session 3 (to pull out a very wide bus you have to sit the chips very close together) gets its answer here in TSVs, interposers and stack bonding. The memory problem and the packaging problem were the same problem.

Primary sources

SK hynix Newsroom, "Semiconductor Back-End Process Episode 6: The Eight Steps of Assembling Conventional Packages" · ScienceON, "Artificial Intelligence Semiconductor and Packaging Technology Trend" (2023, in Korean) · ScienceON, "Advances and Research Trends in 3D Packaging-Based High-Bandwidth and Large-Capacity Memory Technologies for Next-Generation AI Hardware" (2026, in Korean) · Siemens EDA, "Comprehensive 3D IC guide to heterogeneous integration" · TSMC 3DFabric (CoWoS, InFO, SoIC) · JEDEC JESD47 standard page · SK hynix, 12-high HBM4E samples shipped (2026-06-18) · UCIe specifications page

Learning objectives

  1. Explain how the purpose of traditional back-end processing differs from that of advanced packaging.
  2. Calculate the gains and losses of chiplet partitioning with a yield model.
  3. Explain which physical problem each of TSVs, interposers and hybrid bonding solves.
  4. Tell 2.5D and 3D apart precisely, and choose the approach that fits a design goal.
  5. Explain why CoWoS capacity is the bottleneck of AI chip supply.

0. Self-study guide — for readers working alone

This session is where the previous five sessions meet

Bandwidth from Session 2, HBM from Session 3, yield from Session 4 and the reticle limit from Session 5 merge here into a single problem: "If you cannot make a big chip but need big performance, what do you do?" Exercise 1 (optimal chiplet partitioning) gives the answer in numbers. Four of this session's five exercises reuse tools from earlier sessions, so if you understood those, they go surprisingly fast.

What this session brings over from earlier ones — it leans on them heavily

From What
Session 4 Y=e−AD0 and the GDPW formula — used as is in Exercise 1
Session 5 Exercise 5 Reticle limit 858 mm², 429 mm² for High-NA
Session 3 Exercise 2 pJ/bit — used as is in Exercise 2
Session 3 HBM stack structure, TSVs, stack yield yn, the stacking methods in volume production (TSV + microbumps, MR-MUF and TC-NCF) and the next-generation candidate, hybrid bonding
Session 2 Why bandwidth is everything

If you have not done Exercise 4 (chiplet gains and losses) of Session 4, go back and do it now. Exercise 1 of this session generalizes it.

Prerequisite check

Concept One-line answer
Parasitic capacitance The electrical capacitance a wire has without meaning to. Roughly proportional to length; charging and discharging it costs energy
E=12CV2 The energy needed to charge a capacitance C to a voltage V
Thermal resistance R=t/(kA) The resistance heat meets when passing through a layer of thickness t, thermal conductivity k and area A [K/W]. θJA and θJC, which roll a whole package into one value, come in section 7
Pitch The center-to-center distance between neighboring wires or bumps
Signal integrity Whether a transmitted signal arrives without distortion or noise

Reading order (130 minutes in total recommended)

Step Sections Time Note
1 Sections 1–3 (overview of the back end, why split) 25 min An extension of Session 4
2 Sections 4–6 (2.5D and 3D, TSVs, bonding) 35 min The HBM structure is completed here
3 Exercise 1 25 min The heart of this session. Fill in the table yourself
4 Section 7 on heat and reliability + Exercise 4 20 min The bridge to Session 7
5 Sections 8 and 9 on UCIe and signal integrity + Exercises 2, 3 and 5 25 min

The one sentence that runs through this session

Packaging is not "a box to put the chip in" but "an extension of the wiring." How close you place the dies decides bandwidth, power and heat all at once. Exercise 2 shows this with a number: a factor of 200.

A common sticking point — when 2.5D and 3D get confusing

The terms are confusing because the names refer not to geometry but to the way things are connected.

Placement Connection Typical example
2D Side by side, on a substrate Substrate wiring (long) Traditional multichip module
2.5D Side by side, on an interposer Interposer wiring (short) GPU + HBM (CoWoS)
3D Stacked one on top of another TSV + microbumps, or hybrid bonding (shortest) Inside an HBM stack (microbumps today), logic on logic

To remember it: 2.5D is "beside, but very close"; 3D is "on top." And today's AI accelerators use both at once — inside the HBM stack it is 3D, between the GPU and the HBM it is 2.5D.

1. Getting the intuition — the purpose of the back end has changed

The back end of old

Wafer test (electrical test → wafer burn-in → functional test → repair → retest)
  → backgrinding (thinning the back) → dicing (cutting) → die attach → wire bonding
  → molding (resin encapsulation) → ball attach and singulation (for BGA) → package test → shipment

Testing is not one step at the very end. Chips are screened first in wafer form, before cutting, and inspected again after they are packaged. The earlier testing produces the KGD of section 2.

A package does four jobs: ① it protects the chip physically and chemically, ② it distributes power to the chip, ③ it lets signals pass to and from the outside world, and ④ it removes the heat the chip produces. The Semiconductor Packaging volume of the second edition of the Microelectronics Packaging Handbook edited by Tummala and others (Chapman & Hall, 1997), counted as the standard reference in this field, says the same in its publisher's description: "Electronic packaging is defined as interconnection, powering, cooling, and protecting semiconductor chips for reliable systems." (The bibliographic details were confirmed from the publisher's catalog; the text of the book itself was not checked.) The fourth job is the subject of section 7 of this session and of Session 7. In the old days this work was relatively simple, so it was outsourced to OSATs in regions with cheap labor, and it added little value.

Packages are also divided into levels: the die itself, the single package that holds the die (first-level package), the board the package is mounted on (second level), and the system that gathers the boards. Whether the die counts as level zero, and what number the system gets, varies from text to text. Look less at the number and more at which level connects to which. Advanced packaging puts several dies and an interposer inside the first-level package, pulling connections that the board used to make into the package.

Advanced packaging today

The purpose is entirely different: to connect several chips to each other at ultra-high bandwidth so that they behave like one giant chip.

Packaging now decides performance. With the same GPU die, system performance varies widely with how many HBM stacks are attached and what kind of interposer is used. So foundries have begun to absorb packaging themselves (TSMC's CoWoS and SoIC, Intel's Foveros and EMIB, Samsung's I-Cube and X-Cube).

In one sentence: if the front end is "the race to make transistors small," the back end is "the race to put chips close together." And right now the second race is paying off faster.

2. Why the center of gravity moved — three pressures

Pressure ① Yield — a large die cannot be made

Write out the formula from Session 4 again: Y=e−AD0.

Comparing the calculations (assuming D0=0.1/cm²)

Approach Die configuration Individual yield System yield
Single large die 800 mm² × 1 44.9% 44.9%
Chiplet partition 200 mm² × 4 81.9% (each) 0.8194=45.0% ← huh?

Wait — aren't they the same? Calculated naively, they are. In e−AD0, even if you divide the area into four, you need all four, so the yields multiply. Converting the area to cm², (e−2cm2×D0)4=e−8cm2×D0=e−0.8=44.9%, the same (800 mm² = 8 cm²).

This is where it starts to matter. Chiplets win for the following reasons.

  1. KGD screening becomes possible. Small dies are easy and cheap to test individually. Assemble only good ones, and system yield approaches assembly yield. A large die with a defect is thrown away whole.
  2. What you throw away differs. If an 800mm² die is defective, you discard 800mm². If one 200mm² chiplet is defective, you discard only 200mm², and the other three go into inventory.
  3. They are reused. The same I/O chiplet can serve several products. NRE is spread out.
  4. Mixed nodes become possible. See pressure ③.
  5. More dies fit on a wafer, so the share lost at the edge goes down.

Where does KGD come from? From wafer test, at the front of the flow chart in section 1. In wafer form the chips' electrical characteristics are measured, high temperature and voltage are applied to expose in advance the chips that would die early (burn-in), and their functions are checked. Memory does not stop there. Rows and columns with bad cells are swapped for spare rows and columns (repair), and the chips are tested again. Standards give a clue to how long early failures must be screened. JEDEC JESD47I (2012) sets the qualification test that measures the early life failure rate (ELFR) at a junction temperature of 125 °C or higher for 48–168 hours. That is a condition of product qualification testing, not the volume-production burn-in condition itself.

The exact comparison formula: for n chiplets, each of area A/n, with assembly yield yasm after KGD screening,

Ychiplet-system≈yasm,cost per good system≈1yasm[n×cwaferGDPW(A/n)×e−(A/n)D0+cassembly]

The bracket is the cost of one assembly attempt. The good systems that survive carry the cost of the systems lost in assembly, hence the division by yasm. The solution to Exercise 1 sets cassembly to 0 and calculates with this formula.

The price: the interface circuits (PHY) for chiplet-to-chiplet communication eat area and power, and communication across dies is slower and more expensive than on-die communication. Partitioning does not always win — Exercise 4 of Session 4 computed the break-even point.

Pressure ② The exposure field limit — it physically cannot be made

A lithography tool prints only a fixed area at a time (the reticle field). ASML gives the maximum exposure field of its 0.33 NA EUV tools (NXE) as 26 mm × 33 mm. That works out to 858 mm². ASML states: "Because of their anamorphic optics, EXE systems have exposure fields half the size of their NXE predecessors." That works out to about 429 mm². Why it is half was calculated in Session 5.

A chip larger than this cannot, in principle, be made in one shot. Stitching (joining fields together) exists, but overlay errors and yield problems keep it from being common.

★ The link foreshadowed in Session 5: adopting High-NA EUV gains resolution but loses field. So a design that needs a die larger than 429 mm² must, on moving to High-NA, choose between stitching and chiplets, and the incentive to choose chiplets grows. If the required die area fits within 429 mm², if scaling squeezes the same circuit into it, or if you accept the alignment and yield burden of stitching, you need not partition. This link, in which the next step of scaling raises the incentive for a packaging-side solution, ties Session 5 to this session.

Pressure ③ Heterogeneous optimization — not every circuit benefits from scaling

Circuit type Gain from scaling Best choice
Logic (compute) Large Latest node
SRAM (cache) Shrinking — SRAM cell area now scales much more slowly than logic Limited gain from the latest node
Analog, I/O Almost none — needs voltage swing and physical size Mature nodes are far cheaper
Power management None Mature node

Wafers at the latest node cost far more than at mature nodes. Putting circuits that gain nothing from scaling on the latest node is waste. So logic is made at the latest node and I/O at a mature node, and the two are joined. AMD demonstrated this strategy at scale, and it has now become standard in the industry.

3. Dicing — even cutting has become hard

Method Principle Characteristics
Blade Cutting with a diamond blade Traditional, cheap. Chipping (broken edges), kerf (cut width) loss
Laser scribing Cut a groove with a laser, then separate Small kerf, heat-affected zone
Stealth dicing Focus a laser inside the silicon to form a modified layer, then split by expanding the tape Almost no surface damage or particles, suited to thin wafers
Plasma dicing Separation by etching (combined with DBG) Any shape possible, no chipping, excellent die strength

Why it has become hard

  1. Wafers have become thin. Wafers for TSVs and stacking are ground down to a few tens of μm. Something as thin as paper has to be cut and handled without breaking.
  2. Kerf has to shrink. The cut width is area thrown away. The smaller the die, the larger the share of kerf.
  3. Die edge strength has become important. Stacking applies stress, so a microcrack on the cut face leads to failure later.
  4. Low-k dielectrics are weak. The low-permittivity materials in the wiring layers are mechanically fragile and delaminate under blade cutting.

4. TSV — vertical wiring that runs through the silicon

Why it is needed

The problem seen in Session 3: to get bandwidth you must pull out a great many wires, and to do that the chips must be very close. Stacking chips vertically shrinks the distance to the μm scale, but there has to be a passage connecting the upper and lower chips. That passage is the TSV.

Why it is better electrically

Wire delay is roughly proportional to RC, and drive energy is proportional to E=12CV2. A shorter wire reduces both R and C.

  • Wiring that detours through the package substrate: a few mm to a few tens of mm
  • Interposer wiring: a few hundred μm to a few mm
  • TSV (through the thickness of the chip): a few tens of μm

When the length drops 100-fold, parasitic capacitance drops by roughly as much, and the energy to transmit each bit falls sharply. This is the core of why HBM's pJ/bit is much better than GDDR's.

Process flow

1. High-aspect-ratio etching (Bosch process, etc.) — a deep, narrow hole
2. Insulator deposition (ALD/CVD) — electrical isolation from the silicon
3. Barrier/seed layer deposition (ALD/PVD) — blocks Cu diffusion + seed for plating
4. Copper electroplating — fill without voids (bottom-up fill)
5. CMP — remove excess copper from the surface
6. Wafer thinning (backgrinding) — grind the back to expose the TSVs
7. Backside processing — insulation and pad formation

Hard problems

  • Void-free filling: the deep hole must be filled with copper without gaps. If the mouth closes first, a void forms inside. Plating chemistry that uses additives to fill from the bottom up is the key technology.
  • Thermal expansion mismatch (CTE mismatch): copper and silicon have different coefficients of thermal expansion. When the temperature changes, stress builds around the TSV, and that stress shifts the characteristics of nearby transistors. So a keep-out zone is set around each TSV where no devices are placed. This is where area overhead arises.
  • When to drill: drilling before the transistors are made is via-first; after the transistors but before the wiring layers are built, via-middle; after the wiring layers are finished, via-last. The order changes which high-temperature steps the TSV must survive and how the keep-out zone is designed. Stacked memory such as HBM is cited as a typical example on the via-first and via-middle side.
  • Handling thinned wafers (WSS, wafer support system): a wafer a few tens of μm thick cannot hold its shape and warps. So it is temporarily attached to a rigid carrier while its back side is processed. In order: before attaching it to the carrier, the edge of the wafer's front side is trimmed away (edge trimming). The wafer edge is rounded, so if it were attached as is and ground to a few tens of μm, the edge would be left as thin as a knife blade, and the later steps would break it from that tip. Next the wafer is attached to the carrier with a temporary adhesive, the back is ground to expose the TSVs, backside bumps are made, and the carrier is removed (debonding). Debonding must not break the thinned wafer, must not damage the bumps and must leave no adhesive behind, so the process conditions are demanding. Debonding methods can be classified by what neutralizes the adhesive layer: mechanical methods that lift the carrier off by force, thermal methods that soften the adhesive with heat, chemical methods that dissolve it with a solvent, and optical methods that decompose the adhesive layer with a laser. The laser method needs light to pass through the carrier, so it uses a glass carrier. (The process order and debonding methods are summarized from episode 8 of the SK hynix Newsroom series "Semiconductor Back-End Process.")
  • Tested and shipped as a stack: HBM is made by stacking a base die and DRAM dies, molding them, testing them as a stack and shipping them as a KGSD (known good stacked die). What the maker of the GPU package receives is not individual DRAM dies but a verified stack.

TGV and glass substrates

TGV (through-glass via): a via that passes through glass. Why glass substrates draw attention:

Advantage of glass What it means
Low dielectric loss Less loss of high-frequency signals → good for high-speed interconnect
Excellent flatness and stiffness Does not warp even over a large area → good for large packages
Adjustable CTE Can be matched to silicon → less stress
Large-panel processing possible Processed as square panels rather than round wafers → productivity

Remaining challenges: glass is brittle, so cracks propagate easily. Via formation (laser-induced etching and the like), metallization and breakage during handling are the gates to practical use. The schedule is still at the target stage. Announcing its glass substrates in September 2023, Intel said it "is on track to deliver complete glass substrate solutions to the market in the second half of this decade," and in July 2026 it announced a collaboration with the glass-processing company Lens Technology to accelerate development of glass substrate packaging. As of October 2026 we found no official announcement of volume production of glass-substrate packages.

5. Interposers — the board that connects the chips

Types and trade-offs

Type Wiring density Cost Use
Organic substrate Low (wiring at a pitch of a few μm is hard) Low Ordinary packages, low-bandwidth connections
RDL interposer (fan-out) Medium Medium InFO and others. Redistribution layers formed on organic material
Silicon interposer High (fine damascene wiring possible) High The standard for HBM connection. CoWoS-S
Silicon bridge (EMIB, etc.) High (only where needed) Medium Instead of making the whole interposer silicon, a piece of silicon is inserted only at the connection points
Glass interposer High (potentially) ? Under development

Package classification — fan-in and fan-out

To see where the "RDL interposer (fan-out)" in the table above comes from, you first need the classification of packages. The big division is when the wafer is cut. A conventional package first cuts the wafer, attaches each die to a leadframe or a substrate, and encapsulates it. A wafer-level package finishes package steps such as redistribution layers and bumps while still in wafer form, and only then cuts.

Within wafer level there is a further split. In fan-in (WLCSP), the solder balls sit only within the chip's area. If the chip is small, the number of balls is tied to its area. In fan-out, only good dies are picked, laid out again with spacing between them, and the gaps filled with molding compound (EMC) to make a "reconstituted wafer"; the redistribution layers are then spread out over the molding beyond the chip, and the balls placed there. Picking only good dies to lay out shares its root with the KGD logic of section 2. TSMC's InFO (Integrated Fan-Out) is a wafer-level package of this family, and TSMC states that it "has been shipping InFO in high volume since 2016." InFO also has a variant that ties a logic die and HBM together with redistribution layers (InFO_MS), which TSMC presents as offering "a cost/performance alternative to CoWoS for InFO size < 1X reticle."

Two criteria divide the tree: "when is the wafer cut?" and "do the balls go beyond the chip's area?" Redistribution layers, bumps and TSVs are less package types than wafer-stage building blocks that many packages share, so they are grouped separately with a dashed line.

Why HBM needs a silicon interposer

One HBM4 stack is 2,048 bits wide. Eight stacks make 16,384 data wires, with control, power and ground on top. These wires have to be packed densely across a distance of a few mm from the edge of the GPU die to the HBM.

That density is impossible at the wiring pitch of an organic substrate. A silicon interposer is made with semiconductor processes (damascene wiring), so pitches below a μm are possible. In other words, an interposer is "a chip that is nothing but wiring."

The problem this creates: a silicon interposer is also made with semiconductor processes, so it is subject to the exposure field limit. To carry a GPU and eight HBM stacks, the interposer has to be larger than the reticle. Hence:

  • CoWoS-S: a silicon interposer. Stitching is used to make it several times the reticle size. TSMC says it has been in production since 2012, with the interposer reaching up to 3.3 times the reticle (about 2,700 mm² in TSMC's figure; multiplying this book's 858 mm² gives about 2,830 mm²)
  • CoWoS-R: based on RDL (redistribution layers). Can be made larger and is cheaper, but the density is lower. TSMC recommends CoWoS-L or CoWoS-R for interposers larger than 3.3 times the reticle and says -R has been in volume production since 2023
  • CoWoS-L: local silicon interconnect (LSI) bridges inserted into the RDL. Silicon only where high density is needed, RDL elsewhere — combining the strengths of the two. The mainstream for the latest large AI packages. TSMC's "first CoWoS®-L at 3.5X-reticle size has been in volume production since 2024" (TSMC, checked October 2026)

Why CoWoS is the bottleneck of AI chip supply

  1. The process is complex and slow. It is multistage — interposer fabrication + chip bonding + substrate assembly — with yield loss at every stage.
  2. Adding capacity takes time. Ordering, installing and qualifying equipment takes years.
  3. Demand exploded. Each AI accelerator needs a very large interposer area, and shipments surged.
  4. It is effectively concentrated in one particular foundry.

On its CoWoS page TSMC writes: "With the advent of generative AI in late 2022, market demand for CoWoS® solutions has become even greater," and it "continues to expand its advanced packaging capacity" (checked October 2026). The size of that capacity and the allocations by company vary widely from report to report, so this book does not state them as figures.

Why it is not easy to reroute — the assembly order. There are two broad orders for assembling a 2.5D package. CoW-first keeps the interposer in wafer form, attaches the chips onto it first, molds at the wafer level, then attaches the wafer to a temporary carrier, grinds the back to expose the TSVs, builds the backside redistribution layers and bumps, and finally cuts the wafer and mounts the pieces on substrates. There is a process report that actually went through this order with a 300 mm silicon interposer (Ho et al., EPTC 2014). The name CoWoS itself (chip-on-wafer-on-substrate) points to this order. CoS-first cuts the interposer first, attaches it to the organic substrate, and places the chips on top. What separates the two is warpage. Silicon's coefficient of thermal expansion is much smaller than an organic substrate's. If a large silicon interposer is attached to the substrate first, the two layers shrink differently as they cool from the bonding temperature, and warp; when the chips are then placed, tens of thousands of microbumps have to be aligned on that warped surface. CoW-first finishes the fine bonding first on a flat, rigid wafer, which reduces the problem (the warpage of the molded interposer still has to be managed in CoW-first). The larger the interposer, the wider the gap. But CoW-first needs wafer-level molding, thinning and redistribution steps, so places without such equipment and experience cannot easily take over. That is one of the reasons the bottleneck gathers in one place.

The "bottleneck keeps moving" of Session 1 takes concrete form here. Even with room to spare in logic wafer capacity, if CoWoS capacity and HBM supply fall short, only that many AI accelerators can be made. What caps AI chip shipments is not the latest node but packaging and memory.

6. Bonding — a generational change in how chips are joined

The path of evolution

Generation Method Pitch Characteristics
Wire bonding Gold or copper wires connect chip pads to the substrate Tens of μm Connections only at the edge, limited I/O count, high inductance
Flip chip (C4 bumps) The chip is flipped and joined directly with solder bumps ~100 μm The whole face can be used → I/O count soars
Microbumps Small solder bumps ~40 μm or less The workhorse of 2.5D/3D stacking
Microbumps + gap fill (MR-MUF / TC-NCF) MR-MUF: stack all the chips, reflow them all at once to join the bumps, then flow a liquid protective material between the chips and cure it. TC-NCF: lay a non-conductive film on each layer and press the layers on one at a time with heat and pressure Same as microbumps The stacking method of volume-production HBM as of October 2026. The bumps are the same; what differs is how the gap is filled
Hybrid bonding (Cu-Cu) Copper pads bonded directly to each other without bumps + the surrounding dielectric bonded too Sub-10 μm Highest density, lowest resistance, lowest inductance

Stack form and yield — W2W and D2W. Dies are stacked as chip on chip (C2C), die on wafer (D2W, also called C2W) or wafer on wafer (W2W). W2W joins two wafers in one go and is highly productive, but the upper and lower dies must have the same size and layout, and above all you cannot pick good dies to join. A defective die on the upper wafer lands as is on a good die of the lower wafer. So when n layers are stacked, the stack-yield formula of section 5 of Session 3 applies directly.

YW2W=yn×ybondn−1

D2W cuts and tests the dies, then picks only the good ones (KGD) and joins them onto the wafer. Suppose the bottom wafer is also tested in advance and stacking happens only on its good die sites. If screening is perfect, the die-yield term drops out and only the bonding yield remains.

YD2W≈ybondn−1

The denominator of this formula is the good sites of the bottom wafer. If you also stack on the bottom wafer's defective sites, or count those sites in the denominator, the bottom die yield is multiplied in once and the result becomes y·ybondn−1. With the assumed values below and n=8, that is 0.869, which is 2.09 times W2W rather than 2.32 times. The value of the discarded bottom sites remains as a cost.

With die yield y=0.9 and the yield of one bonding step ybond=0.995 (both assumed values; the bonding yield is the same as the example in section 5 of Session 3), the calculation goes as follows.

Stack count n W2W ynybondn−1 D2W ybondn−1 D2W ÷ W2W
2 0.806 0.995 1.23 times
8 0.416 0.966 2.32 times
12 0.267 0.946 3.54 times
16 0.172 0.928 5.40 times

With two layers the gap is in the 20% range, but as layers are added it widens several-fold. That is why W2W suits processes with few layers, dies of the same size and high yield. TSMC, too, presents its wafer-on-wafer SoIC-X as "suitable for high yielding nodes and the same die size applications or design." Even in D2W, though, the value of the discarded defective dies remains as a cost. The yield loss does not disappear; it moves to before stacking, so good dies are no longer thrown away along with bad ones. It is the KGD logic of pressure ① in section 2, extended in the stacking direction.

The figure below shows eight layers stacked with the assumed values of the table above (y=0.9, ybond=0.995). In the screen edition you can change the die yield, the bonding yield and the stack count.

Why hybrid bonding matters

The problem with bumps: bumps have a physical size. To shrink the pitch you have to make the bumps smaller, but small solder joints are less reliable and have higher electrical resistance. The underfill material that fills the space between bumps also becomes hard to inject as the space narrows. Bump-based methods hit a wall at a pitch of roughly a few tens of μm.

How hybrid bonding works: the surfaces of two wafers (or dies) are made flat at the atomic level, and surfaces where the copper pads and the dielectric (mainly SiO₂) are exposed together are pressed face to face. At room temperature the dielectric surfaces bond first (van der Waals → covalent bonds); a later anneal makes the copper expand and diffusion-bond to the copper opposite.

What you gain: the pitch drops into the sub-10 μm range, so the number of connections per unit area exceeds that of microbumps (about 40 μm) by more than 16 times (100 times at a 4 μm pitch), the resistance and parasitics of the joint fall dramatically, and the stack becomes lower.

What it demands (extreme)

  • Surface flatness: on the scale of angstroms. CMP quality decides everything
  • Cleanliness: a single particle ruins the bond at that spot
  • Alignment accuracy: a few hundred nm or less. Die-to-die alignment equipment becomes a new bottleneck
  • Copper recess control: the copper must sit slightly below the dielectric, and that amount has to be controlled at the nanometer level

Where it is used: CMOS image sensors have been mass-produced this way for many years. 3D logic stacking is moving in this direction too (TSMC's SoIC and others; TSMC states that SoIC's "bond pitch starts from the sub-10µm rule" and that "its 3nm chip stacking technology successfully entered volume production in 2025"). For HBM it is a candidate for next-generation high stacks, because as the layer count rises, the height of the bumps and gap-fill layers runs into the stack height limit. SK hynix said in 2023 that in 2022 it had stacked an 8-high HBM2E with hybrid bonding and completed electrical tests, but the 12-high HBM4E samples it supplied to customers in June 2026 used Advanced MR-MUF. As of October 2026 we found no manufacturer announcement of volume production of HBM using hybrid bonding (the same judgment as in section 4 of Session 3).

A point to note: hybrid bonding demands front-end precision of the back end. This is why foundries, not OSATs, are taking over this area.

7. 2.5D and 3D — the exact distinction

Definitions

  • 2.5D: chips placed side by side (horizontally) on an interposer. The chips do not overlap vertically. Typical: GPU + HBM stacks (CoWoS)
  • 3D: chips overlapped vertically. Typical: the DRAM stacking inside an HBM stack, logic or cache stacked on logic (SoIC, Foveros)

Where the name "2.5D" comes from: not fully 3D, but more integrated than a flat layout. The HBM stack itself is 3D, so a GPU+HBM system is a structure with 3D inside 2.5D.

Comparison

2.5D 3D
Connection distance mm scale (via the interposer) μm scale (direct stacking)
Bandwidth density High Very high
Heat removal Each chip can see the heat sink The upper chip covers the lower one and traps the heat
Area Large interposer area Small footprint
Process difficulty Medium High
Design complexity Medium High (heat, power and EDA alike)

The greatest enemy of 3D — heat

This is the fundamental hard problem of 3D stacking.

  • Overlapping chips multiplies the heat per unit area by the number of layers.
  • The heat of the lower chip has to pass through the upper chip to get out, and the silicon and bonding layers have thermal resistance. The chip on top effectively acts as a blanket.
  • As temperature rises, leakage current grows, and as leakage grows, more heat is produced: a positive feedback loop.
  • So 3D logic stacking usually puts the layer that generates less heat on top (for example, cache SRAM on logic). Overlapping high-power logic with high-power logic is still hard.

The same problem in HBM: in a 12–16-high stack, the heat of the bottom die does not escape well. Together with the stack height limit, this constrains the number of layers. Manufacturers advertise this value too. When SK hynix supplied 12-high HBM4E samples in June 2026, it said it had lowered thermal resistance by about 17% compared with HBM4.

Heat leaving the package — θ and ψ. The R=t/(kA) seen so far is the thermal resistance of a single layer. Datasheets roll the whole package into a few numbers. θJA (junction to ambient air), θJC (junction to case) and θJB (junction to board), defined in the JEDEC JESD51 family, are the difference between the junction temperature Tj and the temperature at a reference point, divided by the power dissipated P. For example, since θJA=(Tj−Ta)/P, it follows that Tj=Ta+PθJA. But θJA is measured on a standard test board in still air or at a fixed air speed, so the value changes when the board and airflow change. A Renesas technical brief notes that a test board with two copper planes (1S2P) lowers θJA by roughly 20–40% or more compared with a board with none (1S0P), and TI notes that θJA is a value for comparing packages under the same conditions, not for calculating Tj in an actual design. To work backward to Tj from the temperature of the top of the package or of the board on a real board, you use ψJT and ψJB. The formula looks the same as θ's, but since not all the heat flows between those two points, it is not a true thermal resistance but a characterization parameter.

Seeing it as a series chain. In a package with a heat sink attached, heat flows in turn from the junction → case → TIM → heat sink (or cold plate) → ambient (air or coolant). Being in series, the resistances add.

Tj=Ta+P(θJC+θTIM+θSA)

θSA is the thermal resistance from the heat sink to ambient. Take one worked example. The values below are all assumed values, not those of any particular product. With P = 1,000 W, Ta = 35 °C (you may read it as the coolant inlet temperature), θJC = 0.015 K/W, θTIM = 0.025 K/W and θSA = 0.020 K/W, the sum is 0.060 K/W. The temperature differences at each stage are 15 K, 25 K and 20 K, 60 K in total, so Tj = 95 °C. This has to be below the maximum junction temperature Tj,max that each product's datasheet sets. The assumed values give the largest share to the TIM to preview the point of section 3 of Session 7: the thin layer between chip and cold plate easily becomes the bottleneck of the whole chain.

On to Session 7: the data center cooling problem is the heat problem extended from inside the chip to the scale of the rack.

The figure below shows how temperature builds up from ambient to junction with the assumed values of the worked example above. In the screen edition you can change the power dissipated, the ambient temperature and the three thermal resistances, and enter a datasheet's maximum junction temperature to see whether it is exceeded.

The structure of a real AI accelerator package

What to check here

  • Inside the HBM stack = 3D; the relation between GPU and HBM = 2.5D
  • The whole package area is several times the reticle → extension techniques such as CoWoS-L are needed
  • One such package draws power in the kilowatt range, and that heat has to leave through the cold plate (Session 7)

Package reliability — how much heat and moisture can it take?

Heat does not stop at raising the temperature. Long exposure to heat degrades materials, and each power cycle makes materials expand and contract by different amounts, fatiguing the joints. Moisture brings corrosion. So new products go through qualification tests that deliberately break them under harsh conditions before shipment. Below are the main items taken from Table 1 (device tests) and Table 2 (tests for nonhermetic packages) of JEDEC JESD47I (July 2012 edition). JEDEC issued JESD47N in August 2026. We did not check against the text of the latest edition.

Test Standard Conditions (JESD47I) Sample and pass criterion Failure targeted
HTOL (high temperature operating life) JESD22-A108 Junction temperature ≥ 125 °C, ≥ maximum supply voltage, 1,000 hours 3 lots × 77 units, 0 fails Failures from heat and voltage during operation
ELFR (early life failure rate) JESD22-A108, JESD74 Junction temperature ≥ 125 °C, 48–168 hours ELFR sample table Early failures in the first months after shipment
HTSL (high temperature storage life) JESD22-A103 150 °C, 1,000 hours 3 lots × 25 units, 0 fails Material degradation such as diffusion, oxidation and intermetallic growth
THB (temperature humidity bias) JESD22-A101 85 °C, 85% relative humidity, bias applied, 1,000 hours 3 lots × 25 units, 0 fails Corrosion and ion migration from moisture
HAST (highly accelerated stress test) JESD22-A110 130 °C or 110 °C, 85% relative humidity, bias applied, 96 hours or 264 hours 3 lots × 25 units, 0 fails A shortened, accelerated THB
UHAST (unbiased HAST) JESD22-A118 96 hours at 130 °C and 85%, or 264 hours at 110 °C and 85% 3 lots × 25 units, 0 fails Corrosion
TC (temperature cycling) JESD22-A104 e.g., condition B is −55 to +125 °C, 700 cycles 3 lots × 25 units, 0 fails Thermomechanical damage from thermal expansion differences

Source: selected from Tables 1 and 2 of JEDEC JESD47I (2012-07). The layout of the table and the "Failure targeted" column are this book's own summary.

There are rules outside the table, too. THB, HAST, TC and UHAST (and autoclave) are preceded by preconditioning: following JESD22-A113, the parts are soaked in moisture according to their moisture sensitivity level (MSL) under J-STD-020 and put through reflow, giving them in advance the stress of being soldered to a board. Autoclave, which steams parts in saturated vapor, can cause damage that does not occur in real use, so it is not recommended as a qualification test, and HAST is required instead for organic-substrate packages. There is also a note that the TC conditions that go below freezing, G, B and C, may not suit organic-substrate flip-chip packages. The thermal expansion mismatch and warpage that trouble 3D stacks and large interposers are exactly the failures TC targets. The keep-out zone of section 4 and CoW-first in section 5 both came from the same physics.

How many years is 1,000 hours? — the Arrhenius conversion. For failures accelerated by temperature, test time is commonly converted to use time with the Arrhenius equation.

AF=exp[Eak(1Tuse−1Tstress)]

Ea is the apparent activation energy, k=8.617×10−5 eV/K is Boltzmann's constant, and temperatures are absolute (K). With a test at 125 °C (398.15 K), use at 55 °C (328.15 K) and Ea = 0.7 eV, AF≈77.7. HTOL's 1,000 hours correspond to about 77,700 hours; dividing by 8,760 hours a year gives about 8.87 years. JESD47I, in a note to Table 1, gives the same conditions as an example with an acceleration factor of 78.6, about 9 years (the last digit differs because of the constant and rounding).

Change only Ea under the same conditions and the conclusion swings widely.

Ea Acceleration factor AF Equivalent use period of 1,000 hours of HTOL
0.5 eV 22.4 about 2.56 years
0.7 eV 77.7 about 8.87 years
0.9 eV 269.3 about 30.7 years

Between 0.5 eV and 0.9 eV, the equivalent use period of the same test differs about 12-fold. Ea differs by failure mechanism. That is why one test cannot tell you "this chip will last nine years." JESD47I itself adds the caveat that this period may be shorter than actual use requirements and depends on the failure mechanism and use environment, and says long-term wear-out mechanisms should be covered by wafer-level reliability data. JEDEC JEP122 collects acceleration models by failure mechanism.

The figure below is for Ea = 0.7 eV, 125 °C → 55 °C, 1,000 hours. In the screen edition you can change Ea, the test and use temperatures, and the test time.

8. Heterogeneous integration and the chiplet standard (UCIe)

The dream of a chiplet ecosystem

If chiplets could be connected through a standard interface, systems could be built by combining chiplets made by different companies. You would assemble a chip the way you assemble a computer.

UCIe (Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express) is the standard for this. It places PCIe/CXL protocols on top of a die-to-die physical layer and specifies separate versions by package type (standard package / advanced package). An industry consortium announced its launch in March 2022, and version 2.0 in August 2024 added 3D packaging aimed at hybrid bonding (UCIe-3D) and a management and test architecture that spans chiplets. As of October 2026, the latest edition on the official specifications page is 3.0, released on August 5, 2025. 3.0 added data rates of 48 GT/s and 64 GT/s, doubling the top speed of 32 GT/s in 2.0.

Understanding it through a software analogy

Chiplet concept Software counterpart
Chiplet Microservice
UCIe Standard API / RPC protocol
Interposer Service mesh / network
Heterogeneous integration Polyglot architecture (the best language for each service)
Die-to-die latency Network hop latency

And the trade-offs are the same. A monolith gets internal communication for free but has to be deployed whole; splitting it allows reuse and independent development but costs something every time a boundary is crossed.

Why it is still hard

  1. Testing and quality assurance. If one chiplet is defective, the whole package already assembled is lost. Complete KGD assurance before assembly is essential, but it is hard to test fine, high-speed interfaces completely before assembly.
  2. Liability. If you combine chiplets from several companies and the system does not work, whose fault is it? A real barrier to a commercial ecosystem.
  3. Integrated thermal and power design. Each chiplet produces a different amount of heat, and power delivery has to be designed at the package level.
  4. Physical compatibility. Even with the same protocol, the bump pitch, die thickness and package process have to match. A standard that fixes only the protocol is not enough.
  5. EDA tools. Tools for designing and verifying several dies together (multi-die STA, coupled thermal-electrical simulation) are still maturing.

The reality: as of 2026, chiplets are used mainly within one company (in-house chiplets). A truly open chiplet market has not formed yet. But as standardization proceeds, the direction is clear. Version 2.0's addition of a test and management architecture to the standard is aimed at problem 1 above (testing and quality assurance).

9. Signal integrity — familiar ground if you have a communications background

As wires multiply into the tens of thousands and speeds rise, an electrical signal is no longer "0 and 1" but a high-frequency transmission-line problem.

Phenomenon Cause Remedy
Insertion loss Conductor skin effect, dielectric loss. Worse at higher frequency Low-loss materials, equalization (EQ)
Reflection Impedance discontinuities Impedance matching, termination resistors
Crosstalk Capacitive and inductive coupling between neighboring wires Wire spacing, ground shielding, optimized wire ordering
Simultaneous switching noise (SSN) Many outputs switch at once and the power network shakes Decoupling capacitors, power network design
Jitter Fluctuation in clock and data timing CDR, equalizers
Skew Arrival times misaligned by differences in wire length Length matching

The evaluation tool: an eye diagram is drawn by cutting the received waveform into one-bit lengths and overlaying them. The larger the open "eye" in the middle, the larger the margin before 0 and 1 are misread; as loss, reflection, noise and jitter grow, the eye closes. The remedies use the ideas of digital communication as they are. The CDR (clock and data recovery) in the table above is a circuit that recovers the clock timing from the transition points of the received data waveform without a separate clock line. Among equalizers, a CTLE (continuous-time linear equalizer) boosts again, with an analog filter at the receiver, the high-frequency components the channel ate away, and a DFE (decision feedback equalizer) estimates and subtracts the tails (intersymbol interference) left by preceding bits already decided as 0 or 1. Pre-emphasis, which boosts the signal at the moment of transition before sending it from the transmitter, and coding, which plants rules in the signal, serve the same purpose.

This completes the logic of Session 3. Why did HBM choose width over frequency? Because every problem in the table above worsens with frequency. Widening the bus gives the same bandwidth at a lower frequency, easing signal integrity and power problems together. HBM is a packaging answer to the signal integrity problem.

10. Common misconceptions

Misconception 1: "The back end is easier than the front end" → Hybrid bonding demands angstrom-level flatness and nanometer alignment. Advanced packaging demands front-end-level precision.

Misconception 2: "2.5D is a kind of 3D, so they are roughly the same" → Their thermal characteristics are completely different. That difference decides the range of feasible designs.

Misconception 3: "Splitting into chiplets always makes it cheaper" → There are the area and power overhead of interface circuits, assembly costs and assembly yield loss. If the die is small, splitting is a loss.

Misconception 4: "Memory companies make all of HBM" → The memory companies make the HBM stacks, but the 2.5D packaging that joins them to the GPU is done by foundries (mainly TSMC). The supply chain is split, and both sides can be bottlenecks.

Misconception 5: "Now that UCIe is out, the era of buying chiplets and assembling them is near" → A protocol standard alone is not enough. Testing, quality assurance, liability and physical compatibility remain.

Misconception 6: "A TSV is just a hole filled with copper" → Stress from thermal expansion mismatch shifts the characteristics of the surrounding transistors and creates the design constraint called the keep-out zone. It is a mechanical problem, not an electrical one, that constrains the design.

Misconception 7: "Packaging capacity is easier to add than fab capacity" → Advanced packaging equipment also has long lead times and needs a yield ramp. In practice it has been a bottleneck of AI chip supply.

Misconception 8: "Today's HBM is stacked with hybrid bonding" → As of October 2026, volume-production HBM and the customer samples manufacturers have announced are stacked with TSVs and microbumps, with the gaps between chips filled by MR-MUF or TC-NCF. Hybrid bonding is a next-generation candidate for higher layer counts (section 6).

Misconception 9: "It passed 1,000 hours of HTOL, so its lifetime is nine years" → That conversion hangs on a single activation energy Ea, and Ea differs by failure mechanism. Under the same conditions, 0.5 eV gives about 2.6 years and 0.9 eV about 31 years (section 7, reliability).

11. Quantitative exercises

Exercise 1 — Chiplet gains and losses, the full version With D0=0.1/cm², split a total area of 800 mm² into (a) 1, (b) 2, (c) 4 and (d) 8 pieces, and for each find the following. Write costs as multiples of W, the price of one wafer (the same symbol as in Session 4; not the power unit W, the watt).

  • Yield per die and good dies per wafer
  • Interface overhead (+5% area per additional split)
  • Assembly yield (×0.99 for each additional die)
  • Total cost

Calculate these and find the optimal number of splits. How does the optimum shift if D0 is changed to 0.05 or 0.2?

Exercise 2 — Wiring energy Assume the parasitic capacitance of a 10mm wire (substrate) and a 50μm wire (TSV) is proportional to length, and use E=12CV2 to find the ratio of energy per bit. What is the power difference when transmitting 1012 bits per second?

Exercise 3 — Interposer area With a GPU die of 800 mm² and eight HBM stacks (about 100 mm² each), estimate the interposer area needed, allowing for spacing between the stacks. How many times the reticle limit is it? Which CoWoS variant is needed?

Exercise 4 — The 3D heat problem If one chip has a power density of 1 W/mm², what is the heat flux per unit footprint when chips are stacked two and four high? Allowing for the thermal resistance of passing through 50μm of silicon, roughly estimate the temperature difference between layers. (Thermal conductivity of silicon about 150 W/m·K)

Exercise 5 — Counting the wires How many data wires alone are needed to attach eight HBM4 stacks? If power, ground and control are assumed to be twice the data wires, how many in total? If the HBM stacks are attached four each to two opposite sides of the GPU die (each side about 30 mm), and these wires come out in a single row along the edges of those two sides, what pitch is needed?

12. Discussion questions

  1. If the field reduction of High-NA EUV raises the incentive to choose chiplets, are scaling and integration rival strategies or complementary ones?
  2. How does the trend of foundries absorbing packaging change the OSAT industry? What is left for OSATs?
  3. What has to be solved first for an open chiplet market to form? Is there anything to learn from the history of software ecosystems?
  4. Is the heat problem of 3D logic stacking one that cooling can solve, or one that has to be avoided by design?
  5. Can glass substrates replace silicon interposers? If they do, what changes will follow in the industry's structure?
  6. Seeing that the bottleneck of AI chip supply has moved from logic → CoWoS → HBM, where do you think the next bottleneck will be?

13. Further study

  • Standard textbook: Lau, Semiconductor Advanced Packaging (Springer, 2021) and the same author's series of books on 3D ICs and fan-out — the most systematic body of material in this field
  • Introductory series: SK hynix Newsroom, "Semiconductor Back-End Process," 11 episodes (2022-09 to 2023-09 in the Korean original) — from Episode 1: Understanding Semiconductor Testing to Episode 11: Reliability Tests and Standards for Semiconductor Packages. It covers, in order, testing, package types, conventional and wafer-level processes, materials and reliability. Check its figures and terms against this book's primary sources as you read
  • Hybrid bonding: public presentations from imec and CEA-Leti, papers from ECTC (Electronic Components and Technology Conference)
  • Industry technical material: TSMC's 3DFabric (CoWoS/InFO/SoIC) technology pages, Intel's advanced packaging (Foveros/EMIB) pages, Siemens EDA's 3D IC guide to heterogeneous integration
  • Chiplet standard: UCIe specifications (1.0–3.0, available on request)
  • Reliability and heat: JEDEC JESD47 (the backbone of qualification testing; the text is based on JESD47I of July 2012, and the current edition is JESD47N), JEDEC JESD51-12 (guidelines for reporting and using thermal information), Renesas TB379, "Thermal Characterization of Packaged Semiconductor Devices" — explains θ and ψ with drawings of the test boards
  • Signal integrity: Bogatin, Signal and Power Integrity — Simplified — well regarded for its intuitive explanations. Hall & Heck, Advanced Signal Integrity for High-Speed Digital Designs (advanced)
  • Conferences: ECTC, IEEE 3D-IC Conference, Hot Chips (product-level architecture disclosures)

Self-study appendix A — solutions to the quantitative exercises

Solution to Exercise 1 — Chiplet gains and losses, the full version

SolutionSolution

Setup: a total silicon area of 800 mm² is split into n pieces. Each split adds 5% interface area overhead cumulatively (total area =800×[1+0.05(n−1)]), assembly yield is 0.99n−1, and D0=0.1/cm². The cost is the silicon cost of one good system, written as a multiple of W, the price of one wafer (cassembly=0 in the exact comparison formula of section 2). The W in the tables below is not the watt.

GDPW(A)=πd2/4A−πd2A≈706.9A−94.252A(d=30 cm, A in cm2)

The values in the tables were computed with unrounded π. Computing with the rounded coefficients 706.9 and 94.25 changes the last digit in a few cells (for example, GDPW 466.3 for n=8, and a cost of 0.03434W for n=1 at D0=0.1). The conclusions do not change.

At D0=0.1

n Chiplet area GDPW Yield Good dies Systems/wafer Assembly yield Effective Cost
1 8.00 cm² 64.8 0.449 29.1 29.1 1.000 29.1 0.03435W
2 4.20 135.8 0.657 89.2 44.6 0.990 44.2 0.02264W
4 2.30 263.4 0.795 209.3 52.3 0.970 50.8 0.01970W
8 1.35 466.2 0.874 407.4 50.9 0.932 47.5 0.02107W

The optimum is n=4, a 42.6% saving over a single die. What matters is that it gets worse again at n=8 — interface overhead and assembly yield loss begin to eat up the yield gain.

Change D0 and the optimum moves — the key finding of this exercise

n D0=0.05 D0=0.1 D0=0.2
1 0.02302W 0.03435W 0.07644W
2 0.01836 0.02264 0.03446
4 0.01756 0.01970 0.02479
8 0.01969 0.02107 0.02412
Optimum n=4 n=4 n=8
Saving 23.7% 42.6% 68.5%

This table compares only the four values the exercise picked. Widening the calculation to every integer number of splits from 1 to 16, the optimum is n=3 at D0=0.05 (0.01754W, a 23.8% saving), n=4 at D0=0.1 (unchanged; almost the same as 0.01971W for n=5), and n=6 at D0=0.2 (0.02364W, a 69.1% saving). The direction is the same: the more defects, the finer the split. Near the optimum, though, the curve is flat. At D0=0.1, n=4~6 all come within 2% of the optimum.

Three conclusions

  1. The more defects there are, the more it pays to split finely. At D0=0.2 the optimal split moves to 8, and the saving reaches 68.5%.
  2. With few defects, the advantage of chiplets fades. At D0=0.05 the saving shrinks to 23.7%, and adding assembly and interposer costs can reverse it.
  3. An optimal number of splits exists. Split without limit and the overhead wins. The shape of this curve is why real products cluster in the range of 2–8 chiplets.

Implications — reading it as industrial strategy

In cost terms, chiplets are a tool that lets you use the latest node early, while its yield is still poor. That those trying to enter the latest node first, and AI accelerators that need large dies, adopted chiplets early fits this direction. Conversely, for small chips at mature nodes the yield gain is small, and on cost alone chiplets are likely to lose. But what this exercise shows is a single cost motive coming from yield. Area beyond the reticle limit (pressure ②), heterogeneous integration that uses a different process for each block (pressure ③) and design reuse are also reasons to use chiplets (the same scope as the solution to Exercise 4 of Session 4), so this calculation alone cannot decide where chiplets are used and where they are not.

Combine this with Exercise 5 of Session 5 and the picture is complete. High-NA shrinks the largest die that can be printed in one shot to 429 mm². If you need a circuit of 800 mm², you must choose between stitching and partitioning, and this exercise shows that under its assumptions partitioning is also the economical choice. The incentive to choose chiplets grows accordingly.

The figure below shows the assumptions of this exercise with D0=0.1 and n=4. In the screen edition you can change D0, the number of splits, the overhead and the assembly yield, and you can also switch to the assumptions of Exercise 4 of Session 4 (10% overhead per chiplet, an assembly yield of 0.95 applied once).

Solution to Exercise 2 — Wiring energy

SolutionSolution

If parasitic capacitance is proportional to length,

CsubstrateCTSV=10 mm50 μm=200 times

From E=12CV2, at the same voltage the energy per bit is also 200 times.

At 1012 bits per second

Taking the energy per bit on the TSV side as 0.05 pJ/bit:

Path pJ/bit Power at 1 Tbit/s
TSV (50 μm) 0.05 0.05 W
Substrate wiring (10 mm) 10 10 W

A difference of about 10 W. On its own this does not look large. Scale it up to real size, though, and the story changes.

When one HBM stack runs at 4 TB/s =3.2×1013 bit/s

Path Power
Interposer/TSV level 1.6 W
Substrate wiring level 320 W

With eight stacks it is 12.8 W vs 2,560 W. As seen in section 7, one such package draws power in the kilowatt range (the worked example in section 7 also used 1,000 W). Spending 2.56 kW on memory wiring alone would exceed the whole power budget of the package, so under this assumption the design does not work.

Conclusion: putting HBM on the interposer right next to the GPU is not a convenience but a necessity. If you cannot shorten the distance, that bandwidth cannot be delivered within the power budget.

This is where it connects to Session 3. Exercise 2 of Session 3 said the choice of "many slow pins" was made because of power. But using many pins needs room to attach them, and making that room needs an interposer. Bandwidth → power → distance → packaging line up in one chain.

Caution: the factor of 200 comes from assuming the same capacitance per unit length and the same voltage. Real wires differ in cross-section, insulator, parasitics and driver circuits, so this ratio does not come out as is. To note just one direction of difference: substrate I/O often uses a higher voltage swing for signal integrity, so the gap can widen further through the V2 term.

The figure below is for 10 mm of substrate wiring vs 50 μm of TSV, 0.05 pJ/bit on the TSV side and 1012 bits per second. In the screen edition you can change the two lengths, the energy per bit and the bit rate (including one HBM stack at 4 TB/s).

Solution to Exercise 3 — Interposer area

SolutionSolution

Estimating the area needed

Component Area
GPU die 800 mm²
8 HBM stacks × 100 mm² 800 mm²
Subtotal 1,600 mm²
Allowance for spacing between stacks, molding and peripheral wiring (25%) 400 mm²
Total about 2,000 mm²

Compared with the reticle limit

2,000858≈2.3 times

It cannot be made with a single exposure. The interposer itself is silicon, and the wiring of a silicon interposer is also made by lithography, so it faces the same 858 mm² constraint.

Three solutions

Approach What it does Character
Stitching Joins several fields to make a large interposer Alignment accuracy and defects are the issue
Local bridges (CoWoS-L / EMIB family) Instead of a full silicon interposer, small silicon bridges are inserted only where connections are needed. The layer around the bridge differs by structure. CoWoS-L puts the bridge (LSI) inside an RDL interposer, and that interposer is in turn mounted on the package substrate. Intel EMIB has no interposer. Intel describes it as "Silicon bridge embedded in package substrate for shoreline-to-shoreline connection"; the bridge joins the facing edges of two dies Gets around the area constraint. The current mainstream direction
Large-area RDL substrate Covers the whole with organic redistribution layers Wiring density lower than silicon

Enlarging a silicon interposer as a whole adds a yield burden on top of the reticle limit. Let us only gauge how large it could get. Applying a logic die's D0=0.1/cm² as is to a 2,000 mm² (20 cm²) interposer gives e−2.0=13.5% by the formula of Session 4. There is no basis for assuming that a passive interposer carrying only wiring has the same real defect density as a logic die, so 13.5% is not an actual manufacturing yield but a sensitivity example under the assumption of the same defect density. The direction is from "silicon everywhere" to "silicon only where needed." TSMC keeping the silicon interposer (CoWoS-S) to 3.3 times the reticle and offering, for larger packages, the RDL-based CoWoS-R and CoWoS-L with local bridges (3.5 times, in volume production in 2024) follows this direction as well.

This is why AI accelerator supply runs into CoWoS capacity before logic wafers — the substance of the bottleneck foreshadowed in section 5 of Session 1.

Solution to Exercise 4 — The 3D heat problem

SolutionSolution

Heat flux per unit footprint

Stack chips with a power density of 1 W/mm² and it multiplies directly.

Stack Heat flux per footprint
1 layer 1 W/mm²
2 layers 2 W/mm²
4 layers 4 W/mm²

For reference, 4 W/mm² =400 W/cm². For a sense of scale, take an electric stove that puts out 2 kW from a burner 20 cm in diameter and divide the power by the burner area: about 6.4 W/cm² (a calculation with assumed values). The heat flux per footprint of a four-layer stack is more than 60 times that.

Thermal resistance of 50 μm of silicon (per 1 mm²)

R=tkA=50×10−6150×10−6=0.333 K/W

Temperature differences between layers in a four-layer stack (heat removed upward only, each layer dissipating 1 W/mm²)

The heat of the lower layers has to pass through all the layers above.

Segment Heat passing ΔT
Layer 1 → layer 2 1 W 0.33 K
Layer 2 → layer 3 2 W 0.67 K
Layer 3 → layer 4 3 W 1.00 K
Layer 4 → heat-removal surface 4 W 1.33 K
Total 3.33 K

An unexpected result: the silicon alone accounts for only 3.3 K. Silicon conducts heat very well.

Then where does the heat problem of 3D stacking come from? — the interfaces

Silicon is not all that lies between layers. There are microbumps, underfill and adhesive layers, and their effective thermal conductivity is about 1–5 W/(m·K), around 1/50 of silicon's. Taking a thickness of 20 μm and k=3 W/(m·K),

Rinterface=20×10−63×10−6=6.67 K/W

How many interfaces are there? With four layers there are three between layers, and one more bonding layer between the top die and the heat-removal surface. Here all four are taken to be the same material (20 μm, k=3). The heat crossing each interface is 1, 2, 3 and 4 W, as for the silicon segments, so (1+2+3+4)×6.67=66.7 K. If the top bond is counted separately as a different material such as a TIM and only the three internal interfaces are included, (1+2+3)×6.67=40 K, and 43.3 K with the silicon added.

Silicon 3.3 K vs interfaces 66.7 K — a factor of 20. Together, the temperature difference between the bottom layer and the heat-removal surface is about 70 K (four-interface model).

Two conclusions

  1. The thermal bottleneck of 3D stacking is not the silicon but the bonding interfaces. So the remedy lies less in thinning the silicon than in lowering the thermal resistance of the interfaces.
  2. Hybrid bonding is a strong candidate. Instead of layers of bumps and underfill, it joins copper and dielectric directly, so the bonding layer becomes much thinner. Hybrid bonding is usually introduced as "a technology for shrinking pitch," but it also matters a great deal from a thermal point of view. That is as far as this calculation goes, however. Removing the interfaces in the figure below drops 70 K to 3.3 K, but that is an idealization that sets the thermal resistance of all four interfaces, up to the top heat-removal bond, to 0. A hybrid bond still leaves two bonded surfaces, copper and dielectric (section 6), and their effective thermal conductivity and the copper area fraction were not calculated here. Volume-production HBM is also lowering thermal resistance by improving gap-fill materials (section 6; about 17% for SK hynix's 12-high HBM4E samples). To state the actual improvement, you would have to recalculate with the material values of the bonding layer.

This logic of a thermal-resistance chain extends directly into Session 7. The path from chip to coolant has the same structure, and there too the bottleneck is the layer that conducts heat worst (the TIM).

The figure below shows the temperature difference that builds up in each segment for four layers of 1 W/mm² chips, 50 μm of silicon and interfaces of 20 μm at 3 W/(m·K). In the screen edition you can change the number of layers, the power density, the thicknesses and thermal conductivities, and remove the interfaces.

Solution to Exercise 5 — Counting the wires

SolutionSolution

Data wires

Taking the data bus of one HBM4 stack as 2,048 bits,

8 stacks×2,048=16,384 wires

Assuming power, ground and control are twice the data wires

16,384×2=32,768 wires

Total=16,384+32,768=49,152 wires

What if they come out in a single row along the edges of two sides (30 mm each)?

With four stacks on each of two opposite sides, as the exercise sets out, each side carries 49,152 ÷ 2 = 24,576 wires.

Pitch=30 mm24,576=1.22 μm

(If all eight stacks were attached to a single side, 49,152 wires would have to fit into 30 mm, giving 0.61 μm.)

That is unrealistic with today's connection methods. The pitch of the microbumps that join the GPU and HBM to the interposer is about 40 μm (section 6), and 1.22 μm is a 33rd of that. On the pitch number alone it falls within the sub-10 μm range claimed for hybrid bonding, but as seen in section 6, hybrid bonding is not the volume-production method for HBM connections as of October 2026, and that pitch is the pad pitch of an area array, not a value that assumes a single row along an edge.

So what is actually done — a two-dimensional area array

The connections are laid out not in one row along the edge but as a grid over the whole underside of the die. The area needed is

Pitch Area needed Relative to the GPU die (800 mm²)
40 μm (microbumps) 49,152×(0.04)2=78.6 mm² 9.8%
9 μm (hybrid bonding) 4.0 mm² 0.5%

Two conclusions

  1. The shift from peripheral I/O to area-array I/O was not a choice. This number of connections cannot be pulled out in one row at microbump pitch. This is the fundamental reason flip chip and microbumps became the standard.
  2. Bump pitch presses down on the ceiling of bandwidth. Under this exercise's assumption (connections three times the data wires), a 40 μm-pitch area array uses 9.8% of the die area. If the number of connections grows several-fold (a new HBM generation, more stacks), this share grows by the same factor and eats into the die. Hybrid bonding, which shrinks the pitch, is a strong path for that moment. But the real limit is set not by pitch alone but together by the interposer's wiring density, the HBM interface specification and the yield of the bonding process.

Here is the price of choosing "wide and slow" in Exercise 2 of Session 3. Wide means many wires, many wires means pitch, and pitch means bonding technology. The memory bandwidth roadmap and the packaging roadmap are the same curve.

Self-study appendix B — leads for the discussion questions

Question type Core axis Leads
Why the back end suddenly became important Diminishing returns to scaling While the gains from the front end shrank and its costs soared, the gains available from packaging (bandwidth, integration) are still in an early phase. The marginal returns crossed over; packaging did not suddenly get better
Will the chiplet standard (UCIe) succeed? Who benefits Standardization favors late entrants and small design firms and disadvantages the leading integrators. Leaders have an incentive to keep their own interfaces, so the standard is likely to settle not as "what everyone uses" but as "the alliance of those who are not the leader." Compare it with the history of PC and server standards
OSAT vs foundry Is packaging a process or an assembly step? The moment advanced packaging uses lithography and etching, it is no longer assembly but an extension of the front end. That is why foundries are absorbing this area and OSATs are being pushed toward mature packages. It is a question of where value added moves
Is heat the ceiling of 3D stacking? Which level's thermal resistance Exercise 4 gives the answer — silicon is not the problem; the interfaces are. Lowering interface thermal resistance with hybrid bonding and the like raises the ceiling. How far it rises has to be calculated with the material values of actual bonding layers. Stacking logic on logic (both high-power) is still hard, though, and the realistic answer is an asymmetric design that puts the lower-power part on top
When will the supply bottleneck ease? Equipment and the learning curve CoWoS capacity can be expanded with capital, but hybrid bonding equipment has few suppliers and needs yield learning. The logic of Exercise 1 of Session 3 applies here too — you can forecast only if you separate a capacity problem from a learning problem

Self-study appendix C — key terms

Term One-line definition
Back end (assembly & test), packaging The stage that cuts the wafer, turns chips into packages and tests them. Different from BEOL, the forming of wiring layers within wafer processing (Session 5)
Dicing The step that cuts a wafer into individual dies
Flip chip Flipping the die and attaching it directly to the substrate with bumps
Microbump A fine solder bump connecting dies. Pitch about 40 μm
Hybrid bonding Direct copper-to-copper bonding without bumps. Sub-10 μm pitch (TSMC SoIC). Used in CIS and 3D logic; for HBM, a next-generation candidate as of October 2026
MR-MUF / TC-NCF (mass reflow molded underfill / thermal compression non-conductive film) The stacking methods of volume-production HBM. One stacks everything, reflows it all at once and fills the gaps with a liquid protective material; the other lays a film on each layer and thermocompresses it
Fan-in WLCSP / fan-out Fan-in if the balls are only within the chip's area; fan-out if the wiring is spread beyond the chip over a reconstituted wafer of rearranged good dies (e.g., TSMC InFO)
Via-middle TSV A TSV drilled after the transistors are made but before the wiring layers are built. Before that is via-first; after, via-last
WSS (wafer support system) Handling a wafer to be thinned by attaching it to a carrier with a temporary adhesive, and removing it (debonding) after backside processing
KGSD (known good stacked die) HBM tested as a whole stack. Memory makers ship it in this form
CoW-first / CoS-first (chip-on-wafer first / chip-on-substrate first) 2.5D assembly orders. Whether the chips are attached first onto the interposer wafer, or the interposer is first cut and attached to the substrate
W2W / D2W (wafer-to-wafer / die-to-wafer) Joining wafers to wafers cannot pick good dies, so yields multiply as yn; picking and joining only good dies leaves only the bonding yield
θJA · θJC · ψJT (junction-to-ambient / junction-to-case thermal resistance, junction-to-top characterization parameter) The difference between junction temperature and a reference temperature, divided by power. θJA is a comparison value under standard test conditions; ψ is a characterization parameter, not a true thermal resistance
HTOL (high temperature operating life) A qualification test that operates parts for 1,000 hours at a junction temperature of 125 °C or higher (JESD47I)
Acceleration factor How many hours under use conditions one hour under test conditions corresponds to. In the Arrhenius equation it depends heavily on Ea
Interposer An intermediate substrate on which several dies sit and are connected to each other
TSV (through-silicon via) Wiring that passes vertically through silicon
TGV (through-glass via) Wiring that passes through a glass substrate. A candidate to replace silicon
2.5D Placing dies side by side on an interposer
3D stacking Stacking dies vertically
CoWoS (chip-on-wafer-on-substrate) TSMC's family of 2.5D packaging
EMIB / bridge (embedded bridge) Connecting only the necessary sections with a small piece of silicon
RDL (redistribution layer) A wiring layer that relocates pad positions
Heterogeneous integration Integrating dies of different processes and functions in one package
UCIe (universal chiplet interconnect express) The interface standard between chiplets
KGD (known good die) A good die verified before assembly
Underfill Resin that fills the space between bumps for mechanical reinforcement
TIM (thermal interface material) The heat-transfer material between chip and heat sink
Signal integrity The degree to which a signal is delivered without distortion or noise
Warpage The bending of a package caused by differences in thermal expansion

Session 7

AI Data Centers

Key takeaway

The heat and power problems that began at the chip become the final ceiling at the level of the building. As the power density of AI racks jumped to ten times that of a conventional data center, cooling, power distribution and the building itself all had to change, and the constraint on AI infrastructure is turning from chip supply into grid connection and land. Data center efficiency metrics (PUE, WUE) cannot be compared unless you check the measurement boundary. PUE has a structural trap: the less efficient the IT equipment, the better it looks. Finally, this session returns to the question posed in Session 1, "where is the bottleneck?", and gathers the answers of all seven sessions into one.

Primary sources

IBM Think, "What Is an AI Data Center?" · Bloom Energy, "Data Center Cooling for Hyperscale and AI Workloads" · Bloom Energy 2026 Data Center Power Report: Mid-Year Pulse · Counterpoint, "Global DRAM and HBM Market Share" · KISTEP, "K-Cloud Technology Development Project Using AI Semiconductors" (in Korean, title translated from Korean; ScienceON TRKO202500001876) · IEA, Key Questions on Energy and AI (2026-04) · LBNL press release on its 2024 U.S. data center energy report · Uptime Institute Global Data Center Survey 2025 · NVIDIA technical blog on 800 VDC

Learning objectives

  1. Explain what is fundamentally different about an AI data center compared with a conventional one.
  2. Describe the power chain from the grid to the transistor and understand the losses at each stage.
  3. Use heat transfer to explain why liquid cooling becomes unavoidable above a certain density.
  4. Read efficiency metrics such as PUE and WUE critically.
  5. Make rough estimates of power, cooling and memory demand from a rack specification.

0. Self-study guide — for readers working alone

This is the session where everything lands

The tools built up over six sessions come together here into a single facility. In particular, Exercise 5 packs the content of all seven sessions into one problem. If you are short of time, skip the other exercises if you must, but do Exercise 5. That one problem is the final check of this book.
