One sentence that runs through this session

All power ends up as heat, and all heat has to go somewhere. The ceiling of a data center is set by these two sentences, not by its computing capacity.

Where readers get stuck — "why water, all of a sudden?"

Why a rise in rack power from 10 kW to 120 kW forces a change of cooling method is explained by one difference in the properties of water and air.

Density Specific heat Heat capacity per volume
Air 1.18 kg/m³ 1,005 J/(kg·K) 1,186 J/(m³·K)
Water 997 kg/m³ 4,186 J/(kg·K) 4,173,000 J/(m³·K)

4,173,0001,186≈3,500×

To carry the same heat, water needs 1/3,500 of the volume that air does. Removing 120 kW with air means pushing 6.75 m³ per second (about one small room's worth, roughly 14,300 CFM) through a 1.2 m² rack face, which gives an average face velocity of about 5.6 m/s. That airflow is about 7.5 times what a single top-performing floor tile delivers (1,900 CFM, see section 3). The fan power, noise and pressure loss of forcing that much air through the servers grow with it. Exercise 1 checks this in numbers.

In one line: liquid cooling was adopted not because it is a better technology but because at this density the airflow, fan power and noise that air cooling needs exceed the practical range.

1. Getting the intuition — when density changes, everything changes

What changed

A conventional data center filled each rack with servers drawing a few kilowatts and cooled them with air. An AI rack is denser by an order of magnitude or more.

Item Conventional data center AI data center
Rack power density 5–10 kW class tens of kW to over 100 kW (the latest systems go higher)
Cooling Air cooling (CRAC/CRAH) Liquid cooling required (direct-to-chip, immersion)
Load profile Relatively smooth Synchronized swings of training jobs — thousands of machines ramp load up and down together
Network Mainly north-south traffic Explosion of east-west traffic (collective communication between nodes)
Siting constraint Latency (closeness to users) Whether power can be secured
Bottleneck Land and buildings Grid connection

In one sentence: the binding question for an AI data center has changed from "where would we like to build?" to "where can we draw power from?"

The gap between two worlds (as of October 2026). Across facilities as a whole, density is still low. Uptime Institute's 2025 survey (published July 2025) reports that "Average server rack power densities continue to rise slowly, driven by greater adoption of racks in the 10 kW to 30 kW range. Few facilities exceed 30 kW, and extreme densities remain rare." The people building AI racks see ten times that. In a May 2025 technical blog post, NVIDIA wrote that "As racks exceed 200 kilowatts," today's 54 V in-rack distribution "begins to hit physical limits" and announced a move to 800 V direct-current distribution "to support 1 MW IT racks and beyond, starting in 2027" (section 2). The "over 100 kW" in the table above refers to the AI side of these two worlds.

Why density went up — continued from Session 6

This is not an arbitrary change but a direct consequence of the earlier sessions.

  1. Compute and memory must sit close together to perform (Session 2, Session 3, Session 6) → GPU and HBM are integrated in one package → power per package reaches the kilowatt class
  2. Communication between nodes is a bottleneck → nodes must be physically close for high-bandwidth links (NVLink and the like) → they are packed into the rack
  3. Result: GPUs that must form one group over high-bandwidth links (the scale-up domain of section 5) perform poorly if spread out, so within that group density cannot be lowered. Within that scope, density is not a choice but a requirement of the architecture. How large a group to put in one rack remains a design branch that depends on the performance target (8 versus 72 accelerators per rack in Exercise 5 (d)).

2. The power chain — from the grid to the transistor

[Transmission grid (tens to hundreds of thousands of V)]
        ↓ receiving substation
[Medium-voltage distribution (thousands to tens of thousands of V)]
        ↓ transformer
[Low-voltage distribution (hundreds of V)]
        ↓ UPS (uninterruptible power supply) + generator backup
[PDU / busbar (rack distribution)]
        ↓
[Rack power (trending toward DC distribution)]
        ↓ PSU
[Board power]
        ↓ VRM (voltage regulator module)
[Chip (1 V or less, hundreds to thousands of A)]
        ↓ package power network → on-die power network
[Transistors]

Losses multiply at each stage

If there are several stages with efficiency ηi , the overall efficiency is ∏iηi . Even at 97% per stage, five stages give 86%. Every loss becomes heat that must in turn be cooled. That is why better distribution efficiency pays twice: it also lightens the cooling load.

This is why high-voltage direct current (HVDC) distribution and rack-level power integration are being pursued. Fewer conversion stages mean less loss and less heat.

800 V DC — when one rack becomes a megawatt. Inside today's AI rack, power shelves produce direct current and copper busbars carry it to the compute trays. This is commonly called "48 V distribution" (48 V is the nominal voltage of the industry standard OCP Open Rack V3). NVIDIA's documents give the in-rack bus voltage as 54 V. This session groups the two together as the 48 V-class system. In its May 2025 technical blog post, NVIDIA judged that this approach hits its limits once a rack exceeds 200 kW and announced a move to 800 V direct current (800 VDC) distribution supporting IT racks of 1 MW and more, starting in 2027. The same post states that "The physics of using 54 VDC in a single 1 MW rack requires up to 200 kg of copper busbar." Raising the voltage lowers the current for the same power, and resistive loss falls with the square of the current (the solution to Exercise 4 shows this in numbers). The same post claims that the design "Improves end-to-end efficiency by up to 5%" and can cut "total cost of ownership (TCO) by up to 30%". These are NVIDIA's claims, not independently verified values.

The last centimeter is the hardest — the link to Session 5

A chip must be supplied with hundreds to thousands of amperes at 1 V or less. In P=VI , a small V means a large I .

The problem: the wiring resistance R produces a voltage drop ΔV=IR (IR drop). With a large current this drop is no longer negligible, and transistors in the middle of the chip fail to receive their specified voltage. The resistive loss Ploss=I2R also grows with the square of I .

Remedies

  • Devote many metal layers to the on-die power delivery network (PDN) → it competes with signal wiring for space
  • Absorb sudden load swings with decoupling capacitors
  • Backside power delivery (BSPDN) — the one we met in Session 5. Moving the power network to the back of the wafer relieves congestion on the front and reduces IR drop

★ The book's loop closes here. The power problem of the data center changes the structure of the transistor (BSPDN), and that change in turn raises the difficulty of the process (wafer thinning, alignment). This session and Session 5 are each other's cause and effect.

3. The physics of cooling — why air is not enough

The basic formula

The heat a cooling fluid can take away per unit time, that is, the heat transfer rate Q [W], is

Q=m˙cpΔT

  • m˙ : mass flow rate [kg/s]
  • cp : specific heat [J/(kg·K)]
  • ΔT : temperature difference between fluid inlet and outlet

Multiplying the units gives kg/s × J/(kg·K) × K = J/s = W. The Q in this session is not thermal energy [J] but the rate at which heat flows.

The heat transfer rate from a surface into the fluid is

Q=hAΔTsurface

  • h : convective heat transfer coefficient [W/(m²·K)]
  • A : heat transfer area

Air vs. water

Property Air Water Ratio
Density (kg/m³) ~1.2 ~1000 about 830×
Specific heat cp (J/kg·K) ~1005 ~4180 about 4×
Volumetric heat capacity ρcp (kJ/m³·K) ~1.2 ~4180 about 3,500×
Thermal conductivity (W/m·K) ~0.026 ~0.6 about 23×
Convective heat transfer coefficient h (typical) 10–100 1,000–10,000 10–100×

For the same volume flow, water carries about 3,500 times as much heat as air. Cooling 100 kW with air needs an unrealistic airflow, and the fan power to produce that airflow becomes enormous in its own right (fan power scales roughly with the cube of airflow).

Quick exercise: to air-cool a single 30 kW rack with an inlet-outlet temperature difference of 15 K, what airflow is needed? V˙=Q/(ρcpΔT)=30000/(1.2×1005×15)≈1.66 m³/s ≈ 3,500 CFM. At 100 kW, one rack needs more than three times that. Given the area of a rack's front face, the air velocity becomes unrealistic.

The spectrum of cooling methods

Method Applicable density (roughly) Principle Pros and cons
Air cooling (CRAC/CRAH) Roughly 30 kW/rack (depends on conditions) Separate cold and hot aisles, fan circulation Simple and cheap. Clear density limit
Rear-door heat exchanger (RDHx) ~40 kW/rack Water-cooled coil in the rack's rear door Can be used alongside existing air-cooling infrastructure
Direct-to-chip cooling (D2C, cold plate; also called direct-to-chip liquid cooling) tens of kW to 175 kW/rack A cold plate on top of the chip circulates coolant The de facto standard for AI racks. Needs CDUs, leak detection and piping. Components other than the chip still need air cooling
Single-phase immersion cooling High Servers submerged in a dielectric liquid No fans, uniform cooling. Issues with maintenance, fluid cost and compatibility
Two-phase (boiling) immersion cooling Very high Liquid absorbs heat as latent heat while boiling Best at handling heat flux. Fluid regulation (PFAS etc.) and system complexity

Status in 2026: in high-density AI racks, direct-to-chip cooling has become the de facto standard, and immersion cooling is used only in limited, specific applications.

Why the air-cooling limit is not pinned to one number. The ceiling of air cooling depends on how air is supplied (raised-floor tiles, hot-aisle containment, in-row coolers) and on the allowed temperature difference, so sources differ. The 2021 white paper of ASHRAE TC 9.9 states: "Air flows of a 40 to 50 kW rack could be up to 5000 cfm. Floor tile best-in-class is 1900 cfm." Redoing the quick exercise above with an air density of 1.18 kg/m³, removing 40 kW at ΔT=15 K takes about 4,760 CFM, which agrees with that figure. Even the quick exercise's 30 kW (about 3,500 CFM) is more than one tile can supply. For such racks the white paper says designers must check whether the number of floor tiles the aisle space allows would actually deliver enough airflow, and it names supplemental cooling such as overhead or in-row cooling and rear-door heat exchangers as alternatives. This session therefore reads the air-cooling limit as roughly 30 kW per rack with floor-tile supply alone. A 40–50 kW rack needs supplemental cooling unless the layout lets several tiles supply the required airflow. The concentration of field deployments below 30 kW in the Uptime survey in section 1 reflects deployment status, not a physical limit, but it points the same way.

Cold water as a place to dump heat — water-source cooling. Instead of cooling towers, some sites draw cold water from deep in a reservoir behind a dam or from a deep lake or the sea and use a heat exchanger to cool the coolant. The principle is the same formula, Q=m˙cpΔT . With assumed values, drawing 1 m³/s of cold water (about 1,000 kg/s) and returning it only 5 K warmer carries 1,000×4,186×5≈20.9 MW. Removing the 15.6 MW facility power of the 10,000-accelerator cluster in Exercise 5 under these conditions takes, by calculation, about 745 kg/s. If the water stays cold and steady all year, the chiller load falls. In exchange come intake and discharge permits and the ecological effect of warmer discharge water. Trap 4 in section 4 (trading water for electricity) applies here too.

The link to Session 6 — heat was a problem inside the chip from the start

The problem in 3D stacking of heat from the lower chip having to pass through the upper chip (Session 6, section 7) becomes here the problem of heat passing from the chip through the cold plate into the coolant, and on to the CDU and the cooling tower. The thermal resistances form one chain in series, and a large resistance anywhere blocks the whole chain.

ΔTtotal=Q×(Rjunction-case+RTIM+Rcoldplate+Rfluid+⋯)

This is why the TIM (thermal interface material) matters more than you would expect. The tiny gap between chip and cold plate can become the bottleneck of the entire chain.

4. Reading efficiency metrics critically

Definitions

PUE=total data center powerIT equipment power

The ideal value is 1.0. The larger the value, the more the supporting systems such as cooling and power distribution consume.

WUE=annual water use [L]IT equipment energy [kWh],CUE=total CO2 emissionsIT energy

The structural traps of PUE — the core of this section

Trap 1: the denominator is IT power. If the supporting systems carry a fixed load unrelated to IT power, then the more inefficient the servers, the larger the denominator and the better the PUE (Exercise 3). At the extreme, adding servers that do no work and only draw power improves PUE. PUE does not reflect the amount of useful work at all.

Trap 2: the measurement boundary is arbitrary.

  • Are generation losses included? Transmission losses?
  • How is on-site generation or on-site renewable power counted?
  • Are office space and security systems included?
  • At which point is IT power measured (UPS output? PDU? server input?)

Measured at different points, the same facility has different PUEs.

Put two real numbers side by side and the boundary problem appears. In Uptime Institute's 2025 survey, "respondents' annual PUE had a weighted average of 1.54" (681 responding facilities), "marking the sixth consecutive year that this headline figure has virtually stood still." In the same survey, "Facilities commissioned within five years of the survey (from around early 2020) achieved an average PUE of 1.48." Google publishes a 2025 fleet-wide average PUE of 1.09 for its own data centers. It states the boundary: a trailing twelve-month (TTM) average, including all overheads, covering large-scale facilities in stable operation. The difference between the two contains a real difference in efficiency, but one is a weighted average of survey responses and the other is a single company's measurement within a boundary it set itself. Before subtracting the two and reading the result as "how much more efficient Google is," check how their samples and boundaries differ. For reference, putting the two values into the 13 MW IT cluster of Exercise 5 gives a facility power of 20.02 MW at 1.54 and 14.17 MW at 1.09 (by calculation).

Trap 3: timing and conditions. Is it a design PUE or a measured annual average? Which season? At what load factor? PUE gets much worse at partial load.

Trap 4: trading water for electricity. Evaporative cooling uses less power but much more water. PUE alone looks better, but WUE gets worse. Optimizing one metric shifts the cost onto another resource.

A frame for readers trained in statistics: PUE is a textbook case of Goodhart's law — when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to function as a measure. The arbitrariness of the measurement boundary is a problem of comparability. Comparing values measured with different boundaries is statistically meaningless.

Better metrics?

  • Energy per unit of work (e.g., kWh per training run, kWh per million inference tokens) — puts useful work in the denominator
  • Hourly matching of carbon intensity — whether clean power was matched hour by hour, not netted against an annual total
  • Marginal emissions — what generation this data center actually caused to be added (marginal, not average)

5. Networks — scale-up and scale-out

Two axes

Scale-up Scale-out
Scope Inside a node/rack Between nodes, between racks
Technology NVLink, proprietary interconnects InfiniBand, Ethernet (RoCE)
Bandwidth Very high Relatively low
Latency Very low High
Scaling limit Physical proximity (tens of GPUs) Tens of thousands

How parallelization strategies map onto them (the part familiar to AI readers)

  • Tensor parallelism (TP): splits one layer across several GPUs. Needs an all-reduce at every layer → the traffic is enormous, so it must stay inside the scale-up domain
  • Pipeline parallelism (PP): places groups of layers on different GPUs. Little traffic → can scale out. In exchange, bubbles (idle time) appear
  • Data parallelism (DP): splits the batch. A gradient all-reduce at the end of each step → communication can overlap with computation
  • Expert parallelism (EP, MoE): all-to-all communication → the irregular pattern makes network design hard

Why this decides data center design: tensor parallelism requires GPUs to be physically close. So they are packed into the rack as densely as possible, which raises rack power density, which in turn requires liquid cooling. It is a causal chain in which the model's parallelization strategy decides the design of the building.

Where collective communication becomes the bottleneck

In a ring all-reduce over N GPUs, each GPU sends and receives roughly 2N−1N× (parameter size), which converges as N grows. The problem is that latency grows in proportion to the number of hops. That is why large systems use hierarchical all-reduce (within the rack first, then between racks).

Optical interconnect (CPO — co-packaged optics)

Electrical signals lose more and burn more power the farther they travel (Session 6, section 9). Light loses far less with distance.

The idea of CPO: put the optical transceiver in the same package as the switch chip so that electrical signals travel as short a distance as possible. This can cut power substantially.

Challenges: temperature sensitivity of optical devices, laser reliability, serviceability (once inside the package, parts cannot be replaced individually), and cost. This is where the packaging technology of Session 6 extends into the network.

How far commercialization has come (as of October 2026, from manufacturer announcements only). On October 8, 2025, Broadcom announced that it had begun shipping its third-generation CPO switch (Tomahawk 6 – Davisson), which packages optical engines together with a 102.4 Tb/s Ethernet switch chip. The 70% reduction in optical-interconnect power compared with conventional pluggable modules is the company's claim. In March 2025, NVIDIA announced the Quantum-X Photonics CPO switch for InfiniBand and the Spectrum-X Photonics CPO switch for Ethernet, with the former slated for later in 2025 and the latter for 2026. Whether shipments have actually begun could not be confirmed from an official NVIDIA announcement as of October 2026. Both companies' announcements concern switches with attached optical engines.

6. Macro figures and their uncertainty

Why the numbers diverge so much

Estimates of data center power consumption vary widely by institution, year and definition. Taking one institutional outlook as a reference point: the International Energy Agency's Key Questions on Energy and AI (April 2026) sees global data center electricity consumption "roughly doubling from 485 TWh in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030, accounting for around 3% of global electricity demand by that date" (its reference scenario, the Base Case). Growth in 2025 alone was 17%. For the United States alone, a December 2024 report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL), supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, estimates 176 TWh in 2023 (4.4% of U.S. electricity) and 325–580 TWh in 2028 (6.7–12%). That the 2028 value comes as a range nearly two-fold wide is itself the size of the uncertainty. Misconception 6 in section 6 of Session 1 uses the same figures to separate efficiency from total volume. To add one sense of scale: a 1 GW power plant running at a 90% capacity factor produces about 7.9 TWh a year, by calculation. Figures from private research firms, however, differ considerably from these.

Sources of the differences

  1. Whether cryptocurrency mining is included — this alone moves tens to hundreds of TWh
  2. Scope — commercial colocation only, or corporate in-house server rooms too? Telecom facilities?
  3. AI-only vs. total — how is an "AI data center" distinguished? What about mixed-workload facilities?
  4. Estimation method — estimating from accelerators shipped × rated power × utilization is highly sensitive to the assumptions
  5. Publication date — outlooks are revised substantially every six months. Even without a revision, the number that gets quoted changes. The IEA's 2025 Energy and AI projected a path from about 415 TWh in 2024 to about 945 TWh in 2030; the edition a year later still describes its Base Case in the main text as "growing from around 415 TWh in 2024 to around 950 TWh in 2030" while its summary starts from the 485 TWh of 2025: "roughly doubling from 485 TWh in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030" (the annex table gives 416 TWh for 2024, 485 TWh for 2025 and 945 TWh for 2030). The IEA itself says its central projection "remains close to the trajectory set out in the IEA's 2025 report." What changed is not the 2030 outlook but which year is quoted as the starting point, and the rounding. Before putting the two numbers side by side and reading "the outlook went up," align the base years
  6. Interests of the publisher — regulatory debates, fundraising and environmental campaigns each carry different incentives

The lesson of Session 1 repeats. What this book settles is trends and structure, not particular numbers. What can be settled: ① data center power consumption is rising fast, ② the main driver of that rise is AI workloads, ③ rack power density is rising steeply, ④ as a result, liquid cooling has become standard.

The power grid as the new bottleneck

Even with chip and packaging capacity secured, the grid connection queue becomes the bottleneck. New transmission lines and grid interconnection approvals take years. The IEA's April 2026 report states that "Waiting times for grid connections can be as long as five to ten years in many jurisdictions." It also writes that in the United States slow connections are leading more data center projects to add on-site gas generation. Hence:

  • Preference for sites near power plants
  • Consideration of self-generation (gas turbines, fuel cells)
  • Interest in nuclear power (power purchase agreements with existing plants, longer-term plans for SMRs)
  • Flexible load (demand response) — the idea that training workloads, being less sensitive to latency, can be adjusted to the grid's headroom

This book does not cover the economic, policy and legal issues at this point.

7. Back to the memory market — the last link

The book returns to the memory market in its last session because this is where the loop closes.

The causal chain

AI data center build-out
      ↓ more demand for accelerators
Each accelerator needs several HBM stacks
      ↓
HBM demand surges
      ↓ HBM consumes far more die area than ordinary DRAM
      │  (more wafers are needed for the same number of bits)
Supply of ordinary DRAM is crowded out
      ↓
Prices rise across memory
      ↓
Data center build-out costs rise in turn

The core mechanism: from the same wafer capacity, HBM production yields far fewer bits than ordinary DRAM (TSV area, stack yield losses, larger dies). In other words, shifting capacity to HBM reduces the total supply of DRAM bits. This is the path by which AI demand spills over into the memory market as a whole.

Final discussion — does the cycle repeat?

Arguments for "this time is different"

  • Inference demand, unlike training, is continuous and an operating expense. A service, once deployed, keeps running
  • HBM volumes are fixed under long-term contracts with customers, unlike the traditional spot market
  • GPU leasing, too, is locked into long-term commitments. In the fiscal 2025 annual report (10-K) of the GPU cloud company CoreWeave, committed contracts are "typically structured as 'take-or-pay' agreements, requiring payment regardless of the level of utilization." Committed contracts accounted for 88% of revenue in 2023, 96% in 2024 and over 98% in 2025. The weighted-average contract duration is approximately five years, and the company uses these commitments as collateral to raise asset-level debt and buy equipment
  • Barriers to entry are much higher (advanced packaging, stacking technology)

Arguments for "it will turn out the same"

  • The structure of build-out lead time (2–3 years) lagging behind demand signals has not changed
  • All three companies are expanding HBM capacity substantially
  • AI capital spending itself may be cyclical. And the plans move within months. In its earnings release of January 28, 2026, Meta put its 2026 "capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases," at USD 115–135 billion, and in its July 29 release it changed the range to USD 130–145 billion (the July release describes this as "narrowed from our prior outlook" of USD 125–145 billion). Taking the midpoints of the ranges, it rose 10% in half a year. A number that moves this fast on the way up can move just as fast on the way down
  • In the past, too, there was always a claim that "this time the demand is structural"

If you read this as a group: split into two teams and have them debate. The content of all seven sessions comes into play naturally. Yield (Session 4), the cost structure of HBM (Session 3), packaging capacity (Session 6) and power constraints (this session) all become arguments.

8. Common misconceptions

Misconception 1: "A low PUE means environmentally friendly" → PUE looks only at the efficiency of the supporting systems. It reflects neither the amount of useful work, nor the source of the power (coal or renewables), nor water use.

Misconception 2: "Liquid cooling is a risky, exotic technology" → In high-density AI racks it is already the standard. Water cooling was used in the mainframe era as well.

Misconception 3: "Build a data center in a cold region and cooling is free" → Free cooling with outside air helps, but in high-density racks the thermal resistance from chip to coolant dominates, so outside temperature alone does not solve the problem. There are also issues of the power grid, network latency and staffing.

Misconception 4: "Secure the power and you can build a data center" → Grid connection approval, site permits, water supply and local acceptance are all constraints.

Misconception 5: "AI data centers will bring down the grid / their impact is negligible" → Both are exaggerations. In total they are a fraction of all electricity, but concentrated in one area, they are a large shock to that area's grid. Distinguish the total from the local impact.

Misconception 6: "If HBM sells well, every memory company does well" → Converting capacity to HBM reduces the supply of ordinary DRAM. The structure of the whole market changes, and winners and losers separate.

9. Quantitative exercises

Exercise 1 — Deriving cooling requirements from a rack specification For a rack drawing 120 kW: (a) What airflow is needed to hold ΔT=15K with air cooling? Assuming a rack front area of 0.6×2m, what is the air velocity? Is it realistic? (b) What coolant flow is needed to hold ΔT=10K with water cooling? (L/min)

Exercise 2 — Losses in the power chain With transformer (99%) → UPS (96%) → PDU (99%) → PSU (94%) → VRM (90%), what is the overall efficiency from the grid to the chip? To supply 1 MW of IT power, how much must be drawn from the grid? Since every loss becomes heat, how does it add to the cooling load?

Exercise 3 — Calculating and gaming PUE What is the PUE of a facility with 10 MW of IT power, 3 MW of cooling and 1 MW of distribution losses? Now if the IT equipment is made more efficient and does the same work with 8 MW, what happens to PUE? Work the two cases separately. (A) Cooling and distribution losses fall in full proportion to IT power. (B) Of the 3 MW of cooling, 1 MW, and of the 1 MW of distribution losses, 0.2 MW, are fixed loads unrelated to IT power, and only the rest falls in proportion. Confirm that the work is the same, yet PUE stays the same or even gets worse.

Exercise 4 — IR drop Supplying 1V and 500A to a chip, what is the voltage drop if the equivalent resistance of the power network is 0.2 mΩ? What voltage actually reaches the core? What would you have to do to halve this drop?

Exercise 5 — Estimating the scale of a data center (synthesis) Assume a training cluster of 10,000 accelerators and estimate the following. (a) Total IT power (assume 1 kW per accelerator + 30% for supporting equipment) (b) Total facility power and annual energy at a PUE of 1.2 (c) Total HBM capacity and number of stacks required (d) Number of racks and rack power density at 8 accelerators per rack, and the cooling method required The content of all seven sessions enters this single problem.

Exercise 6 — Cost of an inference service Combine the decoding-ceiling formula from Session 2 with the power figures above to make a rough estimate of the power cost of generating one million tokens. How does it change as the batch size changes?

10. Discussion questions

  1. Is the real bottleneck of AI data centers the chip, packaging, memory or power? How has it moved over time, and where does it go next?
  2. If you were to design a metric to replace PUE, what would you put in the numerator and denominator? How would you prevent it from being gamed?
  3. Can the flexible-load character of training workloads be used to stabilize the grid? What conditions would that require?
  4. If density keeps rising, where is the physical limit of cooling? When that limit is reached, how must the architecture change?
  5. Is the memory cycle different this time? (See section 7 — make the case for both sides before you judge.)
  6. Wrap-up: on the value-chain map you drew in Session 1, mark the bottlenecks learned over the seven sessions. Where would putting resources be most effective?

11. Further study

  • Data center infrastructure: ASHRAE data center resources (Datacom Series) — the industry standard for temperature and humidity guidelines and cooling design. For the background to the shift to liquid cooling, see the TC 9.9 white paper "Emergence and Expansion of Liquid Cooling in Mainstream Data Centers" (2021)
  • Efficiency metrics: The Green Grid's white papers on PUE and WUE (definition documents from the body that created the metrics; e.g., "PUE: A Comprehensive Examination of the Metric"). Uptime Institute's annual data center survey (2025 edition)
  • Energy outlook: IEA, Energy and AI (2025) and its follow-up Key Questions on Energy and AI (2026-04) — the most widely cited institutional outlook. Be sure to read the methodology chapter alongside it. The U.S. data center energy report (2024-12) of LBNL (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory) is worth consulting for its transparent methodology
  • Networks and systems: Barroso, Hölzle & Ranganathan, The Datacenter as a Computer (3rd ed.) — the standard textbook on warehouse-scale computing. Especially recommended for readers with a computing background
  • Communication in distributed training: the parallelization sections of the Megatron-LM (arXiv:1909.08053) and DeepSpeed ZeRO (arXiv:1910.02054) papers
  • Optical interconnect: CPO talks at OFC (Optical Fiber Communication Conference)

Self-study appendix A — Solutions to the quantitative exercises

Solution to Exercise 1 — Deriving cooling requirements from a rack specification

SolutionSolution

(a) Air cooling, 120 kW, ΔT=15 K

m˙=QcpΔT=120,0001,005×15=7.96 kg/s

Converting with an air density of 1.18 kg/m³ (about 25 °C):

V˙=7.961.18=6.75 m3/s=405 m3/min≈14,300 CFM

Air velocity across the rack front of 0.6×2=1.2 m²:

v=6.751.2=5.6 m/s

Is it realistic? No. Three problems bite at once.

Problem Detail
Noise Fan noise scales roughly with the 5th to 6th power of air velocity. Doubling the velocity with the same fan makes it tens of times louder (2⁵–2⁶ = 32–64 times)
Fan power Fan power consumption scales with the cube of the flow. The power spent on cooling turns back into heat, a vicious circle
Pressure loss Pushing air through the server at that speed sends the static pressure soaring, and recirculation and bypass between front and rear racks get worse

The practical limit differs by source and conditions, but with floor-tile supply alone it is roughly 30 kW per rack (section 3, "Why the air-cooling limit is not pinned to one number"). According to the ASHRAE TC 9.9 white paper, the airflow of a 40–50 kW rack is up to 5,000 CFM, 2.6 times one best-in-class floor tile (1,900 CFM). The roughly 14,300 CFM of a 120 kW rack is about 7.5 times one tile and about 2.9 times the maximum airflow of a 40–50 kW rack, so cooling it with floor-tile supply is outside the practical range.

(b) Water cooling, ΔT=10 K

m˙=120,0004,186×10=2.867 kg/s≈2.87 L/s=172 L/min

Comparing the volume flow of the two methods

Method Volume flow
Air cooling 6.75 m³/s
Water cooling 0.00287 m³/s
Ratio about 2,350×

With a 40 mm pipe diameter, the flow velocity is about 2.3 m/s, within the recommended range (1–3 m/s). Narrowing it to 25 mm gives 5.8 m/s, which brings erosion and noise problems.

What to take away: the change of cooling method is a result forced by material properties. And it changes the design of the whole data center — CDUs, secondary piping loops, leak detection and maintenance procedures are all needed anew.

The figure below shows a 120 kW rack cooled by air at ΔT=15 K (air density 1.18 kg/m³) and by water at ΔT=10 K. In the screen edition you can change the rack power, the two temperature differences, the air density, the rack front area and the pipe diameter, and see how airflow, air velocity and coolant flow change against the two ASHRAE white paper reference points (5,000 and 1,900 CFM).

Solution to Exercise 2 — Losses in the power chain

SolutionSolution

Overall efficiency

0.99×0.96×0.99×0.94×0.90=0.796

Step by step: 0.99×0.96=0.9504 → ×0.99=0.9409 → ×0.94=0.8844 → ×0.90=0.7960.

To deliver 1 MW to the chips

10.796=1.256 MW

1.256 MW must be drawn from the grid. All 256 kW of loss becomes heat.

Where this heat is added — location matters

Loss point Efficiency Loss Where the heat comes out
Transformer 99% 12.6 kW Electrical room
UPS 96% 49.7 kW Electrical room
PDU 99% 11.9 kW Around the computer room
PSU 94% 70.9 kW Inside the rack
VRM 90% 111.1 kW On the board, next to the chip

The heat to be removed inside the rack is not the chips' 1 MW but

10.94×0.90=1.182 MW

That is, 18% more. The PSU loss of 70.9 kW and the VRM loss of 111.1 kW come out inside the rack, so they go into the rack's cooling load and enlarge the rack cooling requirement of Exercise 1 by that much. Which path removes that heat depends on the design. If the VRMs share the cold plate, the coolant takes it away; otherwise it remains part of "components other than the chip still need air cooling" in the table in section 3.

The heat load of the whole facility is 1.256 MW — every bit of power that comes in leaves as heat (computation stores no energy).

Design implication: efficiency gains win twice. They cut the electricity bill, and they cut the heat to be removed (the cooling load) by the same amount. Raising VRM efficiency from 90% to 94% cuts VRM loss from 111 kW to about 64 kW, a reduction of about 47 kW (and because the earlier stages carry less power, the power drawn from the grid falls from 1.256 to 1.203 MW, about 53 kW), and the heat the facility must remove falls by the same 53 kW. What falls is the heat load, not the power the cooling plant itself consumes. How much the cooling plant's consumption falls depends on the chiller's coefficient of performance (COP) and the fixed loads of pumps and fans, and cannot be settled from this exercise's assumptions alone.

The figure below shows 1 MW delivered to the chips through five stages at 99, 96, 99, 94 and 90% efficiency. In the screen edition you can change the efficiency of each stage and the chip power, or set all five stages to 97%, and see how much loss each stage produces and where its heat comes out.

Solution to Exercise 3 — Calculating and gaming PUE

SolutionSolution

The original facility

PUE=10+3+110=1410=1.40

(A) IT made efficient at 8 MW — if the supporting systems are fully proportional

Cooling 3×0.8=2.4, distribution 1×0.8=0.8

PUE=8+2.4+0.88=11.28=1.40

PUE is unchanged. Total power fell 20%, from 14 to 11.2 MW, yet the metric does not move at all.

(B) In reality it is worse — the supporting systems have fixed loads

Split cooling's 3 MW into 1 MW fixed + 2 MW variable, and distribution's 1 MW into 0.2 fixed + 0.8 variable.

Item IT 10 MW IT 8 MW
IT 10 8
Cooling 3.0 1+2×0.8=2.6
Distribution 1.0 0.2+0.8×0.8=0.84
Total 14.0 11.44
PUE 1.40 1.43

The facility does exactly the same work and cut total power by 18%, yet PUE got worse.

The structural traps of PUE — three of them

  1. The denominator is IT power. If the supporting systems are fully proportional to IT, making IT more efficient leaves PUE unchanged ((A)); if fixed loads remain, only the denominator shrinks further and the metric gets worse ((B)). PUE does not measure IT efficiency, and in a facility with fixed loads it even penalizes improvements in IT efficiency.
  2. The amount of work is absent. At the same PUE of 1.2, a facility producing ten times the tokens cannot be told apart from one that does not.
  3. It can be gamed by where the boundary is drawn. The value changes depending on whether transformer losses are counted on the IT side or the supporting side, and whether generation losses are included.

Alternative metrics

Metric Content
Energy per unit of computation J/token, J/FLOP, MWh per training run — the amount of work goes into the denominator
Absolute total power When discussing grid and site constraints, the answer is the absolute amount, not a ratio
TUE (total-power usage effectiveness) A metric that extends PUE inside the IT equipment. It multiplies ITUE (total IT equipment power ÷ power reaching the computing components inside, which captures PSU, VRM and fan losses) by PUE to give total facility power ÷ power of the computing components. For example, with a PUE of 1.2 and a delivery efficiency of 0.9 inside the IT equipment, ITUE ≈ 1/0.9 and TUE ≈ 1.2/0.9 ≈ 1.33
WUE / CUE Water and carbon. Reflect local constraints

The lesson when using a metric for judgment: a ratio metric can always be gamed when its denominator is a policy variable. The habit of first asking "what is the easiest way to make this metric look good?" — the training that began in section 4 of Session 1 is completed here.

The figure below shows IT of 10 MW (cooling 3 MW = 1 fixed + 2 variable, distribution 1 MW = 0.2 fixed + 0.8 variable) reduced to 8 MW while doing the same work. In the screen edition you can change the fixed and variable parts and the reduced IT power, and compare "fully proportional" with "fixed loads present."

Solution to Exercise 4 — IR drop

SolutionSolution

Voltage drop

ΔV=IR=500×0.2×10−3=0.1 V

The voltage that actually reaches the core

1.0−0.1=0.9 V(10% drop)

Why it is serious

Effect Detail
Slower speed Transistor drive current is roughly proportional to (V−Vth)α . If Vth is 0.3 V, the effective drive voltage falls from 0.7 to 0.6 V, a 14% decrease
Collapse of timing margin The drop is not uniform but varies with position and time (switching noise), so the clock has to be lowered to assume the worst case
Power loss I2R=5002×0.2×10−3=50 W — if the chip draws 500 W, 10% of it disappears as heat in the power network

Three ways to halve the drop

Method Principle Cost
Halve the resistance R Thicker, wider power wiring, more metal layers Eats into signal wiring space — competition for front-side routing resources
Backside power delivery (BSPDN) Moves power wiring to the back of the wafer and gives the whole front side to signals. Paths become shorter and thicker, and R falls sharply Requires new processes (wafer thinning, backside alignment)
Raise the voltage and lower the current For the same power, doubling V halves I , halves ΔV=IR , and cuts the I2R loss to 1/4 The final step-down has to happen close to the chip → on-package voltage regulators (IVR), 48 V DC distribution

The link to Session 5 — why BSPDN matters as much as GAA

Section 3 of Session 5 called backside power delivery only "the next turning point." The reason lies in this calculation. With current rising steadily (V cannot be raised while P rises in P=VI , so only I grows), the only way to hold ΔV=IR in check is to reduce R , and front-side wiring alone has reached its limit. BSPDN is not a performance-boosting technology but a technology that lifts the physical limit of power delivery.

And this carries all the way to the data center. Moving rack distribution to 48 V and moving voltage regulators onto the board are both applications of the same formulas (ΔV=IR, loss =I2R) at different levels.

The same calculation at the rack level. This puts the 800 V DC discussion of section 2 into numbers. Feeding a 1 MW IT rack at 54 V, the bus voltage of the 48 V-class system, the current is

I54=1,000,00054≈18,519 A≈18.5 kA

At 800 V it is

I800=1,000,000800=1,250 A

The currents differ by a factor of about 14.8. For conductors of the same resistance, the resistive loss I2R differs by a factor of

(80054)2≈219

Put the other way round, matching the 800 V loss at 54 V would require cutting conductor resistance to about 1/219, which for the same length means a cross-section about 219 times larger. NVIDIA's statement that feeding a 1 MW rack at 54 V takes up to 200 kg of copper busbar is the physical form of this calculation. In real designs the conductor size differs by voltage, so the factor of 219 is a comparison that carries the condition "if the same conductor were used."

The figure below covers only the rack-distribution part of this solution. The 0.1 V, 0.9 V and 50 W of the chip IR drop at the start are not in it. It shows a 1 MW IT rack fed at 54 V and at 800 V. In the screen edition you can change the rack power and the two voltages (including the OCP nominal 48 V) and see the currents and the ratio of resistive losses when the same conductor is used.

Solution to Exercise 5 — Estimating the scale of a data center (synthesis)

SolutionSolution

This problem is the final check of this book. A training cluster of 10,000 accelerators.

(a) Total IT power

Item Calculation Value
Accelerators 10,000×1 kW 10 MW
Supporting equipment (CPU, storage, network) 30% 10×0.3 3 MW
IT total 13 MW

Comparing with real systems. "1 kW per accelerator + 30% supporting" is an assumed value for practice. Switching to a manufacturer's system specification: DGX B200 lists the maximum power of its 8-GPU system as about 14.3 kW. 10,000 accelerators means 1,250 systems, and by calculation a maximum of 17.875 MW. DGX B300, with 8 GPUs and 2.1 TB of memory, is listed at about 14 kW, so the same calculation gives 17.5 MW. Being system-boundary maximums, these exceed the assumed 13 MW. One real installation for comparison: the University of Florida's fourth-generation HiPerGator, with 63 DGX B200 systems (504 GPUs), went into service for the fall 2025 semester. 63 systems times 14.3 kW gives a maximum IT power of about 0.90 MW (by calculation). The GPU portion of a university research supercomputer (63 DGX B200 systems) stays under 1 MW at maximum, and the cluster in this exercise is about 20 times that by GPU count (10,000÷504≈19.8).

(b) Total facility power and annual energy

Pfacility=13×1.2=15.6 MW

Eannual=15.6 MW×8,760 h=136,656 MWh≈137 GWh

Assuming 90% utilization, about 123 GWh.

Getting a feel for the scale: taking a rough 3,000 kWh as the annual electricity consumption of one Korean household,

136,656,000 kWh3,000≈45,600 households

A single cluster of 10,000 accelerators uses as much electricity as a small city.

Comparable cases elsewhere. Household consumption differs a great deal between countries, so the household count depends on where you stand. The U.S. Energy Information Administration puts the average annual electricity sold to a U.S. residential customer in 2022 at 10,791 kWh; on that basis the same 136,656 MWh corresponds to about 12,700 U.S. households (our calculation) (source).

(c) Total HBM capacity and number of stacks

Taking 192 GB per accelerator (B200 class):

Item Calculation Value
Total HBM capacity 10,000×192 GB 1.92 PB
Number of stacks 8 stacks per accelerator × 10,000 80,000 stacks
DRAM dies 8-high per stack → 80,000×8 640,000 dies

192 GB is the chip's published figure. NVIDIA's Blackwell Architecture Technical Brief (V2.1) gives the GPU memory of HGX B200 as "Up to 192 GB," but the specification of the finished DGX B200 server is 1,440 GB for the eight together, or by calculation 180 GB per GPU (Session 2, section 6, "Capacity also differs between chip and system"). This exercise uses the chip figure, 1.92 PB. Counting by DGX system usable capacity gives 10,000×180 GB =1.80 PB (the same as 1,250 systems × 1,440 GB). In the same way, with DGX B300 (2.1 TB for eight) it is 1,250 systems × 2.1 TB =2.625 PB (by calculation).

Apply Exercise 1 of Session 3 here. Stacking 8-high without KGD at a die yield of 0.95 gives a stack yield of 66%. Securing 80,000 stacks would require attempting 121,000 stacks, and hundreds of thousands of good dies would be thrown away along the way. This 66% is not an actual yield but the value under the assumption "if dies are not screened before stacking." What the example shows is how much die screening and stack yield can cut supply; this one number cannot explain the actual supply bottleneck behind news that "accelerators can't be built for lack of HBM."

(d) Racks and density — here the design branches

8 per rack (conventional) 72 per rack (high density)
Racks 1,250 racks 139 racks
Rack power about 10.4 kW about 94 kW
Cooling Air cooling possible Liquid cooling required (Exercise 1)
White space (at 4 m² per rack) about 5,000 m² about 560 m²
Communication distance between nodes Long → larger share of optical transceivers Short → more spans possible in copper

A single choice of density decides the cooling method, the size of the site and the network cost all at once. The advantage of high density is not saving space but shortening communication distance — in training, communication between nodes governs performance, so putting things physically close together is performance. The logic of Exercise 2 in Session 6, "distance sets energy," repeats at rack scale.

(e) The real bottleneck — what appears once you calculate this far

15.6 MW is the incoming power capacity of a mid-sized industrial park. But

Item Lead time
Procuring accelerators months to 1 year
Constructing the building 1–2 years
New substation and transmission line 3–7 years

The lead times in the table are rough orders of magnitude. The IEA's April 2026 report notes that "lead times for transformers average between two and three years" and that the wait for grid connection alone can reach five to ten years in many jurisdictions (section 6). That means it may be longer than the 3–7 years in the table above.

The longest item is the power grid. That is why new data center sites are chosen not by "where the internet is fast" but by "where power can already be brought in," and why self-generation, power purchase agreements (PPAs) and sites next to nuclear plants come up.

Back to the question of Session 1: the bottleneck has moved from EUV → CoWoS → HBM. What this calculation says is that the next bottleneck lies outside semiconductors, in the power grid. And neither capital nor technology resolves it quickly.

The figure below uses the assumptions of Exercise 5 (10,000 accelerators, 1 kW each + 30% supporting, PUE 1.2, 192 GB each). In the screen edition you can switch the IT power boundary to the DGX B200 or B300 system maximum, PUE to the 1.54, 1.48 or 1.09 of section 4, and memory per accelerator to the DGX B200 system's 180 GB or to DGX B300. The household count, the share of a 1 GW plant's annual output and the flow for water-source cooling in section 3 move with them.

Solution to Exercise 6 — Cost of an inference service

SolutionSolution

Setup: a 70B INT8 model, an 8×H100 node (total B=26.8 TB/s), node power 6.4 kW, PUE 1.2 → 7.68 kW at the facility level. Electricity at USD 0.08/kWh.

The node power of 6.4 kW is an assumed value for practice. It differs from the manufacturer's specification of 10.2 kW maximum input power for DGX H100. 10.2 kW is a maximum at the system boundary (Exercise 4 of Session 2 distinguishes the chip and server boundaries the same way). Using 10.2 kW makes every power cost below about 1.6 times larger, but the conclusion that capital cost dominates stays the same.

Applying the decoding ceiling from Session 2

tokens/s≲26.8×10127×1010×Bsz=383×Bsz

Setting actual bandwidth utilization at 60% gives an effective 230×Bsz tok/s.

Cost of generating one million tokens, by batch

Batch Effective throughput Time Energy Power cost
1 230 tok/s 4,353 s (1.21 h) 9.29 kWh USD 0.743
8 1,840 544 s 1.16 kWh USD 0.093
32 7,350 136 s (0.038 h) 0.290 kWh USD 0.023

Batch 32 is exactly 32 times cheaper than batch 1. Power cost is inversely proportional to batch size — the node uses the same power over the same time while doing 32 times the work.

But power is only part of the cost — add capital

Taking an 8×H100 node at USD 250,000, depreciated over 3 years, at 80% utilization:

250,0003×8,760×0.8=$11.9 /hour

At batch 32, one million tokens takes 0.038 hours, so capital cost is USD 0.45.

Cost item Per million tokens (batch 32) Share
Power USD 0.023 4.9%
Capital (depreciation) USD 0.45 95.1%

Capital cost is about 20 times the power cost.

What this result says — one of the practical conclusions of this book

  1. This is why "don't let the GPUs sit idle" is the first principle. The dominant cost is a fixed cost per hour, so utilization is cost. The economic value of serving optimizations that enlarge batches and cut waiting time far exceeds that of saving power. The capital cost above is 250,000/(3×8,760)≈$9.51 per calendar hour divided by utilization. At 80% utilization it is USD 11.9 per hour used; at 50% it becomes USD 19.0. Who bears this risk is decided by the contract. A customer who leases GPU cloud capacity under a take-or-pay commitment pays for the committed capacity whether it is used or not (in the CoreWeave case of section 7, over 98% of 2025 revenue came from such commitments). Then the cost of idle GPUs falls on the customer, not the leasing company, and the company borrows against those commitments to buy the next GPUs. The risk does not disappear; it moves to the customer and, if the commitments are concentrated in a few large customers, to those customers' credit (in the same 10-K, approximately 67% of 2025 revenue came from the single largest customer).
  2. This does not mean power is unimportant. Power acts not as a cost but as a constraint — as Exercise 5 showed, if you cannot bring in electricity, you cannot install accelerators even if you can buy them.
  3. It explains quantitatively why quantization and batch optimization are pursued so aggressively. Both are ways of getting more tokens out of the same capital.

Caution: the above looks only at power and capital. Real service cost adds labor, network, storage, unused capacity and safety margins, and API prices add margin and recovery of development costs. This calculation gives a lower bound, not a price.

The figure below is for batch 32, node power 6.4 kW (assumed) and 80% utilization. In the screen edition you can change the batch, node power (DGX H100 maximum 10.2 kW), utilization (including the 50% of the take-or-pay paragraph) and unit price, and see how the power cost and capital cost per million tokens diverge.

Self-study appendix B — Leads for the discussion questions

Question type Core axis Lead
Is power the real ceiling? What can be substituted? Semiconductor bottlenecks yield to capital and time. The power grid carries non-market constraints — siting, permitting and grid stability — and is different in kind. The lead-time table in Exercise 5(e) is the evidence
Do efficiency gains reduce total demand? Jevons paradox When energy per unit of computation improves, unit prices fall and demand rises. Historically, cases in IT where efficiency gains reduced total power consumption are rare. But when growth runs into a physical ceiling, the story changes
What to watch instead of PUE? What goes in the denominator? The conclusion of Exercise 3 — use a metric that contains the amount of work (J/token) together with absolute volume (total MW). In regulatory and disclosure contexts, the key point is that requiring only ratio metrics guarantees they will be gamed
Siting constraints in Korea Grid and cooling water Concentration in the Seoul capital region and grid headroom move in opposite directions. The shift to liquid cooling makes water use (WUE) a variable too. Regional dispersion is a heavy constraint for training clusters because of communication latency but is actually an advantage for inference services — the nature of the workload decides the site. Tariffs are a variable too. Article 45 of the Special Act on the Promotion of Distributed Energy (in Korean) (headed "Region-specific electricity rates"; current text, in force from 2026-09-18) allows the electricity retailer, for purposes such as balanced national development, to set electricity rates differently when drawing up its basic supply terms, taking transmission and distribution costs and the like into account
Feedback with the memory market AI eats into the general market The theme of section 7. When HBM production eats into general DRAM capacity, consumer memory prices rise. This crowding-out between demands is a structure absent from past cycles, and the strongest argument for discussion question 5 of Session 1

Comparable cases elsewhere. Other jurisdictions have managed new data center load through grid-connection policy or capacity allocation rather than through tariffs. Ireland's energy regulator (CRU) decided on December 12, 2025 that new data centers connecting to the network "will continue to be required to provide generation and/or storage capacity, either onsite or local in proximity to match the requested data centre maximum import demand capacity"; system operators must also consider whether a requested connection "is in a constrained or unconstrained location" (source). Singapore lifted a temporary pause on data center growth in 2022 and, through a pilot call for applications, provisionally awarded about 80 MW to four companies out of more than 20 proposals (EDB, July 14, 2023) (source).

Self-study appendix C — Key terms

Term Definition
PUE (power usage effectiveness) Total facility power ÷ IT power. 1.0 is the ideal
WUE / CUE (water / carbon usage effectiveness) Water use / carbon emissions per unit of IT energy
White space The computer-room floor area where racks actually stand
Rack power density Power drawn by one rack [kW/rack]
Air / liquid cooling Carrying heat away with air / with liquid
Direct-to-chip liquid cooling Liquid cooling with a cold plate attached directly to the chip
Immersion cooling Submerging servers in an insulating fluid
CDU (coolant distribution unit) A unit that separates and distributes the primary and secondary cooling loops
Cold plate A metal plate pressed against the chip that passes heat into the coolant
TIM (thermal interface material) Heat-transfer material between chip and cold plate. A common bottleneck in the chain
Thermal resistance R=t/(kA) [K/W]. Adds in series
UPS / PDU / PSU / VRM Uninterruptible power supply / power distribution unit / power supply unit / voltage regulator module
IR drop Voltage drop caused by wiring resistance, ΔV=IR
BSPDN (backside power delivery network) Moving the power wiring to the back of the wafer
PPA (power purchase agreement) A long-term electricity purchase contract signed directly with a generator
RDMA (remote direct memory access) A transfer method in which the network card reads and writes another node's memory directly without going through that node's CPU. Used by InfiniBand and RoCE. NVIDIA's GPUDirect RDMA opens a path for PCIe devices such as network cards to exchange data directly with GPU memory
take-or-pay A contract under which the buyer pays for the committed capacity whether it uses it or not. Utilization risk passes from supplier to buyer
Jevons paradox The phenomenon in which improved efficiency increases total consumption

  • ☐ I can explain from material properties why water is 3,500 times better than air by volume → Self-study guide
  • ☐ I can multiply power-chain efficiencies to calculate the power drawn from the grid, and tell where losses become heat → Exercise 2

  • ☐ I can propose two or more alternatives to PUE and give the reasons → Exercise 3
  • ☐ I can calculate IR drop and explain why BSPDN is needed, linking it to Session 5 → Exercise 4 ★
  • ☐ I can estimate the power, HBM and rack count of a 10,000-accelerator cluster on my own → Exercise 5 ★★

If you can work the ★★ item (Exercise 5) to the end on your own, you have reached the goal of this book.

Closing — the seven sessions in one line

If you read alone, finish by reconstructing this chain without looking. This is the final test.

  1. A transformer is a mass of matrix multiplications (Session 1).
  2. But decoding reads the whole set of weights for every token, so performance is set by bandwidth, not computation (Session 2).
  3. Raising bandwidth requires a wide, slow bus, which requires stacking and TSVs, and the yield of that stacking sets the price of HBM (Session 3).
  4. Meanwhile the chip itself becomes superlinearly more expensive with area, so large chips cannot be made (Session 4).
  5. The physics of lithography (the reticle limit, stochastic defects) tightens that limit further (Session 5).
  6. So the only way is to split and join, and the joining distance in turn sets power (Session 6).
  7. All that power becomes heat, and the ability to remove the heat and the ability to bring in electricity become the final ceiling (Session 7).

If you can attach one number to each arrow from one step to the next (1 → 2, 2 → 3 …), your study of this book is done.

Arrow Number to attach
1 → 2 I*≈295 FLOP/byte; at batch 32, utilization 11%
2 → 3 Making 4 TB/s with high-speed pins costs 96 W per stack
3 → 4 With 12-high stacking, 43% of good dies are wasted
4 → 5 8 times the area for 20 times the cost, A50=ln2/D0
5 → 6 High-NA field 429 mm², 132 ppm per step
6 → 7 200 times the wiring distance = 200 times the energy; interface thermal resistance 20 times that of silicon
7 → end 15.6 MW = 45,600 households; substation lead time 3–7 years

Appendix

Appendix I — Formula Summary and Exercise Index

This appendix gathers, session by session, the equations the book actually uses, and attaches to each the conditions under which it holds. If you can rebuild these tables without looking, the book has done its job.

1. Compute and bandwidth (Session 2)

Equation Meaning Watch out for
Pattainable(I)=min(Ppeak,B×I) Roofline. The performance ceiling is the lower of the compute limit and the bandwidth limit It bounds a kernel in steady state. It says nothing about latency, communication or overhead
I*=Ppeak/B Ridge point. Where compute-bound and memory-bound split Always compute it from dense specifications
I≈M (prefill) Weights read once serve M tokens. I is in FLOP/byte An approximation for when reading weights dominates memory traffic and each weight takes 2 bytes (fp16). Activation reads and writes are left out (activations kept on chip or fused). In general I≈2M/b. Because M is large, prefill is compute-bound
I≈Bsz (decode) Weights read once serve only as many tokens as the batch size Same conditions as above (2-byte weights, weight reads dominate). In general I≈2Bsz/b, and the boundary where decode becomes compute-bound is Bsz=(b/2)I* (compute taken at BF16 peak). Small batches are memory-bound
tokens/s≲BP·b×Bsz Decode ceiling. P is the parameter count, b bytes per parameter B is the combined bandwidth of the N chips the model is split across. In practice, utilization of 60–80% applies and communication overhead comes on top
KV=4·L·S·d·Bsz bytes Size of an fp16 KV cache d is the total dimension of the KV heads. With GQA it shrinks a great deal

Numbers to remember: for current accelerators, I* is around 300 FLOP/byte. At a decode batch of 32, utilization is about 11%.

2. Yield and cost (Session 4)

Equation Meaning
Y=e−AD0 Poisson yield. A is die area [cm²], D0 defect density [defects/cm²]
Y=(1+AD0α)−α Negative binomial yield. Accounts for defect clustering. As α→∞ it becomes Poisson
GDPW≈πd2/4A−πd2A Dies per wafer. The second term is the edge loss. d is the wafer diameter, and A must be in the square of the same length unit as d (A in cm² if d=30 cm, in mm² if d=300 mm)
Cost per die =WGDPW×Y W = price of one wafer
A50=ln2D0 Die area at which yield falls to 50%
N*=CNRE(cG+oG)−(cA+oA) ASIC break-even volume. Assumes one ASIC does the work of one GPU at the same throughput and quality (one-for-one replacement)
Ystack=yn×∏ybond Stack yield (Session 3)

Numbers to remember: at D0=0.1, an 800 mm² die yields 45%. A die with 8 times the area costs 20 times as much. If D0 doubles, the die area allowed for the same target yield halves.

Why clustering raises yield: e−x is convex, so by Jensen's inequality E[e−Λ]≥e−E[Λ]. With the same total number of defects, when they bunch together the remaining dies are clean.

3. Lithography (Session 5)

Equation Meaning
CD=k1λNA Rayleigh criterion. The smallest line width that can be resolved
DOF=k2λNA2 Depth of focus. Inversely proportional to the square of NA
E=hc/λ Photon energy. At the same dose (energy per unit area), a shorter wavelength means fewer photons
Relative fluctuation =1/N The root of stochastic defects
ystep=Y1/n Step yield. n is the number of process steps

Numbers to remember: at k1=0.3, ArF immersion gives 42.9 nm, EUV 12.3 nm, High-NA 7.4 nm. High-NA DOF is 0.36 times that of EUV. EUV delivers 7% as many photons as ArF, with 3.78 times the fluctuation. To hold line yield at 90% over 800 steps, each step may fail at no more than 131.7 ppm.

4. Packaging and heat (Session 6)

Equation Meaning
E=12CV2 Energy to send a signal over a wire. C is roughly proportional to wire length
R=tkA Thermal resistance. t thickness, k thermal conductivity, A area
ΔT=Q×∑R When the same heat flow Q [W] passes through every part of a series path, thermal resistances add in series. If each layer generates its own heat so that the flow differs from segment to segment, ΔT=∑QiRi
Required area =Nwires×(pitch)2 Area needed for an area-array interconnect

Numbers to remember: the energy ratio between a substrate trace (10 mm) and a TSV (50 μm) is 200 times. In a 4-layer stack, the accumulated temperature difference ΔT across the silicon layers is 3.3 K against 66.7 K across the bonding interfaces: the interfaces are the bottleneck. Silicon conducts heat at about 150 W/(m·K); underfill and bump layers at 1–5.

5. Data centers (Session 7)

Equation Meaning
Q=m˙cpΔT Rate of heat carried by a fluid (W)
PUE=total facility powerIT equipment power 1.0 is the ideal
ΔV=IR, loss =I2R IR drop and power-network loss
Overall efficiency =∏ηi Efficiency erodes multiplicatively along the power chain

Numbers to remember: specific heat of air 1,005, of water 4,186 J/(kg·K). Per unit volume, water holds about 3,500 times as much heat as air. A 120 kW rack: air cooling needs 6.75 m³/s (an air speed of about 5.6 m/s across the rack face, outside the practical range) against 172 L/min for liquid cooling. Overall efficiency of the power chain is about 80%. 10,000 accelerators = 15.6 MW = 137 GWh a year.

The five starred exercises are the backbone of the book. If you can solve the double-starred one (7-5) on your own from start to finish, you have reached the goal.

7. The seven sessions in one line

A transformer is a mass of matrix multiplications (Session 1) → but decoding reads every weight for each token, so performance is set by bandwidth, not compute (Session 2) → raising bandwidth takes a wide, slow bus, which takes stacking and TSVs, and the yield of that stacking sets the price of HBM (Session 3) → meanwhile a chip gets superlinearly more expensive with area (Session 4), so you cannot build a big one → and the physics of lithography tightens that limit further (Session 5) → so the industry leans toward splitting chips and joining them, and the distance over which they are joined sets power once again (Session 6) → all that power ends up as heat, and the ability to remove heat and the ability to bring in electricity become the final ceiling (Session 7).

Arrow Number to attach
1 → 2 I*≈295 FLOP/byte; at a batch of 32, utilization 11%
2 → 3 Building 4 TB/s from high-speed pins costs 96 W per stack
3 → 4 In a 12-high stack, 43% of good dies are wasted
4 → 5 8 times the area, 20 times the cost; A50=ln2/D0
5 → 6 High-NA field 429 mm², 132 ppm per step
6 → 7 200 times the wiring distance = 200 times the energy; interface thermal resistance 20 times that of silicon
7 → end 15.6 MW = 45,600 households; substation lead time 3–7 years

Appendix

Appendix II — Glossary Index

This appendix gathers the terms that appear across the seven sessions, in alphabetical order. The Session column shows where each term is first defined; if the definition here is too brief, go to that session's self-study appendix C.

Term Definition Session
2.5D Placing dies side by side on an interposer 6
3D stacking Stacking dies vertically 6
accelerator Umbrella term for chips specialized for particular computations (GPU, TPU, NPU and others) 1
air / liquid cooling Carrying heat away with air / with liquid 7
ALD (atomic layer deposition) Deposition one atomic layer at a time for precise thickness control 5
anisotropy / selectivity How strictly etching goes only downward / how strictly it removes only the intended material 5
arithmetic intensity Operations performed per byte moved from memory [FLOP/byte] 1
ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit) A custom chip built for a fixed purpose 1
back-end (assembly & test), packaging The stage that cuts the wafer, turns chips into packages and tests them. Not the same as BEOL, the forming of wiring layers inside the wafer process 6
bandwidth / capacity How much is moved per second / how much is held. The two axes to keep apart throughout Session 3 3
bank / channel Units of parallel access inside DRAM 3
batch size The number of sequences processed at once 2
binning Testing dies and sorting them into grades. Defect binning switches off some faulty cores and sells the die as a lower grade (yield recovery); speed and power binning sorts defect-free dies by maximum operating frequency and power 4
BSPDN (backside power delivery network) Moving the power wiring to the back side of the wafer 5, 7
bullwhip effect Demand swings that grow larger the further upstream they travel in a supply chain 1
CD (critical dimension) The smallest line width that must be made 5
CDU (coolant distribution unit) A unit that separates the primary and secondary cooling loops and distributes coolant 7
CFET (complementary FET) A next-generation structure that stacks n-type and p-type transistors vertically 5
chiplet Splitting a large chip into several small dies, making them separately and joining them 4
clustering parameter (α) The smaller it is, the more defects bunch together. At ∞ the model becomes Poisson 4
CMP (chemical mechanical polishing) Flattening a surface by chemical and mechanical means 5
cold plate A metal plate pressed against a chip that passes its heat to coolant 7
compute-bound A state in which the compute units are the limit (I>I*) 2
CoWoS (chip-on-wafer-on-substrate) TSMC's flagship 2.5D advanced-packaging method 1, 6
defect density (D0) Number of killer defects per unit area [defects/cm²] 4
deposition A process that lays down a needed film 5
depth of focus (DOF) The range of depth over which focus holds. ∝λ/NA2 5
dicing Cutting a wafer into individual dies 6
die A single chip cut from a wafer 4
direct-to-chip liquid cooling Liquid cooling with cold plates attached directly to the chip 7
dual damascene A wiring process that etches vias and trenches into the dielectric, fills them with copper in one step, and removes the excess by CMP 5
EDA (electronic design automation) Software tools for chip design 1
EMIB / bridge (embedded bridge) Connecting only the regions that need it with a small piece of silicon 6
etching A process that removes unwanted material 5
EUV (extreme ultraviolet) Lithography with extreme ultraviolet light at a wavelength of 13.5 nm 5
fabless A semiconductor company that designs chips and outsources their manufacture 1
FlashAttention A representative kernel that fuses attention to cut round trips to HBM 2
flip chip Turning a die over and attaching it to the substrate directly through bumps 6
foundry A plant that manufactures other companies' designs under contract 1
front-end process (FEOL + BEOL) The whole wafer process that builds transistors (FEOL) and the wiring layers above them (BEOL) on the wafer. Distinct from the back end, which cuts and joins wafers 5
GAA (gate-all-around) A transistor structure in which the gate wraps the channel on all sides 5
GDPW (gross die per wafer) Total number of dies from one wafer (before yield is applied) 4
GEMM (general matrix multiply) General matrix–matrix multiplication 2
good die A die that works. GDPW × yield 4
GQA / MQA (grouped / multi-query attention) Attention variants that reduce the number of KV heads to shrink the KV cache 2
HAR etch (high aspect ratio etch) Etching deep, narrow holes. A hard problem in 3D NAND and TSVs 5
HBF (high bandwidth flash) A proposal to stack NAND the same way to reach large capacity 3
HBM (high bandwidth memory) Memory that stacks DRAM vertically to maximize bandwidth 1, 3
heterogeneous integration Combining dies of different processes and functions in one package 6
High-k A gate insulator with a high dielectric constant. It blocks leakage current 5
High-NA EUV Next-generation EUV with NA raised from 0.33 to 0.55. The field is half the size 5
hybrid bonding Bonding copper directly to copper without bumps. Better on both pitch and thermal resistance 3, 6
hyperscaler A very large cloud operator (Google, AWS, Microsoft, Meta and others) 1
IDM (integrated device manufacturer) A semiconductor company that designs, manufactures and sells 1, 4
immersion cooling Submerging servers in an insulating fluid 7
inspection / metrology Finding whether there are defects / measuring dimensions and thickness 5
interposer An intermediate substrate that carries several dies and connects them 3, 6
ion implantation Driving dopant ions into the material to change its electrical properties 5
IR drop Voltage drop caused by wiring resistance, ΔV=IR 7
Jevons paradox Better efficiency leading to higher total consumption 7
kernel fusion An optimization that merges several operations so intermediate results are not written to memory 2
KGD (known good die) A die verified as good before stacking 3, 6
KV cache (key-value cache) Memory that stores intermediate results for tokens already produced, to avoid recomputing them 1
memory-bound A state in which memory transfer is the limit (I<I*) 2
memory tiering Placing data on different media according to how often it is accessed 3
microbump A tiny solder bump that joins one die to another 3, 6
MoE (mixture of experts) A sparse model structure that activates only some experts for each token 2
multi-patterning Exposing one layer in several passes to get around the resolution limit 5
negative binomial yield model Y=(1+AD0/α)−α. Accounts for clustering 4
node (process node) The name of a process generation, such as "3nm". A marketing label, not a physical dimension 1
NRE (non-recurring engineering) The one-time cost of developing a chip 2, 4
numerical aperture (NA) A measure of the angle over which a lens gathers light 5
OPC (optical proximity correction) Altering the mask in advance to cancel diffraction distortion 5
OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) A contractor specializing in the back end (packaging and test) 1
PDK (process design kit) The bundle of process-specific design rules and models a foundry supplies 4
photoresist A light-sensitive film whose properties change when exposed 5
PIM / PNM (processing in / near memory) Structures that put compute units inside memory / next to memory 3
pJ/bit (picojoule per bit) Energy to move 1 bit. The practical constraint in bandwidth design 3
Poisson yield model Y=e−AD0. Assumes defects are completely random 4
PPA (power purchase agreement) A long-term electricity purchase contract signed directly with a generator 7
prefill / decode The stage that processes the whole input at once / the stage that generates tokens one at a time 2
PUE (power usage effectiveness) Total facility power ÷ IT power. 1.0 is the ideal 7
quantization Representing weights with fewer bits to save capacity and bandwidth 1
rack power density Power drawn by one rack [kW/rack] 7
Rayleigh criterion CD=k1λ/NA. The fundamental limit on resolution 5
RDL (redistribution layer) A wiring layer that relocates pads 6
reduction projection Exposing a mask pattern onto the wafer at reduced size. 4× is standard; High-NA uses 4× and 8× 5
refresh Rewriting the charge in DRAM capacitors before it leaks away 3
reticle limit The largest area a lithography tool exposes in one shot (about 26×33 mm) 4
ridge point The arithmetic intensity at which compute-bound and memory-bound split, I*=Ppeak/B 2
roofline model A model that expresses the performance ceiling as the minimum of the compute limit and the bandwidth limit 2
signal integrity The degree to which a signal arrives free of distortion and noise 6
single point of failure A point whose failure alone stops the whole system 1
stack yield The probability that a whole stack works. Falls steeply as yn 3
stochastic defect A random defect caused by too few photons 5
structured ASIC An intermediate form that customizes only some layers to lower NRE 4
structured sparsity Setting some weights to 0 to cut computation. The main culprit behind inflated spec-sheet figures 2
systolic array A compute structure that streams data through a grid, repeating multiply-accumulate 2
tensor parallelism Splitting the matrices of one layer across several accelerators 2
TGV (through-glass via) A via through a glass substrate. A candidate to replace silicon 6
thermal oxidation Growing an SiO₂ film by oxidizing silicon at high temperature. The thickness follows the Deal–Grove equation 5
thermal resistance R=t/(kA) [K/W]. Adds in series 7
tiling / blocking An optimization that cuts data into pieces small enough to sit on chip and reuses them 2
TIM (thermal interface material) The material that carries heat between a chip and its heat sink 6, 7
training / inference Building a model / using a model that has been built 1
TSV (through-silicon via) A vertical connection through silicon 3, 6
UCIe (universal chiplet interconnect express) An interface standard between chiplets 6
underfill A resin that fills the space between bumps for mechanical reinforcement 6
UPS / PDU / PSU / VRM Uninterruptible power supply / power distribution unit / power supply unit / voltage regulator module 7
warpage Bending of a package caused by differences in thermal expansion 6
white space The floor area of the computer room where racks actually stand 7
WUE / CUE (water / carbon usage effectiveness) Water used / carbon emitted per unit of IT energy 7
yield The fraction of what is made that works 1
yield learning The process by which D0 falls over time 4
