Figure 3-2Session 3 Solution to Exercise 1Stacking 12 dies with a die yield of 0.95 and no screening gives a stack yield of 54.0%, and each failed stack throws away 10.7 good dies on average. The bars are 100 randomly drawn stacks.widgets/hbm.html
Figure 3-3Session 3 Solution to Exercise 2Delivering 4 TB/s per stack over a 1,024-bit bus takes 31.25 Gbps per pin; over a 2,048-bit bus, 15.6 Gbps. With energy per bit set to 3 and 0.75 pJ/bit, memory-interface power for 8 stacks approaches 800 W for (a) and is about 190 W for (b) (about 130–260 W over the 0.5–1 pJ/bit range).widgets/hbm.html
Figure 4-1Session 4 Solution to Exercise 2Laying 800 mm² dies on a 300 mm wafer gives a direct count of 68 (66–71 depending on grid position); the √(2A) approximation gives 64.8. With D₀ = 0.1, yield is 44.9%, good dies number 29.1, and cost per die is 0.03435 times the wafer price, about 19.9 times that of a 100 mm² die. The defect dots are one random sample.widgets/die-cost.html
Figure 4-2Session 4 Solution to Exercise 3At λ = 0.8, splitting the die into 10 cells gives (1 − λ/n)ⁿ = 0.4344, 97% of the limit exp(−0.8) = 0.4493. At the same λ, the negative binomial yield (α = 2) is 51.0%, higher than the Poisson 44.9%, and the variance of defect density is D₀²/α = 0.005.widgets/die-cost.html
Figure 4-3Session 4 Solution to Exercise 5With the assumptions of Exercise 5 (NRE USD 150 million, ASIC USD 4,000 and GPU USD 30,000, 3-year power cost USD 2,000 and 6,000), N* = 5,000 units, which falls inside the band "in-house AI infrastructure at a large company: hundreds to thousands of units."widgets/asic-breakeven.html
Figure 5-1Session 5 Solution to Exercise 2At k₁ = 0.3, CD is 42.9 nm for ArF immersion, 12.3 nm for EUV and 7.4 nm for High-NA EUV. Depth of focus with k₂ = 0.5 is 53, 62 and 22 nm, so High-NA gets 0.36 times the EUV value.widgets/litho.html
Figure 5-2Session 5 Solution to Exercise 3At the same dose, EUV delivers 7% as many photons as ArF, and the relative fluctuation is 3.78 times larger. Raising the dose 14.3 times to match the fluctuation makes exposure 14.3 times longer at the same source power; holding exposure time instead requires source power to rise from 250 W to about 3.6 kW.widgets/litho.html
Figure 5-3Session 5 Solution to Exercise 4To reach 90% line yield over 800 steps, the allowed defect rate per step is 131.7 ppm; over 1,200 steps, 87.8 ppm.widgets/litho.html
Figure 5-4Session 5 Solution to Exercise 5Shrinking the 104 × 132 mm pattern area on the mask 4× in each direction gives a 26 × 33 mm wafer field (858 mm²); High-NA, which shrinks one direction 8×, gives 26 × 16.5 mm (429 mm²). With D₀ = 0.1, the maximum die yields are 42.4% and 65.1%.widgets/litho.html
Figure 6-1Session 6 Section 6Stacking 8 layers with die yield 0.9 and bonding yield 0.995 (assumed) gives a W2W yield of 0.416, while D2W, which bonds only good dies, gives 0.966: a 2.32-fold difference.widgets/chiplet.html
Figure 6-2Session 6 Section 7Removing 1,000 W from a chip to 35 °C ambient through a chain of θJC 0.015, θTIM 0.025 and θSA 0.020 K/W (assumed) gives stage temperature differences of 15, 25 and 20 K and a junction temperature of 95 °C.widgets/thermal.html
Figure 6-3Session 6 Section 7At an activation energy of 0.7 eV, a test at 125 °C and use at 55 °C, the acceleration factor is about 77.7, and 1,000 hours of HTOL equals about 8.87 years. At 0.5 eV it is about 2.56 years; at 0.9 eV, about 30.7 years.widgets/reliability.html
Figure 6-4Session 6 Solution to Exercise 1System cost (as a multiple of the wafer price) when 800 mm² of silicon is split into n dies. With D₀ = 0.1, 5% overhead per split and assembly yield 0.99 for each added die, n = 4 is cheapest at 0.01970, 42.6% cheaper than a single die.widgets/chiplet.html
Figure 6-5Session 6 Solution to Exercise 2A 10 mm wire and a 50 μm TSV differ in length by 200 times, so energy per bit also differs by 200 times. At 0.05 pJ/bit for the TSV, 10¹² bits per second costs 0.05 W versus 10 W.widgets/thermal.html
Figure 6-6Session 6 Solution to Exercise 4Stacking 4 layers of 1 W/mm² chips produces a total temperature difference of 3.33 K across the silicon (50 μm) but 66.7 K across interfaces such as bumps and underfill (20 μm, 3 W/(m·K)), 20 times as much.widgets/thermal.html
Figure 7-1Session 7 Solution to Exercise 1Cooling a 120 kW rack with air (ΔT 15 K) takes 6.75 m³/s (about 14,300 CFM) and an air velocity of 5.6 m/s across the rack face. Liquid cooling (ΔT 10 K) needs only 172 L/min. The two dashed lines are the 5,000 and 1,900 CFM figures from the ASHRAE white paper.widgets/datacenter.html
Figure 7-2Session 7 Solution to Exercise 2With transformer, UPS, PDU, PSU and VRM efficiencies of 99, 96, 99, 94 and 90%, overall efficiency is 0.796, and delivering 1 MW to the chips takes 1.256 MW from the grid. Of the 256 kW lost, the VRM share of 111 kW is the largest.widgets/datacenter.html
Figure 7-3Session 7 Solution to Exercise 3Cutting IT load from 10 MW to 8 MW for the same work lowers total power 14 → 11.44 MW, 18% less, but the fixed load of the facility equipment pushes PUE the wrong way, from 1.40 to 1.43.widgets/datacenter.html
Figure 7-4Session 7 Solution to Exercise 4Feeding a 1 MW rack at 54 V takes about 18.5 kA; at 800 V, 1,250 A. The current is 14.8 times higher, so resistive loss in the same conductor is about 219 times higher.widgets/datacenter.html
Figure 7-5Session 7 Solution to Exercise 510,000 accelerators (1 kW each plus 30% overhead) mean 13 MW of IT load, 15.6 MW for the facility at PUE 1.2, and about 137 GWh a year. Counted with the DGX B200 and B300 system maximums, IT is 17.875 and 17.5 MW, and at 192 GB per chip HBM totals 1.92 PB.widgets/datacenter.html
Figure 7-6Session 7 Solution to Exercise 6Running a 70B INT8 model on an 8×H100 node (26.8 TB/s, bandwidth utilization 0.6) at batch size 32, the power cost of 1 million tokens is about USD 0.023 and the capital cost about USD 0.45, so capital accounts for 95.1%.widgets/datacenter.html

About this book

This self-study guide was made for the semiconductor sessions of the study group Sunday AI.

It began as study material, but it was reworked so that a reader working alone, outside any group, can get to the end. Each session gives a reading order and a time budget, every quantitative exercise comes with a full solution, and each session closes with a checklist for testing yourself.

How this book was made

The editor made this book with Claude Code. Because it is text produced with generative AI, errors may remain even after it was checked against primary sources.

  • Material from the study group's presentations and discussions went in only after it was confirmed against primary sources such as manufacturer announcements, standards documents, agency reports and papers, and was then written afresh.
  • Each session was checked independently. A process separate from the one that revised the text received only the revised text and the primary sources, compared the changed sentences, and fixed what was wrong. The numbers in the calculation exercises were recalculated.
  • Finally, an AI model from a different company (OpenAI Codex), with no knowledge of how the work had been done, read the whole manuscript, the print edition and the figure code. Each of its 125 findings was checked against the originals and by recalculation, and was either fixed or answered with a written reason for leaving it.
  • The interactive figures move only the variables of equations and tables that appear in the text. Each figure's results are checked automatically against the worked solutions in the text, and the book will not build if any of them disagree. The static snapshots in the print edition are the screen-edition figures opened in their initial state and captured.
  • Equations were converted to MathML. No external scripts or fonts are loaded.
  • Diagrams are drawn in inline SVG. They look the same on screen and in print, in light and dark mode.
  • Page numbers, running heads and table-of-contents page numbers in the print edition were computed at typesetting.

How this English edition was made

This English edition was translated from Korean edition 2.0.1 (October 22, 2026) by the editor working with Claude Code. Quotations that were originally in English were restored from the original sources rather than translated back from Korean. Korean-language sources are kept with translated titles and marked "(in Korean)." Numbers were carried over unchanged and checked against the Korean edition; only their notation changed where English needs it (for example, Korean counting units written as thousands or billions, and amounts written as USD). In a few places, boxes headed "Comparable cases elsewhere" add examples from other countries that are not in the Korean edition; each was checked against the primary source cited in the box. Before publication, an AI model from a different company (OpenAI Codex), given only the Korean and English texts and the sources they cite, compared the two editions sentence by sentence; each of its findings was rechecked against the originals and either fixed or answered with a written reason for leaving it.

Acknowledgments

Since January 2022 the editor has been a member of Sunday AI, a study group of graduates and students of the Department of Statistics and Data Science at Korea National Open University. Its members propose a new topic each time one ends, and despite busy lives they take turns presenting and share what they know every week. The editor owes them a great deal and is always grateful. What came out of the presentations and discussions was checked again against primary sources before it went in, and any errors that remain are the editor's.

When you use this book

  • Do not quote the numbers as they stand. Prices, electricity costs and similar inputs in the calculation exercises are assumed values meant to show the direction of a conclusion, and accelerator specifications come from public spec sheets that change with each generation. The details are in "A note on the numbers" at the front of the book.
  • When the numbers date from. Volume-production and shipment status, power-demand projections, standards and product specifications were rechecked as of October 8, 2026. Announcements made after that date are not reflected.
  • Links. The links in the text were checked on October 8, 2026. Company blogs and press releases may disappear or move.
  • Errors and revisions. Please look especially at the arithmetic and units in the calculation exercises and at the specification figures quoted. If you find a statement that differs from its source, please report it through the issue tracker of the public repository. Corrections will be made in a new edition with a new date.
  • A personal study resource. The editor compiled this book as part of personal study. It is unrelated to the views or work of any institution the editor belongs to.
